intro: は (wa) marks the topic, what the sentence is about, while が (ga) marks the subject, often new or focused information. Both come right after a noun: 私は学生です (as for me, I am a student) but 誰が来ましたか (who came?). Note that the particle は is written with the kana for ha but pronounced wa.

formation.example: 私は学生です, 東京は大きい

formation.when: Subject as new or focused information
formation.example: 田中さんが来ました
誰が, 何が, どれがいいですか
肉は食べますが、魚は食べません
母が作ったケーキ

usage: は sets up the topic and then you say something about it. Once a topic is known, you often drop it: (私は) 学生です. が points at one thing as the answer, so it is used with question words and when you introduce something new: あ、バスが来た.
A simple test: if the question is "who?" or "what?", the answer takes が. 誰が作ったの？ is answered with 私が作った. If the question is "what about X?", X takes は.
は also shows contrast. 肉は食べます can imply "meat, I do eat (but other things, maybe not)". This contrast use is common in negative sentences: お酒は飲みません.
Some words take が for their object: 好き, 嫌い, 上手, わかる, できる, ほしい and ある / いる. 猫が好きです means "I like cats". In clauses that describe a noun, the subject takes が, not は: 母が作ったケーキ (the cake my mother made).

examples.romaji: Watashi wa gakusei desu.
examples.en: I am a student.

examples.context: Asking about a dish at a party
examples.romaji: Dare ga tsukutta no?
examples.en: Who made this?

examples.romaji: Zou wa hana ga nagai.
examples.en: Elephants have long trunks.

examples.romaji: Ame ga futte kita.
examples.en: It started raining.

compare.note: も means "also" and replaces は or が: 私も学生です. You never say はも or がも.
を marks the object of most verbs. A few words like 好き, わかる and できる take が instead: 日本語がわかります, not 日本語をわかります.

mistakes: Using は with a question word: 誰は来ましたか is wrong. Say 誰が来ましたか.
Using を with 好き: 私は猫を好きです sounds unnatural. Say 私は猫が好きです.
Using は inside a describing clause: 私は買った本 should be 私が買った本 (the book I bought).

faq.q: What is the difference between は and が?
faq.a: は marks the topic, what you are talking about. が marks the subject, often as new or important information. Question words and their answers take が, and contrast takes は.

faq.q: Why is は pronounced wa?
faq.a: As a particle, は is always read wa. In other words, like はな (flower), it is read ha.

faq.q: Can a sentence have both は and が?
faq.a: Yes. 象は鼻が長い has は for the topic (elephants) and が for the subject of 長い (the trunk). This pattern is very common: 私は頭が痛い (I have a headache).

meaning: object marker; through, out of (a place)
intro: を (o, sometimes romanized wo) marks the direct object, the thing an action is done to: パンを食べる (eat bread). It goes right after the noun. With verbs of movement it can also mark a place you move through or leave: 公園を歩く, 家を出る.

formation.example: 本を読む, 水を飲む
勉強をする, 料理をする

formation.when: After a place you move through
formation.example: 公園を散歩する, 橋を渡る

formation.rule: Place + を + 出る / 降りる
formation.example: 家を出る, 電車を降りる

usage: を is the basic object marker. Most action verbs that take an object use it: 映画を見る, 手紙を書く, 音楽を聞く. Today it is pronounced o, the same as お, but it is written with its own kana.
With movement verbs like 歩く, 走る, 渡る and 通る, を marks the path: この道をまっすぐ行ってください (go straight along this road). With 出る, 降りる and 卒業する, it marks the place you leave.
In casual speech, を is often dropped: ご飯食べた？ (did you eat?). In polite speech and writing, keep it.
Some words that look like verbs take が, not を: わかる, できる, ある, いる, and adjectives like 好き and ほしい. 日本語がわかります, 時間がありますか.

examples.romaji: Maiasa koohii o nomimasu.
examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.

examples.romaji: Kono michi o massugu itte kudasai.
examples.en: Please go straight along this road.

examples.context: A family member asking about plans
examples.romaji: Nanji ni ie o deru no?
examples.en: What time are you leaving the house?

examples.romaji: Shukudai o shinakya.
examples.en: I have to do my homework.

compare.note: わかる, できる, 好き and ほしい take が for what English treats as an object: 猫が好き. With たい, both 水を飲みたい and 水が飲みたい are fine.
公園で走る means running somewhere inside the park. 公園を走る focuses on running through or along it.
に marks where you arrive: 電車に乗る (get on). を marks where you leave: 電車を降りる (get off).

mistakes: Using を with わかる: 日本語をわかります is wrong. Say 日本語がわかります.
Using を with ある or いる: 時間をありますか should be 時間がありますか.
Writing お instead of を: おちゃお飲む should be お茶を飲む. They sound the same, but the particle is always written を.

faq.q: Is を pronounced o or wo?
faq.a: In standard modern Japanese it is pronounced o, just like お. Some speakers say wo when speaking very carefully or singing, but o is the normal pronunciation.

faq.q: Can you drop を in casual speech?
faq.a: Yes. ご飯食べた？ and 何見てるの？ are normal in conversation. Keep を in polite speech and in writing.

meaning: at (a time), to, in (where things are)
intro: に (ni) marks a point: a time (7時に, at 7), a destination (学校に行く, go to school), or the place where something is (部屋に猫がいる). It goes after a noun. It also marks the person who receives something, and the purpose of going somewhere: 買いに行く (go to buy).

formation.example: 7時に起きる, 月曜日に会う

formation.rule: Place + に + 行く / 来る / 帰る
formation.example: 学校に行く, 家に帰る

formation.when: After a place where something exists
formation.rule: Place + に + いる / ある
formation.example: 部屋に猫がいる

formation.rule: Person + に + あげる / もらう / 会う
formation.example: 友達にあげる, 先生に聞く

formation.rule: ます-stem + に + 行く / 来る
formation.example: 買いに行く, 遊びに来る

usage: に marks a point in time or space. Clock times, dates and days of the week take に: 3時に, 5月に, 日曜日に. Words relative to now, like 今日, 明日, 毎日 and 来週, usually take no particle.
With いる and ある, に marks where something is: 駅の前にコンビニがあります. With 行く, 来る, 帰る, 着く and 入る, it marks the goal you reach.
With a person, に marks the receiver (友達にあげる), or the giver with もらう and 借りる (友達にもらった). It also marks the person you meet or ask: 先生に聞く.
に is neutral and used in every register. It is one of the most common particles, so it is worth learning each use with a set phrase.

examples.romaji: Mainichi shichiji ni okimasu.
examples.en: I get up at seven every day.

examples.romaji: Raishuu, Kyouto ni iku yo.
examples.en: I'm going to Kyoto next week.

examples.romaji: Tsukue no ue ni kagi ga arimasu yo.
examples.en: Your keys are on the desk.

examples.romaji: Tomodachi ni tanjoubi purezento o moratta.
examples.en: I got a birthday present from a friend.

compare.note: に marks where something is or where you go. で marks where an action happens: 部屋にいる (be in the room) but 部屋で勉強する (study in the room).
へ stresses direction (toward). For a destination, 日本に行く and 日本へ行く are both fine; に is more common in speech.

mistakes: Using に for the place of an action: 公園に遊ぶ is wrong. Say 公園で遊ぶ.
Adding に to relative time words: 明日に行きます sounds wrong. Say 明日行きます.

faq.q: When do you use に with time?
faq.a: Use it with clock times, dates, months, years and days of the week: 3時に, 日曜日に. Leave it out with words relative to now, like 今日, 明日, 毎日 and 先週.

faq.q: What is the difference between に and へ?
faq.a: Both can mark a destination. に points at the goal you reach, and へ points at the direction. In speech, に is more common.

intro: で (de) marks where an action happens (図書館で勉強する, study at the library) and the means you use to do it (バスで行く, go by bus). It goes right after a noun. It can also mark a language, a cause, or a total: 日本語で, 風邪で, 全部で.

formation.example: 図書館で勉強する, 家で食べる
バスで行く, 箸で食べる
日本語で話す, 英語で書く
風邪で休む, 雨で中止になる
三人で行く, 全部で千円

usage: The most common で marks the stage where something happens. Any action verb works: 駅で会う, 家で寝る, 会社で働く. Events also take で: 東京でコンサートがある.
で also marks how you do something: by train, with a pen, in Japanese. 電車で来ました, ペンで書いてください, 日本語で言ってください.
With a noun of cause, で means "because of": 事故で電車が遅れた. It is neutral and common in news and daily speech alike.
After a number of people, で shows who does it together: 二人で行こう (let's go, the two of us). After 全部 or a price, it means "in total".

examples.context: Telling a coworker about your weekend
examples.romaji: Eki de tomodachi ni aimashita.
examples.en: I met a friend at the station.

examples.context: Asking a friend who just arrived
examples.romaji: Densha de kita no?
examples.en: Did you come by train?

examples.context: Asking a teacher about a word
examples.romaji: Kore, nihongo de nan to iimasu ka.
examples.en: How do you say this in Japanese?

examples.romaji: Kaze de gakkou o yasunda.
examples.en: I stayed home from school with a cold.

compare.note: に marks where something is or where you go: 部屋にいる. で marks where something is done: 部屋で勉強する.
Both can give a reason. で only follows a noun (雨で). から follows a full clause (雨が降ったから) and is more personal.

mistakes: Using で with いる or ある for location: 部屋で猫がいる is wrong. Say 部屋に猫がいる.
Using に for the means: バスに行く is wrong. Say バスで行く.

faq.q: What is the difference between で and に for places?
faq.a: で is for the place an action or event happens. に is for the place something exists or the place you go. 東京に住む (live in Tokyo) but 東京で働く (work in Tokyo).

faq.q: Is the particle で the same as the で in 読んで?
faq.a: No. 読んで is the て-form of a verb, and 学生で is the て-form of だ. The particle で comes after a noun and marks a place, means or cause.

meaning: where something is vs where it happens
intro: に (ni) and で (de) both translate as "in" or "at", but they do different jobs. に marks where something exists or where you go (部屋にいる, 学校に行く), and で marks where an action happens (部屋で勉強する). Both go right after the place noun.

formation.rule: Place + に + いる / ある
formation.example: 公園に犬がいる

formation.rule: Place + に + 行く / 来る / 帰る
formation.example: 日本に行く, 家に帰る
公園で遊ぶ, 家で食べる
東京でコンサートがある

formation.rule: 住む takes に, 働く takes で
formation.example: 東京に住む, 東京で働く

usage: Ask what the verb does. If it says something is there (いる, ある, 住む, 座る), or that you arrive somewhere (行く, 着く, 入る), use に. If it describes an activity (食べる, 遊ぶ, 働く, 会う), use で.
ある can take either one. For things, use に: 机の上に本がある. For events like a party, exam or concert, use で: 学校で試験がある.
Verbs of putting or writing also take に, because they mark where something ends up: ここに名前を書いてください, 机の上に置く.
Both are neutral and appear in all registers, so the choice is about meaning, not politeness.

examples.romaji: Eki no mae ni konbini ga arimasu.
examples.en: There's a convenience store in front of the station.

examples.romaji: Eki no mae de matteru ne.
examples.en: I'll be waiting in front of the station.

examples.romaji: Ane wa Oosaka ni sunde imasu.
examples.en: My older sister lives in Osaka.

examples.context: Explaining why you can't go out
examples.romaji: Ashita, gakkou de shiken ga aru n da.
examples.en: I have an exam at school tomorrow.

compare.note: へ marks direction, like に with movement verbs. It never marks where something exists or where an action happens.
With movement verbs, を marks the path you move along: 公園を歩く (walk through the park). 公園で歩く focuses on walking as an activity there.

mistakes: Using に for an activity: 図書館に勉強します is wrong. Say 図書館で勉強します.
Using で with 住む: 東京で住んでいます is wrong. Say 東京に住んでいます.
Using に for an event: 学校にお祭りがある should be 学校でお祭りがある.

faq.q: Why does 住む take に but 働く takes で?
faq.a: 住む is about where you are, like いる, so it takes に. 働く is an activity, so the place where you do it takes で.

faq.q: Can ある take で?
faq.a: Yes, when the subject is an event. 東京でコンサートがある means a concert takes place in Tokyo. For objects, use に: 東京に大きい駅がある.

intro: へ (e) marks the direction of movement: 日本へ行く means "go to Japan" or "head toward Japan". It goes after a place noun, and it is written with the kana he but pronounced e. Before a noun it becomes への: 母への手紙 (a letter to my mother).

formation.example: 日本へ行く, 家へ帰る
北へ向かう, 右へ曲がる
母への手紙, 未来への道
日本へようこそ

usage: へ goes with movement verbs like 行く, 来る, 帰る, 向かう and 送る. It focuses on the direction more than the arrival point, but for everyday destinations it means the same as に.
In speech, に is used more often for destinations. へ feels a little more formal or written, and is common in signs, letters and announcements.
への is useful because に cannot be followed by の. You can say 友達への手紙 (a letter to a friend) and 東京への旅行 (a trip to Tokyo), but not 友達にの手紙.
Like は, the particle へ is pronounced differently from the kana's usual sound. へ in へや (room) is he, but the particle is e.

examples.romaji: Natsuyasumi ni Okinawa e ikimasu.
examples.en: I'm going to Okinawa over summer vacation.

examples.context: A parent asking a child heading out
examples.romaji: Doko e iku no?
examples.en: Where are you going?

examples.context: Writing at the end of the school year
examples.romaji: Sensei e no tegami o kakimashita.
examples.en: I wrote a letter to my teacher.

examples.romaji: Toukyou e youkoso!
examples.en: Welcome to Tokyo!

compare.note: に can mark a destination, a time, a location of existence and more. へ only marks direction. For 行く and 来る, both work.
まで means "as far as" or "all the way to": 駅まで歩く stresses walking the whole way to the station.

mistakes: Writing え for the particle: 学校え行く is wrong. Write 学校へ行く.
Using へ for where something is: 部屋へ猫がいる is wrong. Say 部屋に猫がいる.
Using にの before a noun: 友達にの手紙 is wrong. Say 友達への手紙.

faq.q: What is the difference between へ and に?
faq.a: へ stresses the direction of movement, and に stresses the goal. With 行く, 来る and 帰る both are correct. に has more uses, such as time and existence, which へ does not have.

faq.q: Why is へ pronounced e?
faq.a: When へ is used as a particle it is always read e. In normal words like へや (room) it is read he.

intro: と (to) joins nouns as "and" (犬と猫, dogs and cats), marks a partner as "with" (友達と行く, go with a friend), and marks quoted words before 言う or 思う. It goes after a noun or a quote. As "and", it gives a complete list.

formation.example: パンと牛乳, 犬と猫
友達と行く, 母と話す

formation.rule: Quote + と + 言う / 思う
formation.example: 行かないと言った, 雨だと思う

formation.rule: A + と + B + と + どちら / どっち
formation.example: 犬と猫とどっちが好き？

usage: As "and", と lists every item: パンと牛乳を買った means you bought bread and milk, and nothing else is implied. If you only want to give examples, use や.
As "with", と marks the person you do something with: 彼女と映画を見た. Some verbs need a partner, like 結婚する and けんかする, and always use と.
Before 言う, 思う, 聞く and 書く, と marks the content of what was said or thought. In casual speech, って often replaces it: 来ないって言ってた.
と only joins nouns. To join verbs or adjectives, use the て-form: 安くておいしい (cheap and tasty). The と that means "when" or "if" after a verb is a different grammar point.

examples.context: Asking a family member to run an errand
examples.romaji: Pan to gyuunyuu o katte kite.
examples.en: Can you go buy some bread and milk?

examples.context: Telling a coworker about your weekend
examples.romaji: Shuumatsu, kanojo to eiga o mimashita.
examples.en: I saw a movie with my girlfriend over the weekend.

examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa konai to itte imashita.
examples.en: Tanaka said they aren't coming.

examples.romaji: Inu to neko to, docchi ga suki?
examples.en: Which do you like better, dogs or cats?

compare.note: や gives examples from a longer list (books, magazines and so on). と lists everything.
友達と会う suggests meeting by arrangement, both sides taking part. 友達に会う focuses on you meeting them, and also covers running into someone.
って is the casual quote marker. 来ないって言ってた is the everyday version of 来ないと言っていました.

mistakes: Joining adjectives with と: 安いとおいしい is wrong. Say 安くておいしい.
Joining sentences with と as "and": 朝ご飯を食べたと学校に行った is wrong. Use the て-form: 朝ご飯を食べて学校に行った.

faq.q: What is the difference between と and や?
faq.a: と lists all the items: りんごとバナナ means exactly apples and bananas. や lists some examples: りんごやバナナ means apples, bananas and things like that.

faq.q: Is と the same as and in English?
faq.a: Only between nouns. English and can join verbs, adjectives and sentences, but Japanese uses the て-form or そして for those.

intro: も (mo) means "also" or "too": 私も行きたい (I want to go too). It goes after a noun and replaces は, が or を. With a negative it means "not either", with a question word and a negative it means "nothing" or "nobody", and after a number it stresses that the amount is large.

formation.example: 私も学生です, 猫もいる
コーヒーも飲む

formation.rule: Noun + に / で / と + も
formation.example: 京都にも行った, 家でも勉強する

formation.rule: 何 / 誰 / どこ + も + negative
formation.example: 何も食べない, 誰もいない
三時間も待った

usage: も adds something to what was already said. If someone says 私は学生です, you answer 私も学生です. In a negative sentence, it means "either": 私も行きません (I'm not going either).
も takes the place of は, が and を, but it sits after other particles like に, で and と: 京都にも行った, 友達とも話した.
A question word with も and a negative verb means "none": 何も知らない (I don't know anything), 誰も来なかった (nobody came), どこにも行かない (I'm not going anywhere).
After a number, も shows surprise that the amount is large: 三時間も待った (I waited a whole three hours). AもBも means "both A and B", or "neither" with a negative.

examples.romaji: Watashi mo ikitai!
examples.en: I want to go too!

examples.context: Telling a doctor how you feel
examples.romaji: Kinou wa nani mo tabenakatta.
examples.en: I didn't eat anything yesterday.

examples.context: Talking about a long line at a popular shop
examples.romaji: Otouto wa nijikan mo machimashita.
examples.en: My little brother waited a whole two hours.

examples.romaji: Kyouto ni mo Oosaka ni mo ikimashita.
examples.en: I went to both Kyoto and Osaka.

compare.note: は marks the topic, and can show contrast. も says the same thing is true of one more item.
Question word + も + negative means none: 誰も来ない. Question word + でも means any at all: 誰でもいい (anyone is fine).
だけ limits to one thing (only). も adds one more (also).

mistakes: Stacking particles: 私はも and コーヒーをも are wrong. Say 私も and コーヒーも.
Using 誰も with a positive verb for "everyone": 誰も来た is wrong. Say みんな来た, or 誰も来なかった for "nobody came".

faq.q: Does 何も always need a negative?
faq.a: In everyday speech, yes. 何も, 誰も and どこにも go with a negative verb to mean nothing, nobody and nowhere. For everything, use 全部 or 何でも.

faq.q: How do you say me neither in Japanese?
faq.a: Use も with a negative: 私も行きません (I'm not going either). In casual speech, just 私も works as a reply to a negative too.

intro: の (no) links two nouns, like 's or of in English: 私の本 (my book), 日本語の先生 (a Japanese teacher). It goes between the nouns. It can also stand for a noun ("one"), turn a verb into a noun (歌うのが好き), and end a casual question (どうしたの？).

formation.example: 私の本, 日本の車
これは私のです, 赤いのがいい

formation.when: After a verb (makes it a noun)
formation.example: 歌うのが好き, 見るのが楽しい
静かなのがいい
どうしたの？, 行くの？

usage: The first noun describes the second: 日本の車 (a car from Japan), 学校の先生 (a school teacher), 母の傘 (my mother's umbrella). The main noun always comes last.
の can replace a noun everyone already knows: この傘は誰の？ (whose is this umbrella?). After an adjective, it means "one": 大きいのをください (the big one, please).
After a plain verb, の makes it a noun, like -ing in English: 料理するのが好き (I like cooking). This is very common in speech.

At the end of a sentence, の asks a casual question or asks for an explanation: どうしたの？ (what's wrong?). Anyone uses it in questions. A statement ending in の, like 行くの。, sounds soft and is used more by women and children.

examples.context: Finding an umbrella at the office
examples.romaji: Kore wa dare no kasa desu ka.
examples.en: Whose umbrella is this?

examples.romaji: Nihongo no sensei wa totemo yasashii desu.
examples.en: My Japanese teacher is very kind.

examples.romaji: E o kaku no ga suki desu.
examples.en: I like drawing.

examples.romaji: Dou shita no? Daijoubu?
examples.en: What's wrong? Are you okay?

compare.note: Both turn a verb into a noun. の is more common in speech and for things you sense directly: 見るのが好き. こと is needed before です in definitions and in set patterns like ことができる.
の at the end of a casual question asks for an explanation. The polite version is んですか: どうしたんですか.

mistakes: Putting の between an い-adjective and a noun: 高いの車 is wrong. Say 高い車.
Using の after a な-adjective: きれいの花 is wrong. Say きれいな花.

faq.q: What is the difference between の and こと?
faq.a: Both make a verb into a noun. の is more casual and used for direct experiences. こと is more abstract and required in patterns like ことができる and 趣味は読むことです.

faq.q: Is の at the end of a sentence feminine?
faq.a: In questions, no: everyone says どうしたの？ In statements, like 明日行くの。, it sounds soft and is used more often by women and children.

intro: から (kara) means "from" and まで (made) means "until" or "as far as". Both go after a noun of time or place: 9時から5時まで (from 9 to 5), 東京から大阪まで (from Tokyo to Osaka). まで can also follow a dictionary-form verb: 雨がやむまで (until the rain stops).

formation.example: 9時から, 5時まで
東京から大阪まで
母から聞いた, 友達からもらった
雨がやむまで待つ, 帰るまで

usage: から marks a starting point and まで marks an end point. You can use either one alone, or both together for a range: 月曜日から金曜日まで (Monday to Friday).
With a person, から marks where something comes from: 先生から聞いた (I heard it from my teacher). With もらう, both に and から work.
まで means an action continues up to a point: 5時まで働く (work until 5). For a deadline, something done by a certain time, use までに instead.
Both are neutral and used everywhere. Don't mix up this から with the から after a verb that means "because": 寒いから (because it's cold).

examples.romaji: Jugyou wa kuji kara hajimarimasu.
examples.en: Class starts at nine.

examples.romaji: Toukyou kara Oosaka made shinkansen de itta.
examples.en: I took the bullet train from Tokyo to Osaka.

examples.romaji: Haha kara tegami ga todokimashita.
examples.en: A letter came from my mother.

examples.romaji: Ame ga yamu made, koko de matou.
examples.en: Let's wait here until the rain stops.

compare.note: まで is for something that continues until a time: 5時まで待つ. までに is a deadline: 5時までに来てください (come by 5).
After a noun, から means from. After a full clause, it means because: 雨だから行かない.
To say "after doing", use the て-form + から: 食べてから行く. 食べたから means "because I ate".

mistakes: Using まで for a deadline: 金曜日まで宿題を出してください should be 金曜日までに宿題を出してください.
Using the た-form for "after": 食べたから出かけた means "I went out because I ate". For "after eating", say 食べてから出かけた.

faq.q: What is the difference between まで and までに?
faq.a: まで marks the end of an action that continues: 10時まで寝た (I slept until 10). までに marks a deadline for a one-time action: 10時までに起きる (wake up by 10).

faq.q: How do I tell から (from) and から (because) apart?
faq.a: Look at what comes before it. A noun of time, place or person means from. A full clause with a verb, adjective or だ means because.

intro: や (ya) means "and" when you list a few examples from a longer list: 本や雑誌 means "books, magazines and things like that". It goes between nouns only. It is often paired with など at the end: りんごやバナナなど.

formation.example: 本や雑誌, 卵や牛乳

formation.when: With など at the end
formation.example: 京都や奈良など

formation.rule: Noun + や + noun + や + noun
formation.example: ペンやノートや消しゴム

usage: や says the list is not complete. 掃除や洗濯をする means you do cleaning, laundry and other chores. If you want to name every item, use と.
Adding など after the last item makes the "and so on" clearer. It is common in polite speech and writing.
や is neutral and works in both speech and writing. In casual conversation, people often use とか instead.
や only joins nouns. To list actions as examples, use たり〜たり: 掃除したり洗濯したりする.

examples.romaji: Kaban ni hon ya nooto ga haitte imasu.
examples.en: There are books, notebooks and such in my bag.

examples.romaji: Shuumatsu wa souji ya sentaku o shimasu.
examples.en: On weekends I do things like cleaning and laundry.

examples.romaji: Kyouto ya Nara nado ni ikitai desu.
examples.en: I'd like to go to places like Kyoto and Nara.

examples.context: Telling a roommate what there is to eat
examples.romaji: Reizouko ni tamago ya gyuunyuu ga aru yo.
examples.en: There are eggs, milk and stuff in the fridge.

compare.note: と lists every item. や gives examples and implies there are more.
とか also gives examples but is more casual, and it can follow verbs and clauses too: 映画見るとか.
など means "and so on" and often closes a や list. It can also follow a single item: 本などを読む.

mistakes: Joining verbs with や: 食べたや飲んだ is wrong. Use たり: 食べたり飲んだりした.
Using や for a complete list: if you bought exactly two things, say パンと牛乳を買った, not パンや牛乳を買った.

faq.q: What is the difference between や and と?
faq.a: と means the list is complete. や means these are just examples and there are other things too.

faq.q: What is the difference between や and とか?
faq.a: Both list examples. や is neutral and only joins nouns. とか is casual and can also follow verbs and sentences.

intro: より (yori) means "than" in comparisons: 今日は昨日より暑い (today is hotter than yesterday). It goes after the thing you compare against, a noun or a plain-form verb. It is often paired with のほうが: 肉より魚のほうが好き. In formal writing, より can also mean "from".

formation.example: 昨日より暑い, 犬より猫

formation.rule: A より B のほうが + adjective
formation.example: 肉より魚のほうが好き
思ったより簡単, 待つより歩くほうが早い
10時より開始, 社長より

usage: The noun before より is the standard you compare against. 東京は大阪より大きい means Tokyo is bigger than Osaka. Japanese adjectives do not change form for comparison, so より does all the work.
AよりBのほうが is the full pattern: AよりBのほうが好き (I like B more than A). You can drop either part when it is clear: 魚のほうが好き, or 肉より魚が好き.
思ったより (than I thought) and 予想より (than expected) are very common set phrases.
In formal announcements and letters, より means "from": 会議は2時より始まります, 田中より (from Tanaka, signing an email). In normal speech, use から for that.

examples.romaji: Kyou wa kinou yori atsui desu ne.
examples.en: It's hotter today than yesterday, isn't it?

examples.romaji: Watashi wa niku yori sakana no hou ga suki desu.
examples.en: I like fish better than meat.

examples.romaji: Omotta yori kantan datta.
examples.en: It was easier than I thought.

examples.romaji: Kaigi wa gogo niji yori hajimarimasu.
examples.en: The meeting will begin at 2 p.m.

compare.note: Use ほど for "not as ... as": 今日は昨日ほど暑くない. より is mainly used in positive comparisons.
Both can mean from. から is the everyday word. より for "from" is formal and written.

mistakes: Flipping the comparison: 東京より大阪は大きい means Osaka is bigger. To say Tokyo is bigger, say 東京は大阪より大きい.
Using より for "not as ... as": 今日は昨日より暑くない is understandable but unnatural. Say 今日は昨日ほど暑くない.

faq.q: What is the difference between より and ほど?
faq.a: より compares in a positive sentence: AはBより大きい. ほど is used with a negative for "not as ... as": AはBほど大きくない.

faq.q: Do I always need のほうが with より?
faq.a: No. 肉より魚が好き is fine. のほうが makes the choice clearer, and it is common when answering "which one?" questions.

intro: だけ (dake) means "only" or "just": 水だけ (only water), 見るだけです (I'm just looking). It goes after a noun, a number, or the plain form of a verb or adjective. Unlike しか, it works with both positive and negative verbs.

formation.example: 水だけ, 私だけ
一つだけ, 少しだけ
見るだけ, 聞いただけ

formation.rule: い-adj + だけ / な-adj + な + だけ
formation.example: 高いだけ, 好きなだけ

formation.rule: Noun + に / で + だけ
formation.example: 君にだけ, ここでだけ

usage: だけ limits something to the item before it, in a neutral way. 水だけ飲む simply means "I drink only water". It does not add a feeling of "too little" the way しか does.
見るだけです (I'm just looking) is a set phrase for shop staff. ちょっとだけ (just a little) is very common in casual speech.
With particles, だけ usually comes after に, で and から (君にだけ), and before or in place of は, が and を (水だけを飲む or 水だけ飲む).
好きなだけ and できるだけ are useful set phrases: 好きなだけ食べて (eat as much as you like), できるだけ早く (as soon as possible).

examples.romaji: Miru dake desu.
examples.en: I'm just looking.

examples.romaji: Hitotsu dake shitsumon shite mo ii desu ka?
examples.en: May I ask just one question?

examples.romaji: Kimi ni dake hanasu ne.
examples.en: I'm only telling you.

examples.context: A host at a dinner party
examples.romaji: Suki na dake tabete ne.
examples.en: Eat as much as you like.

compare.note: しか always needs a negative verb and suggests "not enough": 千円しかない (I only have 1,000 yen). 千円だけある is more neutral.
ばかり means "nothing but" and often complains that something happens too much: ゲームばかりしている.

mistakes: Using だけ with a negative to mean "only": 水だけ飲まない can mean "water is the only thing I don't drink". To say "I drink nothing but water", use 水しか飲まない or 水だけ飲む.
Dropping な after a な-adjective: 好きだけ is wrong. Say 好きなだけ.

faq.q: What is the difference between だけ and しか?
faq.a: だけ works with positive and negative verbs and is neutral. しか must be followed by a negative and stresses that it is less than you want or expect.

faq.q: Is だけ polite?
faq.a: だけ itself is neutral. You can use it with です and ます in polite speech, or alone in casual speech.

intro: しか〜ない (shika ... nai) means "only" or "nothing but": 千円しかない (I only have 1,000 yen). しか goes after a noun, number or particle, and the verb at the end must be negative. It stresses that the amount is small or that there is no other option.

formation.example: 水しか飲まない
千円しかない, 一人しか来なかった

formation.rule: Noun + で / に / と + しか
formation.example: ここでしか買えない
待つしかない, やるしかない

usage: The sentence ends in a negative, but the meaning is positive: 水しか飲まない means "I drink only water". Think of it as "except for water, I don't drink anything".
しか adds a feeling that the amount is too small or less than expected. 三人しか来なかった means only three people came, and the speaker expected more.
しか replaces は, が and を, but goes after に, で and から: ここでしか買えない, 友達にしか言っていない.
Verb + しかない means there is no other choice: もう待つしかない (all we can do is wait). やるしかない (I just have to do it) is a common phrase for facing a challenge.

examples.romaji: Saifu ni gohyaku en shika nai.
examples.en: I only have 500 yen in my wallet.

examples.romaji: Paatii ni wa sannin shika kimasen deshita.
examples.en: Only three people came to the party.

examples.romaji: Kono mise de shika kaenai n desu.
examples.en: You can only buy it at this shop.

examples.context: Stuck waiting for a delayed train
examples.romaji: Mou matsu shika nai ne.
examples.en: All we can do now is wait.

compare.note: だけ is neutral and works with positive verbs: 千円だけある. しか needs a negative and sounds like "only, and that's not much".
ばかり means "nothing but" with a positive verb and often a complaint: 肉ばかり食べている.

mistakes: Using しか with a positive verb: 千円しかあります is wrong. Say 千円しかありません.
Putting を before しか: 水をしか飲まない is wrong. Say 水しか飲まない.

faq.q: What is the difference between しか and だけ?
faq.a: Both mean only. だけ is neutral and works with any verb. しか must take a negative verb and suggests the amount is small or not enough.

faq.q: Why does しか need a negative?
faq.a: しか means "except for". 水しか飲まない is literally "except for water, I don't drink", which gives the meaning "I drink only water".

intro: ばかり (bakari) means "nothing but" or "only", usually with a feeling that it is too much: ゲームばかり means games and nothing else. It goes after a noun, after the て-form with いる (寝てばかりいる), and after the た-form, where it means "just did" (来たばかり).

formation.example: 肉ばかり, 漫画ばかり

formation.when: After a noun with a particle
formation.example: 弟にばかり, 友達とばかり

formation.rule: て-form + ばかり + いる
formation.example: 寝る → 寝てばかりいる, 遊ぶ → 遊んでばかりいる
来る → 来たばかり, 買う → 買ったばかり

usage: With nouns and the て-form, ばかり says one thing fills everything, and it often sounds like a complaint. 弟はゲームばかりしている means your brother plays games all the time and does nothing else. だけ is the neutral word for "only".
After the た-form, ばかり means "just did". 日本に来たばかりです means you arrived in Japan recently. The time can be days or even months, as long as it feels recent to the speaker.
In casual speech ばかり often becomes ばっかり or ばっか: 文句ばっかり言って. Use ばかり in polite speech and writing.
After a number, ばかり can mean "about", as in 千円ばかり. This use is old-fashioned and mostly written. In everyday speech, people say くらい instead.

examples.romaji: Otouto wa geemu bakari shite iru.
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play games.

examples.romaji: Nihon ni kita bakari desu.
examples.en: I just came to Japan.

examples.context: Telling a friend to stop grumbling
examples.romaji: Monku bakari iwanaide.
examples.en: Stop complaining all the time.

examples.romaji: Katta bakari no kasa o nakushichatta.
examples.en: I lost the umbrella I just bought.

compare.note: だけ is a neutral "only" that states a limit: 一つだけ (just one). ばかり means one thing again and again, often with a complaint: 肉ばかり食べる (eat nothing but meat).
たところ means the action finished a moment ago: 今起きたところ (I just this minute woke up). たばかり means it feels recent and can cover a longer time: 先月入ったばかり (I only joined last month).
しか〜ない stresses that there is nothing else, often too little: 千円しかない. ばかり stresses that there is too much of one thing.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form with いる: 寝るばかりいる is wrong. Use the て-form: 寝てばかりいる.
Using ばかり for a neutral limit or a small amount: 一つばかりあります sounds odd. Say 一つだけあります or 一つしかありません.
Using たばかり for something that happened seconds ago when you mean "right this moment": for that, 今終わったところ is more natural than 今終わったばかり.

faq.q: What is the difference between ばかり and だけ?
faq.a: だけ simply means only and is neutral. ばかり means nothing but one thing, over and over, and often sounds like a complaint or criticism.

faq.q: What does たばかり mean?
faq.a: It means just did. 買ったばかり means just bought. The action feels recent to the speaker, even if it was a few weeks ago.

faq.q: What is ばっかり?
faq.a: ばっかり and ばっか are casual spoken versions of ばかり. The meaning is the same, with a bit more emphasis.

meaning: about, around; so much that; at least
intro: くらい or ぐらい (kurai / gurai) means "about" or "around" after an amount, as in 10分くらい (about ten minutes). It also shows a degree ("so much that") or a minimum ("at least"). It goes after numbers, nouns, これ / どの, and the plain form of verbs and adjectives.

formation.rule: Number + くらい / ぐらい
formation.example: 3時間くらい, 1000円ぐらい

formation.rule: Noun + くらい / ぐらい
formation.example: 電話ぐらい, 私くらい

formation.when: After こ / そ / あ / ど words
formation.rule: この / その / どの + くらい
formation.example: このくらい, どのくらい, これぐらい
泣きたいくらい, 痛いくらい
静かなくらい, きれいなくらい

usage: The most common use is a rough amount: 駅まで10分くらいです. くらい and ぐらい mean the same thing, and both are correct. In speech, ぐらい is very common after nouns and numbers.
After a verb or adjective, くらい shows how far something goes: 泣きたいくらい恥ずかしかった (so embarrassed I wanted to cry). The clause before くらい gives a picture of the degree.
After a noun, ぐらい can mean "at least" or "something as small as": 電話ぐらいしてよ (at least give me a call). This often carries a light complaint or a sense that it is easy.
どのくらい asks how much, how long or how far, and works in both casual and polite speech: どのくらいかかりますか (How long does it take?).

examples.romaji: Eki made aruite juppun kurai desu.
examples.en: It's about ten minutes on foot to the station.

examples.romaji: Denwa gurai shite yo.
examples.en: At least give me a call.

examples.romaji: Hazukashikute, nakitai kurai datta.
examples.en: I was so embarrassed I wanted to cry.

examples.romaji: Dono kurai nihongo o benkyou shite imasu ka.
examples.en: How long have you been studying Japanese?

compare.note: ごろ means "around" a point in time: 3時ごろ. くらい is for amounts and lengths: 3時間くらい. In casual speech 3時くらい is also common, but ごろ is the standard for clock times and dates.
ほど also means "about" and "to the extent that", but it sounds more formal. For "not as ... as", ほど is the normal choice: 兄ほど背が高くない.

mistakes: Putting くらい before the number: くらい3時間 is wrong. It always comes after: 3時間くらい.
Using くらい for "not as ... as": 兄くらい背が高くない sounds unnatural to many speakers. Use ほど: 兄ほど背が高くない.
Forgetting な with a な-adjective: 静かくらい is wrong. Say 静かなくらい.

faq.q: What is the difference between くらい and ぐらい?
faq.a: There is no difference in meaning. Both are correct. ぐらい is very common in speech after nouns and numbers, and くらい is common after verbs and adjectives, but you can use either.

faq.q: What is the difference between くらい and ごろ?
faq.a: ごろ is for a point in time, like 5時ごろ (around five o'clock). くらい is for an amount or length, like 5時間くらい (about five hours).

faq.q: What does ぐらい mean in 電話ぐらいして?
faq.a: Here it means at least. The speaker is saying a phone call is a small thing, so you could do at least that.

meaning: such as, and so on, things like
intro: など (nado) means "such as" or "and so on": it shows that the things you named are only examples. It goes after a noun or at the end of a list, often with や: りんごやみかんなど (apples, oranges and so on).

formation.example: 果物など, 本など

formation.when: At the end of a list
formation.example: りんごやみかんなど

formation.rule: など + が / を / に / で
formation.example: 京都などに行った, お茶などを飲む
お菓子なんか, 私なんか

usage: など marks a list as incomplete. 京都や奈良などに行きました means you went to Kyoto, Nara and other places too. It is very common with や, which also lists examples.
など is neutral to formal. You see it in news, signs, business emails and polite speech. With friends, people usually say なんか or とか instead.
After a word for yourself, など is humble: 私などまだまだです (someone like me still has a long way to go). After other words it can sound dismissive, like saying "something like that".
With a negative, など adds emphasis: 嘘などついていません means "I have not told any lie at all", as if the idea itself is out of the question.

examples.romaji: Kyoto ya Nara nado ni ikimashita.
examples.en: I went to places like Kyoto and Nara.

examples.romaji: Nomimono wa, ocha ya juusu nado ga arimasu.
examples.en: For drinks, we have tea, juice and so on.

examples.romaji: Watashi nado madamada desu.
examples.en: Someone like me still has a long way to go.

examples.romaji: Uso nado tsuite imasen.
examples.en: I haven't told any lie or anything like that.

compare.note: や lists examples between nouns: AやB. など usually closes the list: AやBなど. You can use や alone, or add など to make the "and so on" clear.
とか also lists examples, but it is casual and can follow verbs and adjectives too. など is more neutral and more common in writing.
なんか is the spoken form of など. It is casual, and when it follows a person or thing it can sound more dismissive: 宿題なんかやりたくない.

mistakes: Using など for a complete list: if you have exactly one brother and one sister, say 兄と姉がいます, not 兄や姉などがいます.
Using など in casual chat with friends: it sounds stiff. Say お菓子とか or お菓子なんか instead of お菓子など.

faq.q: What is the difference between など and とか?
faq.a: Both list examples. など is neutral to formal and common in writing. とか is casual and spoken, and it can be repeated after each item: AとかBとか.

faq.q: What is the difference between など and なんか?
faq.a: なんか is the casual spoken version of など. It can also sound more dismissive, as in 私なんか (someone like me).

faq.q: Is など polite?
faq.a: など is neutral and fits polite speech and writing well. It is not rude, but after another person's name or work it can sound dismissive, so be careful with that use.

intro: とか (toka) means "things like" or "...or something": it gives examples in casual speech, as in 寿司とか天ぷらとか (sushi, tempura and so on). It goes after nouns and after the plain form of verbs and adjectives, and it can also report something vaguely, like "he said something like...".

formation.rule: A とか B とか
formation.example: 寿司とか天ぷらとか
映画とか, コーヒーとか
寝るとか, 音楽を聞くとか
高いとか安いとか, 静かだとか

formation.rule: Plain form + とか + 言う
formation.example: 来ないとか言ってた

usage: とか is the casual way to list examples. 寿司とか天ぷらとか means sushi, tempura and other things like that. You can say とか after every item, or leave it off the last one.
With one item, とか makes a suggestion or question softer and less direct: 映画とか見に行かない? (Want to go see a movie or something?). The listener can pick something else.
Unlike や, とか can follow verbs and adjectives: 寝るとか音楽を聞くとか. This is a casual way to list actions, similar to たり〜たり.
とか言ってた means "(they) said something like". The speaker reports the idea but not the exact words. とか belongs to casual speech, so use や or など in writing and formal situations.

examples.romaji: Shuumatsu wa eiga toka mi ni ikanai?
examples.en: Want to go see a movie or something this weekend?

examples.romaji: Sushi toka tenpura toka, nihon ryouri ga suki desu.
examples.en: I like Japanese food, like sushi and tempura.

examples.romaji: Tanaka-san, ashita korarenai toka itteta yo.
examples.en: Tanaka said something like they can't come tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Tsukareta toki wa, neru toka ongaku o kiku toka shiteru.
examples.en: When I'm tired, I do things like sleep or listen to music.

compare.note: や lists nouns only and is neutral, fine for writing. とか is casual and can follow verbs and adjectives too.
など usually closes a list and is neutral to formal. とか is the spoken, casual choice.
たり〜たり lists example actions and works in polite speech too: 掃除したり洗濯したりします. とか can do the same, but it is more casual.

mistakes: Using とか in an essay or business email: 会議では予算とか日程とかを話しました sounds too casual. Write 予算や日程などについて話しました.
Using とか after everything you say: answering every question with 〜とか sounds vague, like adding "or whatever" to each sentence in English.

faq.q: What is the difference between とか and や?
faq.a: Both list examples. や only goes between nouns and is neutral. とか is casual and can also follow verbs and adjectives.

faq.q: Is とか casual?
faq.a: Yes. とか is for speech with friends, family and coworkers you are close to. In formal speech and writing, use や or など.

faq.q: What does とか mean at the end of a sentence?
faq.a: It makes the statement vague, like "or something". After a quote, as in 来ないとか, it means the speaker heard something like that but is not giving the exact words.

meaning: casual quote; (they) said; as for, called
intro: って (tte) is a casual particle that quotes what someone said, like "(she) says" or "I heard". It also works as a casual topic marker ("as for", "what is...?") and means "called" in っていう. It goes after the plain form of verbs and adjectives, after nouns, and after any word or phrase being quoted.

formation.example: 来るって, 行かないって, 寒いって
雨だって, 休みだって
日本語って, 納豆って
「推し」って何?
山田さんっていう人

usage: As a quote, って is the casual form of と or と言っていた. 先生、明日休むって means "The teacher says she's off tomorrow." At the end of a sentence it passes on news you heard.

As a topic marker, って replaces は when you talk about what something is like or what it means: 納豆って美味しいの? (Is natto actually good?). It often suggests the speaker is curious or does not know much about it.
っていう is the casual form of という (called): 山田さんっていう人 (a person called Yamada). It is also how people ask about a word: 「推し」って何?
って is casual speech. In formal speech and writing, use と, は, という, or そうです for hearsay. A polite sentence can still use って in friendly speech, as in 「推し」って何ですか, but avoid it with bosses and customers.

examples.context: Passing on a message to a classmate
examples.romaji: Sensei, ashita yasumu tte.
examples.en: The teacher says they're taking tomorrow off.

examples.romaji: Nattou tte oishii no?
examples.en: Is natto actually tasty?

examples.romaji: "Oshi" tte nan desu ka.
examples.en: What does "oshi" mean?

examples.context: Telling a family member about a call
examples.romaji: Yamada-san tte iu hito kara denwa ga arimashita yo.
examples.en: You got a call from someone called Yamada.

compare.note: と is the standard quote particle and fits any register: 明日休むと言っていました. って is the casual spoken version and can drop the verb 言う.
は is the general topic marker. って as a topic sounds casual and often adds curiosity or surprise: 東京って広いね.
そうだ / そうです reports hearsay in a neutral or polite way: 明日休むそうです. Sentence-final って does the same thing casually.

mistakes: Using って with a boss: 部長、田中さん今日休むって is too casual. Say 田中さんは今日休むそうです.
Using って in writing: essays and emails use と, は or という. Write 田中という人, not 田中っていう人.

faq.q: What does って mean at the end of a sentence?
faq.a: It usually means "(someone) said" or "I heard". 雨だって means "They say it'll rain." With rising intonation, it can also mean "Did you say...?"

faq.q: Is って rude?
faq.a: It is not rude, but it is casual. Use it with friends and family. With teachers, bosses or customers, use と, は, という or そうです.

faq.q: What is the difference between って and と?
faq.a: Both quote. と is standard and works in any register, while って is casual and spoken. って can also stand alone at the end of a sentence without 言う.

intro: までに (made ni) means "by" a time: it sets a deadline for something to be done once, as in 金曜日までに (by Friday). It goes after a time word or after the dictionary form of a verb, like 帰るまでに (by the time I get home).

formation.example: 5時までに, 9時までに
金曜日までに, 来週までに, 明日の朝までに
帰る → 帰るまでに, 始まる → 始まるまでに

formation.rule: それ / これ + までに
formation.example: それまでに (by then)

usage: までに is for deadlines. The action happens once, at any point before the time: 金曜日までに出してください means hand it in on Friday or earlier.
まで (without に) is different. It means "until", and the action continues the whole time: 5時まで待つ (wait until five). Many learners mix these up.
After a verb, までに means "by the time" something happens: 母が帰ってくるまでに (before Mom gets home). The verb stays in the dictionary form, even for past events.
までに is common at work, school and in instructions. 〜までにお願いします and 〜までにいただけますか are standard polite ways to set a deadline in emails.

examples.romaji: Repooto wa kin'youbi made ni dashite kudasai.
examples.en: Please hand in the report by Friday.

examples.romaji: Rokuji made ni kaeru ne.
examples.en: I'll be home by six.

examples.context: Talking to yourself in a messy room
examples.romaji: Haha ga kaette kuru made ni heya o katazukenakya.
examples.en: I have to clean my room before Mom gets home.

examples.romaji: Ashita no asa made ni henji o itadakemasu ka.
examples.en: Could I get your reply by tomorrow morning?

compare.note: まで means "until" and goes with an action that continues: 5時まで働く (work until five). までに means "by" and goes with an action done once: 5時までに終わらせる (finish by five).
前に means "before" with no deadline feeling: 寝る前に歯を磨く. までに sets a limit that must not be passed.

mistakes: Using まで for a deadline: 5時まで宿題を終わらせる is wrong. Say 5時までに宿題を終わらせる.
Using までに with a continuing action: 5時までに待ちます is wrong. Say 5時まで待ちます.
Putting a past verb before までに: 着いたまでに is wrong. Use the dictionary form: 着くまでに.

faq.q: What is the difference between まで and までに?
faq.a: まで means until: the action goes on up to that time. までに means by: the action is done once, at some point before that time.

faq.q: Is までに polite enough for a work email?
faq.a: Yes. までに itself is neutral. Make the rest polite: 金曜日までにご提出ください or 金曜日までにいただけますでしょうか.

meaning: sentence-ending: I'm telling you, you know
intro: よ (yo) is a sentence-ending particle that tells the listener something they don't know yet, like "you know" or "I'm telling you". It goes at the very end of a sentence, after a verb, an adjective, or a noun with だ / です: 行くよ, 高いですよ, 学生だよ.

formation.example: 行くよ, 行きますよ, 来たよ
高いよ, 高いですよ

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + だよ / ですよ
formation.example: 学生だよ, 静かですよ
早くしてよ, 行こうよ

usage: よ marks new information for the listener. 電車、もう来ていますよ tells someone the train is here because they may not have noticed. It is used by everyone, in casual and polite speech.
よ adds force, so it can sound warm and helpful or pushy, depending on tone. 大丈夫だよ is comforting. Using よ on every sentence, or to correct a superior, can sound like you are lecturing.
With requests and invitations, よ adds urging: 行こうよ (come on, let's go), 早くしてよ (hurry up already). The second one sounds impatient.
In casual speech, dropping だ before よ (学生よ, きれいよ) sounds feminine or a bit old-fashioned. The neutral casual form is 学生だよ.

examples.romaji: Kono mise, yasukute oishii yo.
examples.en: This place is cheap and tasty, you know.

examples.context: Telling a stranger on the platform
examples.romaji: Densha, mou kite imasu yo.
examples.en: The train's already here.

examples.romaji: Issho ni ikou yo.
examples.en: Come on, let's go together.

examples.romaji: Daijoubu da yo. Shinpai shinaide.
examples.en: It's okay. Don't worry.

compare.note: ね checks that the listener agrees or shares the feeling: 暑いね. よ gives the listener information they may not have: 暑いよ (it's hot out there, just so you know).
よね states something and asks for agreement at the same time: 明日だよね (It's tomorrow, right?).
ぞ and ぜ are stronger, rougher endings used mostly by men in casual speech. よ is neutral and used by everyone.

mistakes: Telling a teacher or boss something they know: 先生、今日は月曜日ですよ sounds like you are correcting them. Leave out よ or use ね if you are checking.
Adding よ to every sentence: it makes you sound insistent. Use it when the information is really new or important to the listener.

faq.q: Is よ rude?
faq.a: No. よ is used by everyone, also in polite speech: ありますよ, 大丈夫ですよ. It only sounds pushy when overused or used to correct someone above you.

faq.q: What is the difference between よ and ね?
faq.a: よ tells the listener something new. ね looks for agreement about something you both know or feel. よね does both: it states and checks.

faq.q: What does よ mean at the end of a Japanese sentence?
faq.a: It works like "you know" or "I'm telling you". It marks the sentence as information or advice for the listener.

intro: ね (ne) is a sentence-ending particle that asks for agreement or shares a feeling, like "isn't it?" or "right?". It goes at the very end of a sentence, after a verb, an adjective, or a noun with だ / です: 暑いですね, きれいだね.

formation.example: 行くね, 行きますね, 来たね
暑いね, 暑いですね

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + だね / ですね
formation.example: 雨だね, きれいですね
気をつけてね, 待っててね

usage: ね invites the listener to agree, or shows that you share a feeling: 今日は暑いですね (It's hot today, isn't it?). It is a big part of friendly small talk.
ね also checks information you think is right: 来週から大阪ですね (You're in Osaka from next week, right?). Staff at shops and offices use it all the time to confirm details.
After your own plan or request, ね softens the sentence: 先に行くね (I'll go ahead, okay?), 気をつけてね (take care, okay?). It sounds warm and friendly.
ね is used by men and women, in casual and polite speech. A long ねえ shows stronger feeling, and ね in the middle of a sentence (昨日ね、...) is a casual filler to keep the listener with you.

examples.romaji: Kyou wa atsui desu ne.
examples.en: It's hot today, isn't it?

examples.romaji: Jaa, mata ashita ne.
examples.en: Okay, see you tomorrow.

examples.context: A parent seeing a child off
examples.romaji: Ki o tsukete kaette ne.
examples.en: Get home safe, okay?

examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa raishuu kara Osaka desu ne.
examples.en: Tanaka-san, you're in Osaka from next week, right?

compare.note: よ gives the listener new information. ね assumes the listener knows or feels the same and asks them to agree.
よね states your view and asks for agreement in one go. It is a bit stronger than ね when you want the other person to confirm.
な is a casual ending close to ね, more common among men, and often said to yourself: いいなあ (I'm jealous).

mistakes: Using ね for information only you know: 私の名前はジョンですね sounds like you are unsure of your own name. Say 私の名前はジョンです.
Treating そうですね as a clear yes: it often means "let me see" and shows the speaker is thinking. A clear agreement is はい or そうです.

faq.q: What is the difference between ね and よ?
faq.a: ね asks for agreement about something shared. よ tells the listener something they may not know. 寒いね means "cold, isn't it?" and 寒いよ means "it's cold, you know."

faq.q: Is ね feminine?
faq.a: No. Everyone uses ね, in polite and casual speech. Dropping だ before ね, as in きれいね, can sound feminine, while な is a bit more common among men.

faq.q: What does ねえ mean?
faq.a: ねえ is a longer ね with more feeling. At the start of a sentence, ねえ is like "hey" to get someone's attention.

intro: よね (yo ne) is a sentence ending that states what you think and checks that the listener agrees, like "right?" or "isn't it?". It goes at the end of a sentence, after a verb, an adjective, or a noun with だ / です: 3時からですよね, 美味しいよね.

formation.example: 行くよね, 行きますよね
言ったよね, 言いましたよね
美味しいよね, 美味しいですよね

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + だよね / ですよね
formation.example: 明日だよね, 簡単ですよね

usage: よね joins よ (I think this) and ね (you agree, right?). You use it when you are fairly sure but want the other person to confirm: 会議は3時からですよね?
With an opinion or feeling, よね invites the listener to share it: このラーメン、美味しいよね. It sounds friendly and is very common in conversation.
With a past verb, よね can remind someone, sometimes with a little blame: 昨日言ったよね? (I told you yesterday, didn't I?). The tone decides how strong it sounds.
ですよね is polite and used everywhere, including at work. On its own, ですよね! is a common reply meaning "I know, right?" or "Exactly."

examples.context: Checking the schedule with a coworker
examples.romaji: Kaigi wa sanji kara desu yo ne?
examples.en: The meeting starts at three, right?

examples.romaji: Kono raamen, oishii yo ne.
examples.en: This ramen is good, isn't it?

examples.romaji: Kinou, chanto itta yo ne?
examples.en: I told you clearly yesterday, didn't I?

examples.romaji: Wakaru, sore muzukashii yo ne.
examples.en: I get it, that's hard, isn't it.

compare.note: ね alone assumes you both already agree: 暑いね. よね adds your own claim first, so it sounds more like checking: 暑いよね (it's hot, right?).
よ only tells. よね tells and then asks for agreement.
でしょう? also asks for agreement, but it can sound more pushy, as if the answer is obvious. よね sounds softer and more friendly.

mistakes: Reversing the order: ねよ is wrong. It is always よね.
Using よね for news the listener cannot know: 新しい仕事が決まったよね sounds like you expect them to know already. To share news, say 新しい仕事が決まったよ.

faq.q: What is the difference between よね and ね?
faq.a: ね shares a feeling you assume is mutual. よね puts your own view first and asks the listener to confirm it, so it is closer to "right?"

faq.q: What does ですよね mean?
faq.a: It is the polite form of よね. Said alone as a reply, ですよね means "I know, right?" or "Exactly."

faq.q: Is ですよね polite?
faq.a: Yes. ですよね is fine with coworkers, teachers and customers. Just be careful with よね on past actions, which can sound like you are blaming the listener.

intro: かな (ka na) means "I wonder" at the end of a sentence, as in 明日晴れるかな (I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow). It goes after the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and directly after nouns and な-adjectives without だ: 雨かな.

formation.example: 来るかな, 来ないかな, 届いたかな
美味しいかな, 高かったかな

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + かな (no だ)
formation.example: 雨かな, 大丈夫かな
早く来ないかな

formation.rule: てくれる / てもらえる + かな
formation.example: 手伝ってもらえるかな

usage: かな is mostly said to yourself. It shows you are wondering or unsure: 荷物、もう届いたかな (I wonder if the package came). It is casual and used by everyone.
Said to someone, かな softens a question or request: ちょっと手伝ってもらえるかな? sounds gentle and less direct than 手伝って.
With the ない-form, かな expresses a wish: 早く夏休みにならないかな means "I can't wait for summer break", not a real question about whether it will come.
かな also makes an answer vague: うーん、3時くらいかな (Hmm, around three, I guess). In polite speech, use でしょうか instead.

examples.romaji: Ashita, hareru ka na.
examples.en: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Nimotsu, mou todoita ka na.
examples.en: I wonder if the package has arrived yet.

examples.romaji: Chotto tetsudatte moraeru ka na?
examples.en: Could you give me a hand for a sec?

examples.romaji: Hayaku natsuyasumi ni naranai ka na.
examples.en: I can't wait for summer break.

compare.note: でしょうか is the polite way to wonder or ask softly: 明日は晴れるでしょうか. かな is the casual version.
かしら means the same as かな but sounds feminine and a little old-fashioned.
かもしれない states a possibility: 雨かもしれない (it might rain). かな shows you are wondering about it: 雨かな (is it going to rain, I wonder).

mistakes: Adding だ before かな: 雨だかな is wrong. Say 雨かな.
Using かな with a boss or customer: 部長、明日来られるかな is too casual. Say 明日いらっしゃいますか or いらっしゃるでしょうか.

faq.q: Is かな feminine?
faq.a: No. かな is used by men and women. かしら is the ending that sounds feminine.

faq.q: What does ないかな mean?
faq.a: With the ない-form, かな usually expresses a wish. 早く来ないかな means "I wish they'd hurry up and come."

faq.q: What is the difference between かな and かも?
faq.a: かも (かもしれない) says something is possible. かな says you are wondering about it. かな can also soften a question to someone, which かも does not do.

intro: っけ (kke) is a sentence ending you use when you are trying to remember something, like "what was it again?". It goes after だ / だった, the past tense, or polite でした / ました: 何曜日だっけ, どこに置いたっけ.

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + だっけ / だったっけ
formation.example: 何だっけ, 明日だったっけ
言ったっけ, 置いたっけ
行くんだっけ, 来るんだっけ

formation.rule: かった + っけ / い + んだっけ
formation.example: 高かったっけ, 高いんだっけ

formation.rule: でした / ました + っけ
formation.example: 何でしたっけ, 言いましたっけ

usage: っけ asks about something you once knew but forgot. あれ、今日何曜日だっけ? is like "Wait, what day is it again?" You can say it to yourself or to someone else.
っけ often comes with the past tense, even about the present or the future: お名前、何でしたっけ? asks someone's name now. The past tense shows you heard it before.
It is casual, but でしたっけ and ましたっけ are fine with coworkers and people you know. In very formal situations, ask directly: もう一度お名前を伺ってもよろしいですか.
In stories and memories, っけ can also show looking back fondly: 子どもの頃、よくここで遊んだっけ (We used to play here a lot, didn't we).

examples.romaji: Are, kyou nan'youbi dakke?
examples.en: Wait, what day is it today again?

examples.romaji: Sumimasen, onamae nan deshitakke?
examples.en: Sorry, what was your name again?

examples.romaji: Kagi, doko ni oitakke.
examples.en: Where did I put my keys?

examples.romaji: Ashita no shuugou tte nanji dattakke?
examples.en: What time are we meeting tomorrow again?

compare.note: かな wonders about something you don't know: 明日晴れるかな. っけ tries to recall something you knew before: 明日って何曜日だっけ.
よね checks something you are fairly sure about: 3時だよね. っけ is for when you have really forgotten: 何時だっけ.

mistakes: Putting っけ right after a non-past verb: 明日行くっけ is unnatural. Say 明日行くんだっけ.
Putting っけ right after a non-past い-adjective: 高いっけ is unnatural. Say 高かったっけ or 高いんだっけ.
Using っけ for something you never knew: っけ means you forgot. If you never heard it, just ask: 何時ですか.

faq.q: Why is っけ often used with the past tense?
faq.a: The past tense shows that you heard or knew the information before. お名前何でしたっけ means "what was your name (that you told me)?"

faq.q: Is っけ polite?
faq.a: Plain だっけ is casual. でしたっけ and ましたっけ are polite enough for coworkers and teachers you know. In very formal settings, ask the question directly.

faq.q: What does 何だっけ mean?
faq.a: It means "What was it again?" People say it when a word or name is on the tip of their tongue.

intro: でしょう (deshou) and だろう (darou) mean "probably" or "I suppose" at the end of a sentence, as in 明日は雨が降るでしょう. With rising intonation they mean "right?". They go after the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and directly after nouns and な-adjectives without だ: 雨でしょう.

formation.rule: Plain form + でしょう / だろう
formation.example: 来るでしょう, 来ないだろう, 来たでしょう

formation.rule: Plain form + でしょう / だろう
formation.example: 寒いでしょう, 高かっただろう

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + でしょう / だろう (no だ)
formation.example: 雨でしょう, 静かだろう

formation.rule: Plain form / noun + でしょうか
formation.example: どちらでしょうか, 大丈夫でしょうか

usage: でしょう is the polite form and だろう is the plain form. Both make a guess: 明日は雨が降るでしょう (It will probably rain tomorrow). Weather forecasts use でしょう all the time. たぶん (probably) often comes earlier in the sentence.
With rising intonation, でしょう? asks the listener to agree, often because the answer seems obvious: だから言ったでしょう? (See? I told you). In casual speech it shortens to でしょ or だろ.
だろう is common in writing and in thoughts. In conversation, だろ and だろう sound masculine and a bit rough. Women and men both use でしょ in casual speech.
でしょうか is a soft, polite question. すみません、駅はどちらでしょうか is gentler than どちらですか and is common with strangers and customers.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furu deshou.
examples.en: It will probably rain tomorrow.

examples.context: A parent after a child spills juice
examples.romaji: Hora, dakara itta deshou?
examples.en: See? That's what I told you.

examples.context: Thinking about a friend who is always late
examples.romaji: Kare wa tabun konai darou.
examples.en: He probably won't come.

examples.romaji: Sumimasen, eki wa dochira deshou ka.
examples.en: Excuse me, which way is the station?

compare.note: かもしれない means "might", a weaker guess, around 50 percent. でしょう / だろう means "probably", a stronger guess.
はず means the speaker expects something based on facts or logic: 3時に着くはずです. でしょう is a more general guess.
よね asks for agreement softly. でしょう? can sound like the answer is obvious, so it may come across as pushy.

mistakes: Adding だ before でしょう: 雨だでしょう is wrong. Say 雨でしょう.
Using だろう when speaking politely: to customers or teachers, 来るだろう sounds rough. Say 来るでしょう or 来ると思います.
Using でしょう? to tell a superior what they should know: 部長、ご存じでしょう? can sound rude. Use ですよね or ご存じですか.

faq.q: What is the difference between でしょう and だろう?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. でしょう is polite and works for everyone. だろう is plain, common in writing, and sounds masculine in casual speech.

faq.q: What is the difference between でしょう and かもしれない?
faq.a: でしょう means probably, so the speaker is fairly sure. かもしれない means might or maybe, so the speaker is less sure.

faq.q: Is でしょ rude?
faq.a: でしょ is casual, not rude, and is used by everyone with friends. But でしょ? can sound like "isn't it obvious?", so tone matters.

intro: じゃない (ja nai) means "is not": it is the casual negative of だ after nouns and な-adjectives, as in 学生じゃない (not a student). At the end of a sentence with the right intonation, it can also mean "isn't it?" or "didn't I?", as in いいじゃない!

formation.example: 学生じゃない, 雨じゃない
静かじゃない, 好きじゃない

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + じゃないです / じゃありません
formation.example: 学生じゃないです, 静かじゃありません
学生ではない

formation.rule: Plain form + じゃない / じゃないですか
formation.example: いいじゃない, 言ったじゃないですか

usage: The basic use is negation. じゃ is a spoken contraction of では, so 学生じゃない is the casual form of 学生ではない. Use じゃないです or じゃありません to be polite, and ではありません in formal speech and writing.
じゃない only negates nouns and な-adjectives. い-adjectives have their own negative: 高い becomes 高くない. Verbs use the ない-form: 行く becomes 行かない.
At the end of a sentence, じゃない can turn a statement into "isn't it?": その服、いいじゃない! (Those clothes look great!). Here it can follow verbs and い-adjectives too, and it is not a negative at all.
じゃないですか is the polite version of that use. だから言ったじゃないですか means "I told you, didn't I?". Using it to state your own opinions too often can sound pushy.

examples.romaji: Watashi wa gakusei ja nai desu.
examples.en: I'm not a student.

examples.romaji: Kono heya, amari shizuka ja nai ne.
examples.en: This room isn't very quiet, is it.

examples.romaji: Sono fuku, ii ja nai!
examples.en: Hey, those clothes look great!

examples.context: A coworker after a mistake you warned about
examples.romaji: Dakara itta ja nai desu ka.
examples.en: I told you so, didn't I?

compare.note: ではない is the full, formal form. じゃない is the spoken contraction. Use ではない in essays and formal writing.
じゃん is an even more casual form of じゃない in its "isn't it?" sense. It never means "is not".
くない is the negative of い-adjectives: 高くない. じゃない is for nouns and な-adjectives: 静かじゃない.

mistakes: Negating an い-adjective with じゃない: 高いじゃない does not mean "not expensive". It means "isn't it expensive!". Say 高くない.
Using じゃないですか to share your own facts with a superior: 私、甘い物が好きじゃないですか sounds like you expect them to know. Say 甘い物が好きなんです.

faq.q: What is the difference between じゃない and ではない?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. じゃない is the casual spoken contraction, and ではない is the full form used in writing and formal speech.

faq.q: What does じゃないですか mean?
faq.a: Usually it means "isn't it?" or "you know", not a negative. 言ったじゃないですか means "I told you, didn't I?". Context and intonation tell you which meaning it has.

faq.q: Is じゃない rude?
faq.a: No. As a negative, じゃない is just casual, and じゃないです is polite. The "isn't it?" use can sound pushy if overused.

intro: じゃん (jan) is a very casual sentence ending that means "isn't it?", "you know" or "see?". It is a short form of じゃない in its "isn't it?" sense, and it goes after the plain form of verbs and adjectives or directly after nouns: いいじゃん, 言ったじゃん, 雨じゃん.

formation.example: 行くじゃん, 言ったじゃん, 来ないじゃん
いいじゃん, 美味しいじゃん

formation.rule: Noun / な-adjective + じゃん (no だ)
formation.example: 雨じゃん, 簡単じゃん

usage: じゃん points out something the speaker thinks is obvious or should be shared: ほら、やっぱり雨じゃん (See, it's raining after all). It often has a "see?" or "come on" feeling.
It also shows surprise at a discovery: 美味しいじゃん、これ! (Hey, this is good!). The speaker did not expect it and wants the listener to notice too.
With a past verb, じゃん can remind someone, sometimes with a little blame: 昨日言ったじゃん (I told you yesterday!).
じゃん is for friends, family and people your age. It is never used with teachers, bosses or customers. The polite way to say the same thing is じゃないですか.

examples.romaji: Oishii jan, kore!
examples.en: Hey, this is good!

examples.romaji: Hora, yappari ame jan.
examples.en: See, it's raining after all.

examples.romaji: Kinou itta jan.
examples.en: I told you yesterday!

examples.context: Talking a friend into going out
examples.romaji: Ii jan, issho ni ikou yo.
examples.en: Oh come on, let's go together.

compare.note: じゃない can mean "is not" or "isn't it?". じゃん only has the "isn't it?" meaning and is more casual.
でしょ also asks for agreement, often in a "right?" tone. じゃん sounds more like "see?" and points to something obvious or newly noticed.
よね checks agreement in a soft, friendly way and works politely as ですよね. じゃん has no polite form.

mistakes: Using じゃん to mean "not": 学生じゃん does not mean "not a student". It means "you're a student, aren't you" or "see, a student". For the negative, say 学生じゃない.
Making it polite with です: ですじゃん is wrong. The polite form is じゃないですか: 美味しいじゃないですか.
Using じゃん with a teacher or boss: it sounds too familiar. Use じゃないですか or ですよね.

faq.q: Is じゃん rude?
faq.a: It is not rude with friends, but it is very casual. With teachers, bosses or people you just met, it sounds too familiar.

faq.q: What is the difference between じゃん and じゃない?
faq.a: じゃん is a casual short form of じゃない in its "isn't it?" sense. じゃない can also mean "is not", but じゃん never does.

faq.q: What does いいじゃん mean?
faq.a: It means "that's nice" or "isn't that great?". It can also mean "come on, what's the harm?" when persuading someone.

meaning: explaining, or asking for an explanation
intro: のです / んです (no desu / n desu) adds an explaining tone: "the thing is..." or "it's that...". It gives a reason, shows surprise, or asks for an explanation. Put it after the plain form, and use なんです after nouns and な-adjectives.

formation.example: 行く → 行くんです, 行った → 行ったんです, 行かない → 行かないんです
痛い → 痛いんです, 高かった → 高かったんです
好き → 好きなんです, 暇 → 暇なんです
学生 → 学生なんです, 雨 → 雨なんです

formation.rule: んだ / のだ, or の in questions
formation.example: 行くんだ, 学生なんだ, どうしたの？

usage: んです links what you say to the situation. 頭が痛いんです does not just state a fact. It explains something, like why you look tired or why you want to leave early.
In questions, んですか asks the listener to explain something you noticed. どうしたんですか (What's wrong?) is asked when someone looks upset. A plain どうしましたか is more neutral, like a doctor asking a patient.
んです is the normal spoken form. のです is more formal and appears in writing and speeches. In casual speech, use んだ in statements and の or んだ in questions: どうしたの？, 何してるんだ？.
It is very common, but do not add it to every sentence. Saying 私はアメリカ人なんです out of nowhere sounds like you are explaining something the listener should already know.

examples.romaji: Doushita n desu ka.
examples.en: What's wrong?

examples.context: Telling your teacher why you need to leave early
examples.romaji: Atama ga itai n desu.
examples.en: I have a headache, you see.

examples.romaji: Jitsu wa, ashita tesuto na n da.
examples.en: Actually, I have a test tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Nihon no bunka ga suki na n desu.
examples.en: The thing is, I really like Japanese culture.

compare.note: です just states a fact politely. んです adds an explanation or connects to the situation. 雨です means "It's rain." 雨なんです means "It's raining, that's the thing."
から states a reason directly. んです implies the reason without a word for "because". The two often combine: 忙しいんですから.

mistakes: Dropping な after nouns and な-adjectives: 好きんです and 学生んです are wrong. Say 好きなんです and 学生なんです.
Using the ます-form before it: 行きますんです is wrong. Use the plain form: 行くんです.
Adding it to plain facts with no context: 私はジョンなんです in a self-introduction sounds like a confession. Say 私はジョンです.

faq.q: What is the difference between です and んです?
faq.a: です states something politely. んです explains it, gives background, or asks for an explanation. The grammar is almost the same, but the feeling is different.

faq.q: Is んです casual?
faq.a: No. んです is polite spoken Japanese. のです is more formal or written. The casual versions are んだ and の.

faq.q: Why do people say どうしたんですか instead of どうしましたか?
faq.a: どうしたんですか reacts to something you noticed, like a worried face, and asks the person to explain. It sounds more caring and personal.

intro: ましょう (mashou) means "let's" in polite Japanese, and ましょうか means "shall I?" or "shall we?". You attach it to the ます-stem of a verb, so 行きます becomes 行きましょう.

formation.example: 行く → 行きましょう, 待つ → 待ちましょう
食べる → 食べましょう, 始める → 始めましょう

formation.rule: し / き + ましょう
formation.example: する → しましょう, 来る → 来ましょう
手伝う → 手伝いましょうか, 開ける → 開けましょうか

usage: ましょう suggests doing something together, or agrees to a plan. 行きましょう can be a suggestion ("Let's go") or a reply to one ("Yes, let's").
ましょうか softens the suggestion into a question. It also offers help: 持ちましょうか means "Shall I carry that for you?"
ましょう is polite. Teachers, guides and announcements use it a lot: 手を洗いましょう on a poster means "Wash your hands." With friends, use the casual volitional form instead: 行こう, 食べよう.
To invite someone, especially a superior, ませんか usually sounds more considerate, because it asks first. Use ましょう once the other person seems to agree.

examples.romaji: Sorosoro ikimashou.
examples.en: Let's get going.

examples.context: Offering help in a stuffy room
examples.romaji: Mado o akemashou ka?
examples.en: Shall I open the window?

examples.romaji: Issho ni shashin o torimashou!
examples.en: Let's take a picture together!

examples.romaji: Dewa, hajimemashou.
examples.en: Well then, let's begin.

compare.note: ませんか invites by asking ("Won't you...?") and leaves room to say no. ましょう assumes you are doing it together.
The volitional form (行こう, 食べよう) is the casual version of ましょう. Use it with friends and family.

mistakes: Attaching it to the dictionary form: 食べるましょう is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 食べましょう.
Using ましょう to invite your boss out of the blue can sound pushy. Ask with ませんか first: 一緒に行きませんか.

faq.q: What is the difference between ましょう and ませんか?
faq.a: ませんか is an invitation that asks what the other person wants. ましょう is a suggestion that assumes agreement. A natural pattern is: 行きませんか → いいですね、行きましょう.

faq.q: What does ましょうか mean?
faq.a: It means "shall I?" or "shall we?". 手伝いましょうか offers help. 何を食べましょうか asks for an opinion about a shared plan.

intro: ませんか (masen ka) makes a polite invitation: "Won't you...?" or "Would you like to...?". It is the negative polite ending ません plus the question marker か, attached to the ます-stem: 行きませんか.

formation.example: 行く → 行きませんか, 休む → 休みませんか
食べる → 食べませんか, 見る → 見ませんか

formation.rule: し / き + ませんか
formation.example: する → しませんか, 来る → 来ませんか
行かない？, 食べない？

usage: Although it uses a negative ending, ませんか is not a negative question here. 映画を見に行きませんか means "Would you like to go see a movie?", not "Aren't you going?"
It is the standard polite way to invite someone. Because it asks what the other person wants, it sounds softer than ましょう. It is safe with coworkers, teachers and people you just met.
A typical reply is いいですね (Sounds good), followed by ましょう: いいですね、行きましょう. To decline politely, people often trail off: すみません、その日はちょっと….
With friends, use the casual ない-form with rising intonation: 行かない？, 食べない？.

examples.context: Asking a coworker about the weekend
examples.romaji: Kondo no shuumatsu, eiga o mi ni ikimasen ka?
examples.en: Would you like to go see a movie this weekend?

examples.romaji: Yokattara, issho ni hirugohan o tabemasen ka?
examples.en: If you like, why don't we have lunch together?

examples.romaji: Sukoshi yasumimasen ka?
examples.en: Shall we take a short break?

examples.romaji: Ocha demo nomimasen ka?
examples.en: Would you like some tea or something?

compare.note: ましょう suggests and assumes agreement. ませんか asks first, so it is the better opener for an invitation.
行かない？ is the casual version for friends. 行かないか is also casual and sounds rougher, more typical of male speech.

mistakes: Answering it like a real negative question: replying はい、行きません to 行きませんか is wrong. Accept with いいですね、行きましょう or はい、ぜひ.
Attaching it to the dictionary form: 行くませんか is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 行きませんか.

faq.q: Why is ませんか negative if it is an invitation?
faq.a: Asking "Won't you...?" is gentler than "Will you...?". It works the same way in English. Japanese uses this pattern as the standard polite invitation.

faq.q: What is the difference between ませんか and ましょうか?
faq.a: ませんか asks whether the other person wants to do something with you. ましょうか asks "shall we?" about a plan, or offers to do something for them.

meaning: do it (firm command from parent or teacher)
intro: なさい (nasai) is a firm but not rude command: "Do it." Parents say it to children, teachers to students, and exams use it in instructions. You attach it to the ます-stem, so 食べます becomes 食べなさい.

formation.example: 書く → 書きなさい, 読む → 読みなさい
食べる → 食べなさい, 寝る → 寝なさい
する → しなさい, 来る → 来なさい
食べな, 早く寝な

usage: なさい comes from someone with authority speaking to someone below them. Think of a parent, a teacher or an older relative. 早く寝なさい is the classic "Go to bed" from a parent.
It is softer and more proper than the plain imperative (食べろ, 寝ろ). It still sounds like an order, so you would never use it to a boss, a customer or a stranger.
Tests and textbooks use it for instructions: 次の質問に答えなさい (Answer the following questions). Here it is neutral, not strict.
In casual speech it can be shortened to the ます-stem + な: 食べな, 寝な. This sounds friendly and a bit rough. Do not confuse it with dictionary form + な (食べるな), which means "don't".

examples.romaji: Hayaku nenasai.
examples.en: Go to bed now.

examples.context: A parent to a child playing games
examples.romaji: Shukudai o shinasai!
examples.en: Do your homework!

examples.romaji: Tsugi no shitsumon ni kotaenasai.
examples.en: Answer the following questions.

examples.context: At dinner with a picky child
examples.romaji: Chanto yasai mo tabenasai.
examples.en: Eat your vegetables too.

compare.note: てください is a polite request you can use with almost anyone. なさい is an order from someone in charge.
食べろ and 行け are blunt and rough. なさい is the more proper, gentler way to give an order.

mistakes: Using なさい to a superior or customer: 待ちなさい to your boss is very rude. Say 待ってください or お待ちください.
Attaching it to the dictionary form: 食べるなさい is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 食べなさい.

faq.q: Is なさい rude?
faq.a: It is not rude between parent and child or teacher and student. It is rude to use it to anyone above you or to strangers, because it is a command.

faq.q: Is おやすみなさい a command?
faq.a: Not in feeling. おやすみなさい is a fixed greeting meaning "good night" and is polite enough to say to anyone. ごめんなさい (I'm sorry) is also a set phrase.

intro: てください (te kudasai) means "please do": a polite request or instruction. You attach ください to the て-form of a verb, so 待つ becomes 待ってください.

formation.example: 待つ → 待ってください, 読む → 読んでください, 書く → 書いてください
食べる → 食べてください, 見る → 見てください

formation.rule: して / 来て + ください
formation.example: する → してください, 来る → 来てください
待って, 見て, 来て

usage: てください is the standard polite way to ask someone to do something. You hear it in shops, offices and classrooms: ここに名前を書いてください.
It is polite, but it is still a request or an instruction. Staff use it with customers to give directions, and hosts use it to offer things: どうぞ、座ってください.
For a real favor from a boss or someone you do not know, more polite forms sound better: ていただけますか or てくださいませんか.
With friends and family, drop ください and just use the て-form: ちょっと待って, 見て見て.

examples.context: On the phone, looking for something
examples.romaji: Chotto matte kudasai.
examples.en: Please wait a moment.

examples.romaji: Mou ichido itte kudasai.
examples.en: Please say that again.

examples.romaji: Koko ni namae o kaite kudasai.
examples.en: Please write your name here.

examples.context: A host serving dinner to guests
examples.romaji: Douzo, takusan tabete kudasai.
examples.en: Please, help yourself to plenty.

compare.note: Noun + をください means "please give me": 水をください. てください asks someone to do an action.
More polite and humble. Use it when asking a favor of a boss, a client or a stranger.
なさい is a command from a parent or teacher. てください is a polite request.

mistakes: Getting the て-form wrong: 待つてください and 書きてください are wrong. Say 待ってください and 書いてください.
Using てください for a big favor from your boss: 推薦状を書いてください can sound like an order. Try 書いていただけませんか.

faq.q: Is てください polite enough for a boss?
faq.a: For simple, expected requests, yes. For a personal favor, use ていただけますか or ていただけませんか, which sound more humble.

faq.q: What is the casual way to say てください?
faq.a: Use the て-form alone: 待って, 見て, 手伝って. Adding ね or よ softens it: 待ってね.

intro: ないでください (naide kudasai) means "please don't": a polite way to ask someone not to do something. You attach でください to the ない-form of a verb, so 吸う becomes 吸わないでください.

formation.example: 吸う → 吸わないでください, 撮る → 撮らないでください
忘れる → 忘れないでください, 見る → 見ないでください

formation.rule: しない / 来ない + でください
formation.example: する → しないでください, 来る → 来ないでください
忘れないで, 心配しないで

usage: ないでください is the polite negative request. It is the opposite of てください: 見てください (please look) and 見ないでください (please don't look).
You see it on signs and hear it from staff: ここでタバコを吸わないでください, 写真を撮らないでください. It is polite but clear.
It is also used kindly, to comfort or care for someone: 心配しないでください (please don't worry), 無理しないでください (don't push yourself).
With friends, drop ください: 忘れないで, 行かないで. Adding ね makes it gentle: 無理しないでね.

examples.context: A staff member at a station
examples.romaji: Koko de tabako o suwanaide kudasai.
examples.en: Please don't smoke here.

examples.context: Reassuring a client after a problem
examples.romaji: Shinpai shinaide kudasai.
examples.en: Please don't worry.

examples.romaji: Shashin o toranaide kudasai.
examples.en: Please don't take photos.

examples.context: To a coworker who has a cold
examples.romaji: Muri shinaide kudasai ne.
examples.en: Don't push yourself too hard, okay?

compare.note: てはいけない states a rule: "you must not". ないでください is a request, so it sounds softer.
Dictionary form + な (吸うな) is a blunt order. ないでください is the polite way to say the same thing.

mistakes: Using なくて instead of ないで: 行かなくてください is wrong. Say 行かないでください.
Attaching ないで to the dictionary form: 吸うないでください is wrong. Use the ない-form: 吸わないでください.

faq.q: What is the casual way to say ないでください?
faq.a: Drop ください: 行かないで, 忘れないで. It sounds soft and is very common with friends and family.

faq.q: What is the difference between ないでください and てはいけない?
faq.a: ないでください asks someone not to do something. てはいけない says it is not allowed. Teachers and rules use てはいけない, while staff and signs usually use ないでください.
