intro: な (na) after the dictionary form of a verb means "don't!": a blunt, strong prohibition. 動くな means "Don't move!" You simply add な to the dictionary form, so 行く becomes 行くな.

formation.example: 行く → 行くな, 動く → 動くな, 触る → 触るな
忘れる → 忘れるな, 諦める → 諦めるな
する → するな, 来る → 来るな
忘れるなよ, 無理するなよ

usage: This な is the negative of the imperative form. Where 行け means "Go!", 行くな means "Don't go!" It is short, strong and direct.
It is mostly used by men, by people in authority, in emergencies, and in sports or action scenes: 動くな！, 諦めるな！. Between close friends it can sound caring rather than harsh, especially with よ: 無理するなよ.
You also see it on warning signs and in slogans, where it acts like "Do not...". In everyday polite speech, use ないでください instead.
Do not mix it up with ます-stem + な (食べな), which is a casual short form of なさい and means "eat". The dictionary form is what makes it "don't".

examples.context: A police officer in a TV drama
examples.romaji: Ugoku na!
examples.en: Don't move!

examples.context: An older brother to a younger one
examples.romaji: Shinpai suru na.
examples.en: Don't worry.

examples.context: A friend reminding you about tomorrow
examples.romaji: Wasureru na yo.
examples.en: Don't forget, okay?

examples.context: A coach shouting to the team
examples.romaji: Saigo made akirameru na!
examples.en: Don't give up until the end!

compare.note: The polite request "please don't". Use it with anyone you are not very close to.
This is a short form of なさい and means "do it". 食べな means "eat", but 食べるな means "don't eat".
行かないで is a casual "don't go" that sounds soft or pleading. 行くな is a firm order.

mistakes: Adding な to the ない-form: 行かないな is wrong for "don't go". Use the dictionary form: 行くな.
Using it with people above you: 遅れるな to your teacher is very rude. Say 遅れないでください.

faq.q: Is な rude?
faq.a: It is blunt and sounds like an order. It is fine between close friends or in emergencies, but rude toward superiors, customers or strangers.

faq.q: What is the difference between 食べな and 食べるな?
faq.a: 食べな (ます-stem + な) means "eat" and is a casual form of 食べなさい. 食べるな (dictionary form + な) means "don't eat".

faq.q: Is this the same な as in いいな?
faq.a: No. いいな and きれいだな use a different sentence-ending な that shows feeling, like "I wish" or "wow". It comes after adjectives and sentences, not as a prohibition.

intro: 〜よう / 〜おう (you / ou) is the volitional form, the casual way to say "let's" or "I'll". Group 2 verbs drop る and add よう (食べよう), and Group 1 verbs change the last sound to an o-sound plus う (行こう).

formation.example: 行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう, 買う → 買おう, 帰る → 帰ろう
食べる → 食べよう, 見る → 見よう

formation.rule: する → しよう, 来る → 来よう (こよう)
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強しよう
行こうと思う, 留学しようと思っています

usage: On its own, the volitional form is a casual "let's": 行こう！, 食べよう！. It is the plain version of ましょう, used with friends and family.
It also expresses your own will or decision, often when talking to yourself: よし、頑張ろう (Alright, I'll do my best).
With か it asks "shall we?" or wonders "should I?": 何を食べようか, どうしようかな.
ようと思う means "I'm thinking of doing". It is a common way to talk about plans and is fine in polite speech: 来年、留学しようと思っています.

examples.romaji: Issho ni kaerou.
examples.en: Let's go home together.

examples.context: Deciding on dinner with your partner
examples.romaji: Nani o tabeyou ka?
examples.en: What should we eat?

examples.context: Telling a teacher about your plans
examples.romaji: Rainen, Nihon ni ryuugaku shiyou to omotte imasu.
examples.en: I'm thinking of studying abroad in Japan next year.

examples.romaji: Yoshi, ganbarou!
examples.en: Alright, let's do our best!

compare.note: ましょう is the polite version: 行きましょう. 行こう is the same idea in casual speech.
つもり states a firm plan. ようと思う sounds like a plan you are still thinking about.

mistakes: Using the Group 2 pattern on Group 1 verbs: 行きよう and 帰よう are wrong. Say 行こう and 帰ろう.
Using the Group 1 pattern on Group 2 verbs: 食べろう is wrong. Say 食べよう.
Using 行こう with your boss. Use the polite 行きましょう or ask 行きませんか.

faq.q: What does ようと思う mean?
faq.a: It means "I'm thinking of doing" or "I plan to". 日本語を勉強しようと思う means "I'm thinking of studying Japanese."

faq.q: What is the difference between よう and ましょう?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. よう / おう is casual, and ましょう is polite.

intro: The て-form (te form) is the connecting form of verbs and adjectives. It links actions ("and"), makes requests (てください), and builds many patterns like ている. Group 2 verbs just drop る and add て, while Group 1 verbs change their ending by rule.

formation.when: Group 1 ending in う, つ, る
formation.rule: う / つ / る → って
formation.example: 買う → 買って, 待つ → 待って, 帰る → 帰って

formation.when: Group 1 ending in む, ぶ, ぬ
formation.rule: む / ぶ / ぬ → んで
formation.example: 読む → 読んで, 遊ぶ → 遊んで, 死ぬ → 死んで

formation.when: Group 1 ending in く, ぐ, す
formation.rule: く → いて, ぐ → いで, す → して
formation.example: 書く → 書いて, 泳ぐ → 泳いで, 話す → 話して (but 行く → 行って)

formation.rule: drop る + て; する → して, 来る → 来て (きて)
formation.example: 食べる → 食べて, 見る → 見て, 勉強する → 勉強して

formation.rule: い-adjective: い → くて; な-adjective and noun + で
formation.example: 安い → 安くて, いい → よくて, 静か → 静かで, 学生 → 学生で

usage: The て-form joins actions in order: 朝ご飯を食べて、学校に行きました (I ate breakfast and went to school). The tense comes only at the end of the sentence.
It is the base for many common patterns: てください (please do), ている (be doing), てもいい (may), てはいけない (must not), てから (after), てしまう, てみる and more.
On its own at the end of a sentence, it is a casual request: ちょっと見て！ (Look at this!). Friends and family use this all the time.

With adjectives and nouns, て joins descriptions: 安くておいしい (cheap and tasty), 静かできれい (quiet and pretty). The sound changes for Group 1 verbs are the same as for the た-form, so learning one gives you the other.

examples.romaji: Asagohan o tabete, gakkou ni ikimashita.
examples.en: I ate breakfast and went to school.

examples.context: Showing a friend something on your phone
examples.romaji: Chotto mite!
examples.en: Look at this!

examples.romaji: Ima, ame ga futte imasu.
examples.en: It's raining now.

examples.romaji: Kono mise wa yasukute oishii desu.
examples.en: This place is cheap and tasty.

compare.note: The た-form has exactly the same sound changes: 書いて and 書いた, 読んで and 読んだ. Replace て / で with た / だ.
Plain て links actions in order. てから stresses "after doing A, then B".

mistakes: Using the く rule on 行く: 行いて is wrong. 行く is the one exception: 行って.
Treating Group 1 る verbs as Group 2: 帰て and 走て are wrong. 帰る and 走る are Group 1, so they become 帰って and 走って.
Adding で to い-adjectives: 高いで is wrong. Change い to くて: 高くて.

faq.q: How do I know if a verb is Group 1 or Group 2?
faq.a: Verbs ending in る after an i-sound or e-sound (食べる, 見る) are usually Group 2. Everything else is Group 1. Some exceptions, like 帰る, 入る and 走る, are Group 1 and must be memorized.

faq.q: Does the て-form have a tense?
faq.a: No. The tense comes from the last verb in the sentence. 食べて寝る is present and 食べて寝た is past.

faq.q: Is ending a sentence with the て-form rude?
faq.a: It is casual, not rude. 待って is fine with friends. With people you should be polite to, add ください.

intro: The ます-form (masu form) is the polite form of Japanese verbs. You use it with people you don't know well, at work and with teachers. Group 2 verbs drop る and add ます, and Group 1 verbs change the last sound to an i-sound plus ます.

formation.example: 書く → 書きます, 飲む → 飲みます, 話す → 話します, 帰る → 帰ります
食べる → 食べます, 見る → 見ます

formation.rule: する → します, 来る → 来ます (きます)
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強します

formation.rule: ます / ません / ました / ませんでした
formation.example: 行きます, 行きません, 行きました, 行きませんでした

usage: The ます-form is the default polite style. Learners usually start with it because it is safe in almost any situation: with strangers, shop staff, coworkers and teachers.
It has four basic forms: ます (do, will do), ません (don't), ました (did) and ませんでした (didn't). ます also covers the future: 明日行きます means "I'll go tomorrow."
The part before ます is called the ます-stem (食べ, 書き). Many patterns attach to it, such as ながら, たい, なさい, やすい and ましょう.
With close friends and family, people switch to the plain form (食べる, 食べた). Inside a sentence, before a noun or と思う, the plain form is used even in polite speech.

examples.romaji: Maiasa koohii o nomimasu.
examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.

examples.context: Explaining your diet to a host
examples.romaji: Niku wa tabemasen.
examples.en: I don't eat meat.

examples.romaji: Kinou, tomodachi ni aimashita.
examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.

examples.romaji: Sumimasen, yoku wakarimasen deshita.
examples.en: Sorry, I didn't really understand.

compare.note: The plain form (食べる, 食べた) means the same thing in casual speech. The ます-form is the polite version.
The ます-form is basic politeness. Keigo goes further with special verbs like いらっしゃる and 申す.

mistakes: Treating Group 2 verbs like Group 1: 食べります is wrong. Say 食べます.
Treating Group 1 る verbs like Group 2: 帰ます is wrong. 帰る is Group 1, so it is 帰ります.
Using the ます-form before a noun: 昨日買いました本 is wrong. Use the plain form: 昨日買った本.

faq.q: What is the ます-stem?
faq.a: It is the verb without ます: 食べ from 食べます, 書き from 書きます. Many grammar patterns attach to it, like ながら, たい and なさい.

faq.q: When should I use the ます-form?
faq.a: With people you don't know well, at work, with teachers, and with anyone older or higher in rank. Use the plain form with close friends and family.

meaning: casual form of verbs, adjectives and だ
intro: The plain form (futsuukei, 普通形) is the casual form of Japanese verbs, adjectives and だ, such as 行く, 行かない, 行った and 学生だ. It is used with friends and family, in writing, and inside longer sentences. Verbs use the dictionary form, ない-form and た-form, and nouns and な-adjectives use だ.

formation.rule: dictionary / ない / た / なかった
formation.example: 行く, 行かない, 行った, 行かなかった

formation.rule: い / くない / かった / くなかった
formation.example: 高い, 高くない, 高かった, 高くなかった

formation.rule: だ / じゃない / だった / じゃなかった
formation.example: 静かだ, 静かじゃない, 静かだった, 静かじゃなかった

formation.rule: だ / じゃない / だった / じゃなかった
formation.example: 学生だ, 学生じゃない, 学生だった, 学生じゃなかった

usage: Plain forms are how people talk to friends, family and children. 明日行く？ (Are you going tomorrow?) is the casual version of 明日行きますか.
Newspapers, essays, diaries and novels also use plain forms. Formal writing often uses である instead of だ.
Inside a sentence, plain forms are used even when the sentence is polite. Before a noun (昨日買った本), before と思う, かもしれない, から and many other patterns, you need the plain form.
In casual speech, だ is often dropped, especially in questions and softer speech: 学生？ rather than 学生だ？. Ending a sentence with a bare だ can sound blunt.

examples.romaji: Ashita, eiga o mi ni iku?
examples.en: Are you going to see a movie tomorrow?

examples.romaji: Kyou wa sugoku atsukatta.
examples.en: It was really hot today.

examples.romaji: Kare wa mada gakusei da yo.
examples.en: He's still a student, you know.

examples.romaji: Kore wa kinou katta hon desu.
examples.en: This is the book I bought yesterday.

compare.note: The ます-form is the polite version: 行きます, 行きません, 行きました. The plain form is casual.
だ is the plain version of です. Unlike です, だ does not follow い-adjectives: 高いだ is wrong, 高い is enough.

mistakes: Adding だ after an い-adjective: 高いだ is wrong. The plain form is just 高い.
Using plain forms with your boss or a stranger. It can sound rude. Use です / ます.
Using polite forms inside a clause: 行きますと思います is wrong. Say 行くと思います.

faq.q: Is the plain form rude?
faq.a: Not with friends and family, where it is normal. With strangers, customers or superiors, it can sound rude or too familiar.

faq.q: What is the difference between the plain form and the dictionary form?
faq.a: The dictionary form (行く) is one of the plain forms: the present positive of a verb. The plain form also includes 行かない, 行った and 行かなかった.

intro: The た-form (ta form) is the plain past tense of Japanese verbs and adjectives: 食べた means "ate". It follows the same sound changes as the て-form, with た / だ in place of て / で, so 書いて becomes 書いた.

formation.when: Group 1 ending in う, つ, る
formation.rule: う / つ / る → った
formation.example: 買う → 買った, 待つ → 待った, 帰る → 帰った

formation.when: Group 1 ending in む, ぶ, ぬ
formation.rule: む / ぶ / ぬ → んだ
formation.example: 読む → 読んだ, 遊ぶ → 遊んだ, 死ぬ → 死んだ

formation.when: Group 1 ending in く, ぐ, す
formation.rule: く → いた, ぐ → いだ, す → した
formation.example: 書く → 書いた, 泳ぐ → 泳いだ, 話す → 話した (but 行く → 行った)

formation.rule: drop る + た; する → した, 来る → 来た (きた)
formation.example: 食べる → 食べた, 見る → 見た, 勉強する → 勉強した

formation.rule: い → かった; な-adjective and noun + だった
formation.example: 高い → 高かった, いい → よかった, 静か → 静かだった, 雨 → 雨だった

usage: The た-form is the casual past: 昨日映画を見た (I saw a movie yesterday). The polite version is ました: 見ました.
It also shows that something has just happened or is completed: あ、バスが来た！ (Oh, the bus is here!), もう食べた (I already ate).
Before a noun, it describes something in the past, even in polite sentences: 昨日買った本 (the book I bought yesterday).
Many patterns are built on it: たことがある (have done before), たら (if, when), たり〜たり (things like), たほうがいい (you should).

examples.context: Chatting with a friend on Monday
examples.romaji: Kinou, nani shita?
examples.en: What did you do yesterday?

examples.context: Telling a friend about a bad day
examples.romaji: Eki de saifu o nakushita.
examples.en: I lost my wallet at the station.

examples.romaji: A, basu ga kita!
examples.en: Oh, the bus is here!

examples.romaji: Nihon ni itta koto ga arimasu ka?
examples.en: Have you ever been to Japan?

compare.note: ました is the polite past: 食べました. た is the casual past: 食べた. Before nouns, only た is used.
The て-form has the same sound changes. If you know 読んで, you know 読んだ.

mistakes: Using the く rule on 行く: 行いた is wrong. Say 行った.
Adding かった to な-adjectives: 静かかった is wrong. Use だった: 静かだった.
Reading 来た as こた. It is きた.

faq.q: Does the た-form always mean past?
faq.a: Mostly, but it can also show completion or a realization: あった！ (Found it!) or バスが来た (The bus is here). Before a noun, it can describe a state: 太った猫 (a fat cat).

faq.q: What is the difference between た and ました?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. た is casual and ました is polite. Inside a sentence, before a noun or と思う, use た even in polite speech.

intro: The ない-form (nai form) is the plain negative of a verb: 行かない means "don't go" or "won't go". Group 2 verbs drop る and add ない, and Group 1 verbs change the last sound to an a-sound plus ない. Verbs ending in う change to わ: 買う → 買わない.

formation.rule: last u-sound → a-sound + ない (う → わ)
formation.example: 書く → 書かない, 飲む → 飲まない, 帰る → 帰らない, 買う → 買わない
食べる → 食べない, 見る → 見ない

formation.rule: する → しない, 来る → 来ない (こない), ある → ない
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強しない
行かなかった, 食べなかった, 来なかった

formation.rule: い → くない; な-adjective and noun + じゃない
formation.example: 高い → 高くない, いい → よくない, 静か → 静かじゃない, 学生 → 学生じゃない

usage: The ない-form is the casual negative: 分からない (I don't understand). The polite version is ません: 分かりません.
With rising intonation, it becomes a casual invitation: 一緒に食べない？ (Want to eat together?). This is the casual version of ませんか.
ない conjugates like an い-adjective: ない, なかった, なくて, なければ. Many patterns are built on it: ないでください, なければならない, なくてもいい, ないほうがいい.
In polite sentences, the ない-form still appears inside clauses and before でしょう or と思う: 雨は降らないでしょう.

examples.context: A friend explains a math problem
examples.romaji: Zenzen wakaranai.
examples.en: I don't get it at all.

examples.romaji: Issho ni tabenai?
examples.en: Want to eat together?

examples.romaji: Kinou wa dare mo konakatta.
examples.en: Nobody came yesterday.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furanai deshou.
examples.en: It probably won't rain tomorrow.

compare.note: ません is the polite negative: 行きません. ない is casual: 行かない.
ないで links "without doing" or makes a casual "don't": 忘れないで. The ない-form ends the sentence or modifies a noun.

mistakes: Forgetting the わ for う verbs: 買あない is wrong. Say 買わない.
Making a ない-form for ある: あらない is wrong. The negative of ある is just ない.
Reading 来ない as きない. It is こない.

faq.q: How do I make the negative in polite speech?
faq.a: Use ません with the ます-stem: 行きません, 食べません. The past is ませんでした.

faq.q: Why does 一緒に食べない？ mean an invitation?
faq.a: With rising intonation, a negative question works like "Won't you...?" in English. It is the casual version of 食べませんか.

intro: The potential form (rareru / eru) means "can": 話せる means "can speak" and 食べられる means "can eat". Group 1 verbs change the last sound to an e-sound plus る, Group 2 verbs drop る and add られる, and する becomes できる.

formation.example: 書く → 書ける, 話す → 話せる, 飲む → 飲める, 買う → 買える
食べる → 食べられる, 見る → 見られる, 起きる → 起きられる

formation.rule: する → できる, 来る → 来られる (こられる)
formation.example: 運転する → 運転できる
書けない, 書けます, 書けません, 食べられない

usage: The potential form talks about ability (日本語が話せる) and about whether something is possible in a situation (明日は来られない).
The object particle を often changes to が: 日本語を話す becomes 日本語が話せる. Both are heard, but が is the textbook choice.
In casual speech, many people drop ら from Group 2 verbs and say 食べれる or 来れる. This is very common, but 食べられる is still the standard form, especially in writing.
ことができる means the same thing and sounds more formal. 見える and 聞こえる mean that something is visible or audible by itself, while 見られる and 聞ける mean you are able to see or hear it.

examples.romaji: Nihongo ga sukoshi hanasemasu.
examples.en: I can speak a little Japanese.

examples.context: Ordering at a restaurant with a friend
examples.romaji: Karai mono wa taberarenai.
examples.en: I can't eat spicy food.

examples.context: Planning a party with a friend
examples.romaji: Ashita, korareru?
examples.en: Can you come tomorrow?

examples.romaji: Unten dekimasu ka?
examples.en: Can you drive?

compare.note: Dictionary form + ことができる also means "can", but it is longer and more formal. 話せる and 話すことができる mean the same thing.
For Group 2 verbs, the potential and passive look the same: 食べられる can mean "can eat" or "be eaten". Context tells you which.
見える means something is visible: 富士山が見える. 見られる means you are able to see it, for example because of time or place.

mistakes: Adding れる to Group 1 potentials: 書けれる is wrong. The potential of 書く is 書ける.
Making a potential of する with られる: 勉強しられる is wrong. Use できる: 勉強できる.
Writing 食べれる in formal writing. It is common in speech, but use 食べられる in essays and business writing.

faq.q: Is 食べれる wrong?
faq.a: It is called ら抜き (ra-less) Japanese. It is very common in everyday speech and many people use it, but it is still considered nonstandard in formal writing. Use 食べられる to be safe.

faq.q: What is the difference between the potential form and ことができる?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. The potential form is shorter and more common in conversation. ことができる sounds more formal and is common in writing.

intro: The passive form (られる / れる, rareru / reru) turns "do" into "be done": 先生がほめた (the teacher praised) becomes 先生にほめられた (I was praised by the teacher). Group 1 verbs change the final -u to -a and add れる, Group 2 verbs drop る and add られる, and the person doing the action is marked with に.

formation.example: 書く → 書かれる, 読む → 読まれる, 言う → 言われる
食べる → 食べられる, 見る → 見られる

formation.rule: する → される, 来る → 来られる (こられる)
formation.example: 紹介する → 紹介される

formation.rule: the new verb is a Group 2 verb
formation.example: 書かれる → 書かれた, 書かれない, 書かれます

usage: The basic use is the direct passive. The subject receives the action, and the doer is marked with に: 弟は母に叱られた means my brother was scolded by my mom.

Japanese also has an "adversative" or suffering passive. It shows that something happened to you and you were bothered by it, even with verbs that have no object: 雨に降られた (I got rained on), 隣の人にたばこを吸われた (the person next to me smoked, and it bothered me). This use is very common in daily conversation.

In news, notices and writing, the passive is used when the doer is unknown or not important: このお寺は800年前に建てられた (this temple was built 800 years ago). Here the doer is often left out, or marked with によって in formal writing.

For Group 2 verbs and 来る, the passive looks exactly like the potential form: 食べられる can mean "can eat" or "be eaten". It is also the same as a light respectful form: 先生が来られる means "the teacher comes" said politely. Context tells you which one is meant.

examples.romaji: Sensei ni homeraremashita.
examples.en: I was praised by the teacher.

examples.romaji: Densha de ashi o fumareta.
examples.en: Someone stepped on my foot on the train.

examples.romaji: Ame ni furarete, bishobisho ni natta.
examples.en: I got caught in the rain and got soaked.

examples.romaji: Kono uta wa sekaijuu de utawarete iru.
examples.en: This song is sung all over the world.

compare.note: For Group 2 verbs the shapes are the same. 魚が食べられる usually means "I can eat fish", while 魚に食べられる means "be eaten by a fish". The particles and context decide.
The passive means something was done to you. The causative-passive means someone made you do something: 待たれた (someone waited for me) vs 待たされた (I was made to wait).

mistakes: Marking the doer with で or が: 先生でほめられた is wrong. Use に: 先生にほめられた.
Adding られる to a Group 1 verb: 書かられる is wrong. Group 1 takes れる after the -a sound: 書かれる.
Forgetting that う becomes わ: 言あれる is wrong. Say 言われる.

faq.q: Why does Japanese use the passive for bad things?
faq.a: The suffering passive is a normal part of Japanese. It shows that an event affected you, usually in a bad way: 子どもに泣かれた means the child cried and it was a problem for me. English has no direct equivalent, so it is often translated with "on me" or "I had someone do...".

faq.q: How do I tell passive られる from potential られる?
faq.a: Look at the particles and the situation. A doer marked with に points to the passive. が on the thing and no doer usually points to the potential. Group 1 verbs have different shapes: 読まれる is passive, 読める is potential.

faq.q: Is the passive form polite?
faq.a: The passive itself is neutral. The same shape can also be used as a light respectful form, as in 部長が来られました (the manager has come). This respectful use is common in business.

intro: The causative form (させる / せる, saseru / seru) means "make someone do" or "let someone do": 子どもに野菜を食べさせる means to make (or let) a child eat vegetables. Group 1 verbs change the final -u to -a and add せる, Group 2 verbs drop る and add させる.

formation.example: 行く → 行かせる, 待つ → 待たせる, 買う → 買わせる
食べる → 食べさせる, 見る → 見させる

formation.rule: する → させる, 来る → 来させる (こさせる)
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強させる

formation.rule: the new verb is a Group 2 verb
formation.example: 行かせる → 行かせた, 行かせない, 行かせて

usage: The causative covers both "make" (force) and "let" (allow). 母は弟に野菜を食べさせた can mean my mom made my brother eat vegetables, and 子どもを公園で遊ばせた means I let the kids play in the park. Context and tone decide which one is meant.

The person who is made or allowed to act is marked with に or を. With a verb that already has an object (を), use に: 学生に本を読ませる. With a verb without an object, を often sounds like forcing and に like allowing: 子どもを行かせる vs 子どもに行かせる.
させてください and させていただけますか ask for permission: "please let me do it". 少し考えさせてください (let me think about it) is very common, and させていただきます is a humble way to say "I will do" in business.
With feeling verbs, the causative means to cause an emotion: 心配させる (make someone worry), 笑わせる (make someone laugh). The set phrase お待たせしました (sorry to keep you waiting) also comes from 待たせる.

examples.romaji: Haha wa otouto ni yasai o tabesaseta.
examples.en: My mom made my little brother eat vegetables.

examples.romaji: Sukoshi kangaesasete kudasai.
examples.en: Please let me think about it a little.

examples.romaji: Omatase shimashita.
examples.en: Sorry to keep you waiting.

examples.romaji: Buchou wa shain o mainichi osoku made hatarakasete iru.
examples.en: The manager makes the staff work until late every day.

compare.note: させる is from the side of the person giving the order: 母が私に掃除させた. させられる is from the side of the person who had to do it: 私は母に掃除させられた (I was made to clean by my mom).
てもらう asks someone for a favor and sounds friendly. Using させる toward a superior or a friend can sound like you are giving orders: 先生に説明してもらった, not 先生に説明させた.

mistakes: Using the potential shape: 食べらせる is wrong. Group 2 takes させる: 食べさせる.
Adding させる to a Group 1 verb: 行かさせる is heard in speech but is considered incorrect. The standard form is 行かせる.
Using it for people above you: 社長に書類を読ませた sounds like you forced the president. Say 社長に書類を読んでいただいた.

faq.q: Does させる mean make or let?
faq.a: Both. Japanese uses one form for forcing and for allowing. Phrases like させてください (please let me) are clearly "let", while scolding or complaining contexts usually mean "make".

faq.q: What does させてください mean?
faq.a: It means "please let me do". 私にやらせてください is "please let me do it". It is polite and used a lot at work and with people you respect.

faq.q: What is the short form 行かす?
faq.a: In casual speech, Group 1 verbs sometimes use a shorter causative ending in す: 行かす, 待たす. It means the same as 行かせる, but it sounds more colloquial.

meaning: be made to do (against your will)
intro: The causative-passive (させられる, saserareru) means "be made to do something", usually something you did not want to do. It combines the causative (させる) and the passive (られる): 飲む → 飲ませられる, often shortened to 飲まされる. The person who made you do it is marked with に.

formation.rule: -a + せられる, or the short form -a + される
formation.example: 飲む → 飲ませられる / 飲まされる, 待つ → 待たせられる / 待たされる

formation.rule: only -a + せられる (no short form)
formation.example: 話す → 話させられる, 出す → 出させられる

formation.rule: drop る + させられる
formation.example: 食べる → 食べさせられる, 覚える → 覚えさせられる

formation.rule: する → させられる, 来る → 来させられる (こさせられる)
formation.example: 掃除する → 掃除させられる

usage: This form tells the story from the side of the person who had to do the action. 私は母に部屋を掃除させられた means my mom made me clean my room, and it shows I did not want to.
Because of this, it often carries a complaining tone. People use it to talk about school, part-time jobs, drinking parties and strict parents: 先輩に飲まされた, 店長に残業させられた.
For Group 1 verbs, the short form (飲まされる, 待たされる, 歌わされる) is much more common in speech than the long form. The long form appears more in writing.
A few verbs of thinking and feeling use it in a positive way: 考えさせられる (be made to think, find something thought-provoking), 感動させられる (be moved). These are common in reviews.

examples.romaji: Kodomo no koro, mainichi piano o renshuu saserareta.
examples.en: When I was a kid, I was made to practice piano every day.

examples.context: The morning after a work party
examples.romaji: Nomikai de senpai ni osake o nomasareta.
examples.en: My senpai made me drink at the party.

examples.context: Complaining to a friend who was late
examples.romaji: Eki de ichijikan mo matasareta yo.
examples.en: I was kept waiting at the station for a whole hour.

examples.romaji: Kono eiga ni wa kangaesaseraremashita.
examples.en: This movie really made me think.

compare.note: The passive means someone did something to you: 母に叱られた (I was scolded by my mom). The causative-passive means you were made to do it yourself: 母に謝らされた (my mom made me apologize).
させる is said by or about the person giving the order: 先輩が後輩に飲ませた. させられる is said about the person who had to obey: 後輩は先輩に飲まされた.

mistakes: Using the short form with す verbs: 話さされる is wrong. Use the long form: 話させられる.
Dropping ら: 食べさせれる is wrong in standard Japanese. Say 食べさせられる.
Mixing up the direction: 母に野菜を食べさせた means I made my mom eat vegetables. If your mom made you, say 母に野菜を食べさせられた.

faq.q: What is the difference between 飲ませられる and 飲まされる?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 飲まされる is the short form for Group 1 verbs and is more common in conversation. 飲ませられる is the full form and sounds a little more formal.

faq.q: Is させられる always negative?
faq.a: Usually it shows you did something unwillingly. With verbs like 考える or 感動する, though, it can be positive: この本には考えさせられた means the book made me think.

intro: The imperative form (命令形, meireikei) is the blunt command form, like 行け (go!) or 食べろ (eat!). Group 1 verbs change the final -u to -e, Group 2 verbs swap る for ろ, and する and 来る become しろ and 来い (こい). It sounds strong and is mostly used in casual, emotional or urgent speech.

formation.example: 行く → 行け, 待つ → 待て, 言う → 言え, がんばる → がんばれ
食べる → 食べろ, 見る → 見ろ, 起きる → 起きろ

formation.rule: する → しろ, 来る → 来い (こい)
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強しろ

formation.rule: Group 2 and する: よ instead of ろ
formation.example: 答える → 答えよ, する → せよ
行く → 行くな, 見る → 見るな

usage: The imperative is very direct. You hear it from coaches, angry parents, people in an emergency, and between close male friends. Said to a stranger or a superior it is rude.
Some uses are not rude at all. がんばれ (go for it!) is a cheer, and road signs say 止まれ (stop). Exam questions use the written style, like 次の問いに答えよ (answer the following questions).
It is also normal when quoting a command: 父に「早く寝ろ」と言われた (my dad told me to go to bed). Here you are only reporting what was said.
For everyday requests, softer forms are used instead: て (待って), てください (待ってください), or なさい (待ちなさい), which parents and teachers use.

examples.context: A parent waking up a teenager
examples.romaji: Hayaku okiro!
examples.en: Get up already!

examples.romaji: Ganbare!
examples.en: Go for it!

examples.romaji: Abunai! Nigero!
examples.en: Watch out! Run!

examples.context: Telling a friend about your dad
examples.romaji: Chichi ni "benkyou shiro" to iwareta.
examples.en: My dad told me to study.

compare.note: なさい (食べなさい) is a firm but standard command used by parents and teachers. The imperative (食べろ) is much rougher.
てください is a polite request: 待ってください (please wait). The imperative 待て is a blunt order.
The imperative tells someone to do something. Dictionary form + な tells them not to: 行け (go!) vs 行くな (don't go!).

mistakes: Using the wrong form for 来る: 来ろ is wrong. The imperative is 来い (こい).
Making する like a Group 1 verb: すれ is wrong. Say しろ.
Using it as a normal request: 先生、ちょっと待て is very rude. Say 先生、ちょっと待ってください.

faq.q: Is the imperative form rude?
faq.a: Usually, yes, when said directly to someone. It is fine in cheers like がんばれ, on signs, in quoted speech, and between close friends who talk roughly. In most situations, use て or てください instead.

faq.q: Do women use the imperative form?
faq.a: It is used more by men in casual speech. Women tend to use softer forms like て or なさい, but anyone can say がんばれ or use it in an emergency.

faq.q: What does がんばれ mean?
faq.a: It is the imperative of がんばる (to do your best). It means "go for it" or "hang in there" and is a friendly cheer, not a rude order.

intro: 敬語 (keigo) is Japanese honorific speech. It has three parts: respectful language (尊敬語, sonkeigo) that raises the other person's actions, humble language (謙譲語, kenjougo) that lowers your own, and polite language (丁寧語, teineigo), which is です and ます. Each part has regular patterns like お〜になる and お〜する, plus special verbs like いらっしゃる and 参る.

formation.rule: お + ます-stem + になる
formation.example: 待つ → お待ちになる, 帰る → お帰りになる
いる / 行く / 来る → いらっしゃる, 言う → おっしゃる, 食べる → 召し上がる, する → なさる, 見る → ご覧になる

formation.rule: お / ご + ます-stem or noun + する
formation.example: 持つ → お持ちする, 案内する → ご案内する
行く / 来る → 参る, いる → おる, 言う → 申す, 食べる → いただく, する → いたす, 見る → 拝見する
行く → 行きます, 学生だ → 学生です

usage: Use respectful language for what customers, teachers, bosses and other people above you do: 社長がいらっしゃいました (the president has arrived). Use humble language for what you do for them: 私がご案内します (I will show you the way).

Who counts as "you" and "them" depends on the group. When talking to someone from outside your company, your own boss is part of your side, so you use humble language and drop the title: 田中はただいま外出しております (Tanaka is out at the moment).
You hear keigo all the time in shops, on the phone, in business emails and in announcements: いらっしゃいませ, かしこまりました, 少々お待ちください. Many of these are fixed phrases you can learn whole.

For daily life as a learner, です and ます are polite enough. Full keigo matters most for jobs, interviews and customer service. There is also a lighter respectful form that looks like the passive: 先生が来られる.

examples.context: A shop clerk to a customer
examples.romaji: Shoushou omachi kudasai.
examples.en: Please wait a moment.

examples.context: Asking a secretary about the schedule
examples.romaji: Shachou wa nanji ni irasshaimasu ka.
examples.en: What time will the president arrive?

examples.context: A business email to a client
examples.romaji: Ashita, shiryou o ookuri shimasu.
examples.en: I will send you the documents tomorrow.

examples.context: Answering the office phone about a coworker
examples.romaji: Tanaka wa tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu.
examples.en: Tanaka is away from their desk right now.

compare.note: です and ます are the polite layer (丁寧語) and are part of keigo. Respectful and humble forms go further and show respect toward a specific person.
来られる or 書かれる is a lighter respectful form with the same shape as the passive. It is less formal than いらっしゃる or お書きになる.

mistakes: Using respectful verbs for yourself: 私が召し上がります is wrong. For your own actions use humble forms: 私がいただきます.
Stacking two respectful forms: おっしゃられる is double keigo and is considered incorrect. おっしゃる is enough.
Using respectful language about your own boss to a client: 田中部長はいらっしゃいません is wrong in that situation. Say 田中はおりません.

faq.q: What are the three types of keigo?
faq.a: 尊敬語 (sonkeigo) raises the other person's actions, 謙譲語 (kenjougo) lowers your own actions, and 丁寧語 (teineigo) is general politeness with です and ます. Some textbooks split the humble group further, but these three are the standard way to learn it.

faq.q: Is です / ます keigo?
faq.a: Yes. です and ます are 丁寧語, the polite part of keigo. When people say keigo is hard, they usually mean the respectful and humble forms.

faq.q: Do I need keigo as a learner?
faq.a: For travel and making friends, です and ます are enough. If you want to work in Japan or with Japanese companies, you will need keigo, especially set phrases for phone calls and emails.

meaning: "is": polite です vs plain だ
intro: です (desu) and だ (da) both mean "is" or "am": 学生です and 学生だ both mean "I am a student". です is polite and だ is the plain, casual version. Both come after nouns and な-adjectives, but い-adjectives take only です, never だ.

formation.example: 学生だ / 学生です
静かだ / 静かです

formation.rule: no だ; add です only to be polite
formation.example: 高い / 高いです (not 高いだ)
雨だった / 雨でした

formation.rule: じゃない / じゃありません (written: ではない)
formation.example: 学生じゃない / 学生じゃありません, 学生じゃないです

usage: The meaning is the same. The difference is politeness. Use です with teachers, coworkers, shop staff and people you do not know well. Use だ with friends and family.

In casual speech, だ is often dropped, especially in questions and by women: 学生? (are you a student?), きれい! (pretty!). Ending a sentence with a bare だ can sound blunt or a bit masculine, so people often add よ or ね: 明日だよ, 大変だね.
In writing, だ is the normal ending for diaries, essays and articles in plain style. Formal writing such as newspapers and reports sometimes uses である instead.
With い-adjectives, です is just a polite marker and adds no meaning. That is why 高いです is fine but 高いだ is wrong: an い-adjective already means "is high".

examples.romaji: Watashi wa gakusei desu.
examples.en: I'm a student.

examples.romaji: Kyou wa nichiyoubi da yo.
examples.en: Today's Sunday, you know.

examples.romaji: Kono heya wa shizuka desu ne.
examples.en: This room is quiet, isn't it?

examples.romaji: Kinou wa ame datta.
examples.en: It rained yesterday.

compare.note: である also means "is" but is used in formal writing like reports and newspapers. It is not used in conversation.
でございます is a very polite form of です used in customer service and announcements: こちらが入口でございます (this is the entrance).

mistakes: Putting だ after an い-adjective: 高いだ is wrong. Say 高い, or 高いです to be polite.
Using だ in a casual question: 学生だか? is wrong. Say 学生? with rising intonation, or 学生なの?
Using だ with a teacher or boss: 明日は休みだ sounds rude to a superior. Say 明日は休みです.

faq.q: Is だ rude?
faq.a: No, it is just casual. Using it with friends is natural. It can sound rude or cold when used with someone you should be polite to, or when it ends a sentence with nothing after it in a sharp tone.

faq.q: Can you say おいしいです?
faq.a: Yes. い-adjective + です is the standard polite form: このケーキはおいしいです. Only おいしいだ is wrong.

faq.q: Why do people drop だ in casual speech?
faq.a: In relaxed conversation, a bare だ can sound strong, so many speakers leave it out or soften it with よ, ね or の: 本当? (really?), 好きなの (I like it).

meaning: is doing; is in a state
intro: ている (te iru) shows an action in progress, like 食べている (is eating), or a state that continues after a change, like 結婚している (is married). You make it with the て-form of a verb plus いる. In casual speech it is often shortened to てる.

formation.example: 読む → 読んでいる, 書く → 書いている, 待つ → 待っている
食べる → 食べている, 見る → 見ている

formation.rule: している / 来ている (きている)
formation.example: する → している, 来る → 来ている
読んでいます, 読んでる, 食べてる
読んでいない, 食べてない

usage: With action verbs, ている means something is happening now: 今テレビを見ている (I'm watching TV now). This is the closest match to English -ing.

With verbs of change, it means the result is still true: 結婚している (is married), 窓が開いている (the window is open), 知っている (know), 日本に来ている (has come to Japan and is here). It does not mean the change is happening right now.
It also shows a habit or a job: 毎朝走っている (I run every morning), 銀行で働いている (I work at a bank).
In conversation, い is usually dropped: 何してる? (what are you doing?), 知ってる (I know). Use ています in polite speech.

examples.romaji: Ima, gohan o tabete imasu.
examples.en: I'm eating right now.

examples.romaji: Ane wa kekkon shite iru.
examples.en: My older sister is married.

examples.romaji: Nani shiteru no?
examples.en: What are you doing?

examples.romaji: Chichi wa ginkou de hataraite imasu.
examples.en: My dad works at a bank.

compare.note: てある is for a state someone created on purpose: 窓が開けてある (someone opened the window). ている with an intransitive verb just describes the state: 窓が開いている (the window is open).
The dictionary form often means future or habit: 食べる (I will eat). ている is for now or a continuing state: 食べている (I'm eating).

mistakes: Using the plain form for something happening now: 今テレビを見る means "I'll watch TV now". For "I'm watching", say 今テレビを見ている.
Reading 結婚している as "getting married": it means "is married". For "getting married", say 結婚する (soon) or 結婚した (just did).
Negating 知っている as 知っていない: the usual negative is 知らない (I don't know).

faq.q: What is the difference between ている and てる?
faq.a: They mean the same. てる is the casual spoken shortening of ている, as in 食べてる or 知ってる. Use ている or ています in polite speech and writing.

faq.q: Does ている always mean -ing?
faq.a: No. With action verbs it is like -ing, but with change verbs it shows a result state: 死んでいる means "is dead", not "is dying".

faq.q: Why is 知っています used for "I know"?
faq.a: 知る means "to come to know". Once you have learned something, that state continues, so "I know" is 知っている. The negative is 知らない.

meaning: has been done (and stays that way)
intro: てある (te aru) means something has been done on purpose and the result is still there: 名前が書いてある means "a name is written (someone wrote it)". You attach ある to the て-form of a transitive verb, a verb that takes an object.

formation.example: 書く → 書いてある, 貼る → 貼ってある
並べる → 並べてある, 入れる → 入れてある
予約する → 予約してある, 準備する → 準備してある
書いてあります, 予約してあります

usage: てある describes the state of a thing, and it shows that a person made it that way. The thing usually takes が: 机の上に花が置いてある (flowers have been placed on the desk).
It is also used for preparations you have done: ホテルはもう予約してある (I've already booked the hotel). Here the object can also take は or を.
書いてある is very common for what a sign, paper or website says: ここに何て書いてある? (what does it say here?).
It only works with transitive verbs like 開ける, 書く, 置く. With intransitive verbs like 開く or 落ちる, use ている instead.

examples.romaji: Kokuban ni namae ga kaite aru.
examples.en: A name is written on the blackboard.

examples.romaji: Resutoran wa mou yoyaku shite arimasu.
examples.en: I've already reserved the restaurant.

examples.context: A note to a family member
examples.romaji: Reizouko ni keeki ga irete aru yo.
examples.en: There's some cake in the fridge for you.

examples.romaji: Kono kami ni nante kaite aru no?
examples.en: What does this paper say?

compare.note: 窓が開けてある means someone opened the window, maybe for a reason. 窓が開いている just says the window is open. てある uses transitive verbs, ている here uses intransitive ones.
ておく is the action of doing something in advance: 予約しておく (I'll book it ahead). てある is the resulting state: 予約してある (it's been booked).

mistakes: Using an intransitive verb: 窓が開いてある is wrong. Say 窓が開けてある or 窓が開いている.
Mixing it up with ている: 手紙を書いている means "I'm writing a letter". 手紙が書いてある means "a letter has been written".

faq.q: What is the difference between てある and ている?
faq.a: Both can describe states. てある uses a transitive verb and implies someone did it on purpose: 電気がつけてある. ている with an intransitive verb just reports the state: 電気がついている (the light is on).

faq.q: What is the difference between てある and ておく?
faq.a: ておく is doing something now to prepare: 飲み物を買っておく. てある is the state after the preparation is done: 飲み物が買ってある (drinks have been bought).

meaning: do in advance; leave as is
intro: ておく (te oku) means doing something in advance to prepare, like 予約しておく (book ahead), or leaving something as it is, like 窓を開けておく (leave the window open). You attach おく to the て-form of a verb. In casual speech it is shortened to とく, or どく after a で-form.

formation.example: 買う → 買っておく, 読む → 読んでおく
調べる → 調べておく, 開ける → 開けておく
予約する → 予約しておく, 準備する → 準備しておく

formation.rule: ておく → とく, でおく → どく
formation.example: 買っておく → 買っとく, 読んでおく → 読んどく

formation.rule: ておきます / ておいてください
formation.example: 調べておきます, 開けておいてください

usage: The main use is preparation: you do something now because it will be useful later. 旅行の前にお金を両替しておく means changing money before a trip so you have it ready.
It also means leaving something in its current state: 電気をつけておいて (leave the light on), そのままにしておいてください (please leave it as it is).
It can mean doing something for now or just in case: とりあえずメモしておく (I'll just make a note for now).
The short forms とく and どく are very common in conversation: やっとく (I'll take care of it), 読んどいて (read it before then). In polite speech, use ておきます. As a helper, おく is normally written in hiragana.

examples.romaji: Ryokou no mae ni hoteru o yoyaku shite okimasu.
examples.en: I'll book the hotel before the trip.

examples.romaji: Mado o akete oite kudasai.
examples.en: Please leave the window open.

examples.context: Getting ready for a party with friends
examples.romaji: Nomimono, kattoku ne.
examples.en: I'll go ahead and buy the drinks.

examples.romaji: Ashita tesuto da kara, mou sukoshi benkyou shite okou.
examples.en: I have a test tomorrow, so I'll study a bit more.

compare.note: ておく is the action of preparing: 飲み物を買っておく. てある is the result: 飲み物が買ってある (the drinks have been bought).
まえに only says when: 旅行の前に予約する. Adding ておく stresses that it is preparation: 旅行の前に予約しておく.

mistakes: Shortening でおく as んとく: 読んとく is wrong. After で the short form is どく: 読んどく.
Writing the helper in kanji: 買って置く looks like you literally put something down. As a helper, write it in hiragana: 買っておく.

faq.q: What does とく mean in Japanese?
faq.a: とく is the casual short form of ておく. 買っとく means 買っておく (I'll buy it in advance), and やっとく means "I'll get it done". With verbs whose て-form ends in で, it becomes どく: 飲んどく.

faq.q: Is ておく polite?
faq.a: ておく is neutral. ておきます is polite, ておいてください is a polite request, and とく is casual.

intro: てしまう (te shimau) means either finishing something completely or doing something you regret, like 財布をなくしてしまった (I lost my wallet, unfortunately). You attach しまう to the て-form of a verb. In casual speech it becomes ちゃう, or じゃう after a で-form: 食べちゃう, 飲んじゃう.

formation.rule: て-form + しまう → ちゃう
formation.example: 行く → 行ってしまう / 行っちゃう

formation.rule: で-form + しまう → じゃう
formation.example: 読む → 読んでしまう / 読んじゃう, 死ぬ → 死んじゃう

formation.rule: て-form + しまう → ちゃう
formation.example: 食べる → 食べてしまう / 食べちゃう

formation.rule: してしまう / しちゃう, 来てしまう / 来ちゃう (きちゃう)
formation.example: 忘れ物する → 忘れ物しちゃう

formation.rule: てしまった → ちゃった, でしまった → じゃった
formation.example: 食べちゃった, 飲んじゃった

usage: One meaning is completion: doing something all the way to the end. 宿題をやってしまった means the homework is completely done. てしまおう is "let's get it done".
The other meaning, and the more common one in conversation, is regret or accident. 寝坊してしまった (I overslept) shows that it was not planned and you feel bad about it.
Sometimes the feeling is "oops" or a playful "I couldn't help it": ケーキ全部食べちゃった (I ate the whole cake).
ちゃう and じゃう are casual and very common with friends. In polite speech or emails, use てしまいました. ちまう is a rougher form you might hear in movies.

examples.romaji: Saifu o wasurete shimaimashita.
examples.en: I forgot my wallet.

examples.romaji: Keeki, zenbu tabechatta.
examples.en: I ate the whole cake.

examples.romaji: Shukudai wa mou yatte shimatta yo.
examples.en: I already finished my homework.

examples.romaji: Densha de nechatte, eki o norisugoshita.
examples.en: I fell asleep on the train and missed my stop.

compare.note: 財布を忘れた just states a fact. 財布を忘れてしまった adds that it was a mistake and you feel bad about it.
ておく is doing something on purpose to prepare. てしまう is often something that happens without meaning to, or getting something completely done.

mistakes: Using ちゃう after a で-form: 読んちゃう is wrong. After ん the short form is じゃう: 読んじゃう.
Using ちゃう in formal writing: 書類を送っちゃいました sounds too casual in a work email. Write 書類を送ってしまいました.

faq.q: Does てしまう always mean regret?
faq.a: No. It can also mean doing something completely: 一日で本を読んでしまった (I read the whole book in one day). Context shows which one is meant, but regret is the more common use.

faq.q: Is ちゃう casual?
faq.a: Yes. ちゃう and じゃう are casual spoken forms of てしまう and でしまう. They are fine with friends and family, but use てしまう or てしまいます in polite situations.

faq.q: What is じゃう?
faq.a: じゃう is the same as ちゃう for verbs whose て-form ends in で: 飲んでしまう → 飲んじゃう, 遊んでしまう → 遊んじゃう.

intro: てみる (te miru) means "try doing something and see what it is like": 食べてみる means to try eating something. You attach みる to the て-form of a verb. It is very common as てみたい (I want to try) and てみて (try it).

formation.example: 書く → 書いてみる, 飲む → 飲んでみる, 行く → 行ってみる
食べる → 食べてみる, 着る → 着てみる

formation.rule: してみる / 来てみる (きてみる)
formation.example: 電話する → 電話してみる

formation.rule: てみたい / てみて / てみてください
formation.example: 行ってみたい, 食べてみて

usage: てみる is about testing something to find out the result: この靴、はいてみる (I'll try these shoes on). It is not about trying hard; for "attempt", use ようとする.
てみたい (want to try) is one of the most common patterns for talking about wishes: 一度富士山に登ってみたい (I'd like to climb Mt. Fuji once).
Requests with てみて or てみてください sound gentle and encouraging: 一回やってみて (give it a try).
The past てみた often comes before a result: 電話してみたけど、誰も出なかった (I tried calling, but no one answered). As a helper, みる is written in hiragana.

examples.romaji: Kono fuku, kite mite mo ii desu ka.
examples.en: Can I try this on?

examples.romaji: Nihon ni itte mitai desu.
examples.en: I'd like to try going to Japan.

examples.romaji: Chotto tabete mite.
examples.en: Try a bit of this.

examples.romaji: Mise ni denwa shite mita kedo, dare mo denakatta.
examples.en: I tried calling the shop, but nobody answered.

compare.note: ようとする means attempting something, often without success: 起きようとしたけど起きられなかった. てみる means doing it to see the result: 早く起きてみた (I tried getting up early).
試す is a separate verb meaning "to test" or "try out" a thing: 新しい方法を試す. てみる attaches to any action verb.

mistakes: Writing it in kanji: 食べて見る is not standard for this meaning. Write 食べてみる in hiragana.
Using it for great effort: 一生懸命起きてみた sounds odd for "I tried hard to get up". Use 起きようとした.

faq.q: What is the difference between てみる and ようとする?
faq.a: てみる is trying something out to see what happens, and the action usually happens. ようとする is attempting or being about to do something, often when you could not do it.

faq.q: Is てみる written in kanji?
faq.a: No. When it means "try", みる is written in hiragana. 見る in kanji is used for the normal verb "see".

meaning: go and come back; come toward; start to
intro: てくる (te kuru) adds the idea of "coming" to a verb. It can mean "go do something and come back" (買ってくる), an action moving toward the speaker (持ってくる, bring), or a change that has been happening up to now (寒くなってきた, it has gotten colder). You attach くる to the て-form of a verb.

formation.example: 買う → 買ってくる, 持つ → 持ってくる, 行く → 行ってくる
借りる → 借りてくる, 増える → 増えてくる
電話する → 電話してくる, 連絡する → 連絡してくる
寒くなってきた, 行ってきます

usage: Go and come back: ちょっとコンビニ行ってくる means "I'm going to the convenience store and will be back". The fixed greeting 行ってきます, said when leaving home, comes from this.
Movement toward the speaker: 持ってくる (bring), 連れてくる (bring a person), 友達が走ってきた (my friend came running).
Change up to now: 寒くなってきた (it has gotten colder), 日本語がわかってきた (I'm starting to understand Japanese), 雨が降ってきた (it started raining). This shows a change you notice now.
Continuing from the past to now: 10年この仕事を続けてきた (I've kept doing this job for 10 years). As a helper, くる is usually written in hiragana.

examples.romaji: Konbini de ocha o katte kuru ne.
examples.en: I'll go get some tea at the convenience store.

examples.romaji: Itte kimasu!
examples.en: I'm off! (said when leaving home)

examples.romaji: Dandan samuku natte kimashita ne.
examples.en: It's been getting colder, hasn't it?

examples.context: A teacher before a school trip
examples.romaji: Ashita, obentou o motte kite kudasai.
examples.en: Please bring a lunch tomorrow.

compare.note: てくる points toward the speaker or up to now: 持ってくる (bring here), 増えてきた (has increased). ていく points away or into the future: 持っていく (take there), 増えていく (will keep increasing).
買いに来る means "come (here) in order to buy". 買ってくる means "go buy it and come back".

mistakes: Mixing up direction: telling a guest to bring food to your home is 持ってきてください, not 持っていってください.
Writing 来る in kanji as a helper: 買って来る is not wrong, but as a helper くる is usually written in hiragana: 買ってくる.

faq.q: What does 行ってきます mean?
faq.a: It literally means "I will go and come back". People say it when leaving home, work or school. The reply is いってらっしゃい (have a good day, come back safely).

faq.q: What is the difference between てくる and ていく?
faq.a: Think of direction in space and time. てくる comes toward you or up to the present. ていく goes away from you or forward into the future.

meaning: go on doing; take; do before going
intro: ていく (te iku) adds the idea of "going" to a verb. It can mean an action moving away from the speaker (持っていく, take), doing something before you leave (食べていく), or a change that will continue from now on (増えていく, keep increasing). You attach いく to the て-form of a verb; in casual speech it is often shortened to てく.

formation.example: 持つ → 持っていく, 歩く → 歩いていく
食べる → 食べていく, 増える → 増えていく
練習する → 練習していく
持ってく, 歩いてく

formation.rule: ていった / ていきます
formation.example: 持っていった, 続けていきます

usage: Movement away from the speaker: 傘を持っていく (take an umbrella), 子どもを公園に連れていく (take the kids to the park), 鳥が飛んでいった (the bird flew away).
Doing something before you go somewhere: 晩ご飯、食べていく? asks if a visitor wants to eat before leaving.
Change or continuation from now into the future: これから寒くなっていく (it will keep getting colder), この仕事を続けていきます (I will keep doing this work). Companies often use this in speeches and plans.
In speech, ていく often becomes てく: 送ってくよ (I'll take you there). Note that 行く is pronounced いく here, and the helper is normally written in hiragana.

examples.context: Checking the weather before going out
examples.romaji: Kasa o motte itta hou ga ii yo.
examples.en: You should take an umbrella.

examples.romaji: Bangohan, tabete iku?
examples.en: Want to stay for dinner before you go?

examples.romaji: Kore kara Nihon ni sumu gaikokujin wa fuete iku deshou.
examples.en: The number of foreigners living in Japan will probably keep growing.

examples.context: Deciding how to get to the station
examples.romaji: Eki made aruiteku.
examples.en: I'll walk to the station.

compare.note: ていく goes away from the speaker or into the future: 持っていく, 増えていく. てくる comes toward the speaker or up to now: 持ってくる, 増えてきた.
買いに行く means "go in order to buy". 買っていく means "buy something and then go", for example on the way to a friend's house.

mistakes: Using ていく for things coming to where you are: if you are at home, ask a friend 飲み物を持ってきて, not 飲み物を持っていって.
Using ていく for a change that has already happened: 最近寒くなっていった sounds odd. For a change up to now, use てくる: 最近寒くなってきた.

faq.q: What does てく mean?
faq.a: てく is the casual spoken form of ていく. 持ってく means 持っていく (take it with me), and 歩いてく means 歩いていく (walk there).

faq.q: What is the difference between ていく and てくる?
faq.a: ていく points away from you in space or forward in time. てくる points toward you or from the past up to now. 寒くなっていく is "will keep getting colder", 寒くなってきた is "has gotten colder".

intro: てあげる (te ageru) means doing something for someone else as a favor: 妹に本を読んであげた means "I read a book to my little sister (for her)". You attach あげる to the て-form of a verb. The giver is you or your side, and the receiver is someone else.

formation.example: 読む → 読んであげる, 貸す → 貸してあげる
教える → 教えてあげる, 見せる → 見せてあげる

formation.rule: してあげる / 来てあげる (きてあげる)
formation.example: 説明する → 説明してあげる

formation.rule: てやる (to animals, plants, rough) / てさしあげる (humble)
formation.example: 犬と遊んでやる, お客様に写真を撮ってさしあげる

usage: Use てあげる when you, or someone you are talking about, does a favor for another person: 友達に傘を貸してあげた (I lent my friend an umbrella).
The receiver is often marked with に, but for verbs that act on a person's thing, use の: 友達の引っ越しを手伝ってあげた (I helped with my friend's move).
Saying てあげる directly to the person you are helping can sound like you are showing off the favor. To a boss or teacher, 持ってあげます is rude. Use the humble お〜します instead: お持ちします (let me carry it).

てやる is the plain, rougher version, used with pets, plants, or younger family members, and sometimes in rough speech. てさしあげる is humbler but can still sound pushy, so people usually avoid it face to face.

examples.romaji: Imouto ni hon o yonde ageta.
examples.en: I read a book to my little sister.

examples.romaji: Michi ga wakaranai nara, oshiete ageru yo.
examples.en: If you don't know the way, I'll show you.

examples.context: Telling a coworker about the weekend
examples.romaji: Tomodachi no hikkoshi o tetsudatte agemashita.
examples.en: I helped my friend move.

examples.context: A parent talking about a birthday
examples.romaji: Kodomo ni omocha o katte ageta.
examples.en: I bought my kid a toy.

compare.note: てくれる is when someone does a favor for you or your side: 友達が教えてくれた (my friend taught me). てあげる goes the other way: I do it for someone else.
てもらう puts the receiver as the subject: 友達に教えてもらった (I had my friend teach me). It focuses on receiving the favor.

mistakes: Using it for favors toward you: 友達が私に教えてあげた is wrong. When you receive the favor, use てくれる: 友達が教えてくれた.
Offering it to a superior: 先生、荷物を持ってあげます is rude. Say 先生、お荷物をお持ちします.

faq.q: What is the difference between てあげる, てくれる and てもらう?
faq.a: てあげる: I (or my side) do something for someone else. てくれる: someone does something for me (or my side). てもらう: I receive a favor from someone, with me as the subject.

faq.q: Is てあげる rude?
faq.a: Not when you talk about what you did for a friend or family member. It can sound condescending when you say it directly to the person, especially someone above you, because it stresses that you are doing them a favor.

meaning: someone does something for me (a favor)
intro: てくれる (te kureru) means someone does something for you or for your group, and you are grateful for it. You attach くれる to the て-form of a verb, so 手伝う becomes 手伝ってくれる (helps me).

formation.example: 書く → 書いてくれる, 買う → 買ってくれる
見る → 見てくれる, 教える → 教えてくれる

formation.rule: して / 来て + くれる
formation.example: する → してくれる, 来る → 来てくれる

formation.rule: てくれます / てくれませんか / てくれない?
formation.example: 手伝ってくれませんか (could you help me?)

usage: The receiver of the favor is always the speaker or someone in the speaker's group, like family. The doer is marked with が or は: 友達が手伝ってくれた means my friend helped me. You usually do not say 私に, because くれる already points the favor toward you.
てくれる adds a feeling of thanks. 母が作った弁当 just states who made it, while 母が作ってくれた弁当 says your mother made it for you. Leaving てくれる out can make a sentence sound cold when someone did you a kindness.
As a question, it is a request. てくれない? is casual and used with friends and family. てくれませんか is polite. With teachers, bosses and customers, the humble-honorific version てくださる / てくださいませんか is safer.
A common pattern is 〜てくれてありがとう (thank you for doing ...). It is a warm, everyday way to thank someone for something specific.

examples.context: Telling a coworker about your morning
examples.romaji: Tomodachi ga eki made okutte kuremashita.
examples.en: My friend took me to the station.

examples.context: Asking a friend for help moving a box
examples.romaji: Chotto tetsudatte kurenai?
examples.en: Can you help me for a sec?

examples.romaji: Haha ga tsukutte kureta obentou wa oishii.
examples.en: The lunch my mom made for me is delicious.

examples.context: Greeting a friend at your party
examples.romaji: Kite kurete arigatou.
examples.en: Thanks for coming.

compare.note: てあげる is the opposite direction: you (or your side) do something for someone else. 友達に教えてあげた means I taught my friend.
てもらう describes the same favor from the receiver's side, with the doer marked by に: 友達に手伝ってもらった. てくれる makes the doer the subject: 友達が手伝ってくれた.

mistakes: Using てくれる for a favor you do: 私が友達に教えてくれた is wrong. Say 私が友達に教えてあげた.
Using it for a favor between two other people with no link to you: 田中さんが山田さんに本を貸してくれた sounds odd unless 山田さん is in your group. Use 貸してあげた instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between てくれる and てもらう?
faq.a: Both mean someone did a favor for you. With てくれる the doer is the subject (友達が手伝ってくれた). With てもらう you are the subject and the doer takes に (友達に手伝ってもらった). てもらう can also suggest you asked for it.

faq.q: Is てくれない rude?
faq.a: No. てくれない? is a normal, friendly request between friends and family. To a stranger or someone above you, use てくれませんか or てくださいませんか.

meaning: have someone do something for you
intro: てもらう (te morau) means you receive a favor: you get someone to do something for you. You attach もらう to the て-form of a verb and mark the person who does it with に, as in 友達に手伝ってもらう (get help from a friend).

formation.example: 待つ → 待ってもらう, 書く → 書いてもらう
見る → 見てもらう, 教える → 教えてもらう

formation.rule: して / 来て + もらう
formation.example: する → してもらう, 来る → 来てもらう

formation.rule: てもらえる? / てもらえますか
formation.example: 待ってもらえますか (could you wait?)

usage: The receiver is the subject, often left out because it is you. The person doing the favor takes に: 先輩に駅まで送ってもらった means my senior gave me a ride to the station.
てもらう can suggest that you asked for the favor or arranged it. 医者に診てもらう means to have a doctor examine you, which is the normal way to say you saw a doctor.
As a request, the potential form is common: てもらえる? with friends, てもらえますか or てもらえませんか in polite speech. With a boss or customer, use the humble version ていただけますか.
In polite speech about people above you, もらう becomes いただく: 先生に教えていただきました. In casual talk and with friends, てもらう is the normal choice.

examples.context: Telling a friend how you finished homework
examples.romaji: Tomodachi ni shukudai o tetsudatte moratta.
examples.en: I got my friend to help me with my homework.

examples.context: Telling your boss how you got here
examples.romaji: Senpai ni eki made okutte moraimashita.
examples.en: My senior gave me a ride to the station.

examples.context: A shop clerk asking a customer
examples.romaji: Sukoshi matte moraemasu ka?
examples.en: Could you wait a moment?

examples.romaji: Isha ni mite moratta hou ga ii yo.
examples.en: You should get a doctor to look at it.

compare.note: てくれる tells the same favor with the doer as subject: 友達が手伝ってくれた. てもらう puts you as subject and the doer with に.
ていただく is the humble, polite version of てもらう, used for favors from teachers, bosses and customers.

mistakes: Marking the doer with が: 友達が手伝ってもらった is wrong. Say 友達に手伝ってもらった, or 友達が手伝ってくれた.
Using てもらってください to ask the listener for a favor: 待ってもらってください means please have someone else wait. To ask the person in front of you, say 待ってもらえますか or 待ってください.

faq.q: What is the difference between てもらう and てくれる?
faq.a: They describe the same favor. てもらう focuses on you receiving it and can hint that you asked. てくれる focuses on the other person's kindness.

faq.q: Is てもらえますか polite?
faq.a: Yes, it is a polite request that works in shops and with coworkers. ていただけますか is more polite, for bosses and customers.

intro: すぎる (sugiru) means "too" or "too much": you did something more than you should, or something is more than you want. Attach it to the ます-stem of a verb (食べすぎる) or to an adjective stem (高すぎる, 静かすぎる).

formation.example: 食べる → 食べすぎる, 飲む → 飲みすぎる
高い → 高すぎる, 暑い → 暑すぎる
静か → 静かすぎる, 真面目 → 真面目すぎる

formation.rule: いい → よすぎる, ない → なさすぎる
formation.example: いい → よすぎる, 時間がない → 時間がなさすぎる

usage: すぎる itself conjugates as a group 2 verb: すぎます, すぎた, すぎない, すぎて. 飲みすぎた means I drank too much, and 食べすぎないで means don't eat too much.
It usually sounds negative, as in a complaint or a regret. In casual speech, young people also use it as praise: かわいすぎる means it is incredibly cute, not that the cuteness is a problem.
The て-form すぎて gives a reason: 暑すぎて眠れない means it is so hot I can't sleep. This is a very common pattern.
The noun form すぎ is also common in speech: 飲みすぎ (drinking too much) or 考えすぎだよ (you are overthinking it).

examples.romaji: Kinou, nomisugita.
examples.en: I drank too much yesterday.

examples.romaji: Kono heya wa atsusugimasu.
examples.en: This room is too hot.

examples.romaji: Kare wa majimesugiru.
examples.en: He's too serious.

examples.context: A parent at a birthday party
examples.romaji: Tabesuginaide ne.
examples.en: Don't eat too much, OK?

compare.note: とても and すごく mean "very" with no judgment: とても高い is just very expensive. 高すぎる means too expensive, more than you accept.
あまりに also means too, but it is an adverb used before the word, often in writing: あまりに高い. すぎる attaches to the end.

mistakes: Keeping the い of an い-adjective: 高いすぎる is wrong. Say 高すぎる.
Using the dictionary form of a verb: 食べるすぎた is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 食べすぎた.
Forgetting the special forms: いいすぎる means to say too much (言いすぎる). For too good, say よすぎる.

faq.q: Is すぎる always negative?
faq.a: Mostly it shows something is excessive. In casual speech it can be strong praise, like おいしすぎる (way too delicious), meaning extremely good.

faq.q: How do you say "too" with a negative, like too little time?
faq.a: Use なさすぎる: 時間がなさすぎる means there is way too little time. For an adjective of quantity, 少なすぎる (too few, too little) is also common.

meaning: easy to do / hard to do
intro: やすい (yasui) means "easy to do" and にくい (nikui) means "hard to do". You attach them to the ます-stem of a verb: 読む becomes 読みやすい (easy to read) or 読みにくい (hard to read).

formation.rule: ます-stem + やすい / にくい
formation.example: 書く → 書きやすい, 読む → 読みにくい

formation.rule: ます-stem + やすい / にくい
formation.example: 食べる → 食べやすい, 覚える → 覚えにくい

formation.rule: し / 来 + やすい / にくい
formation.example: する → しやすい, 来る → 来やすい
わかりやすかった, 使いにくくない

usage: The result is an い-adjective, so it conjugates like one: わかりやすい, わかりやすかった, わかりやすくない. It can also come before a noun: 使いやすいアプリ (an easy-to-use app).
やすい also means "tends to" or "is likely to": 風邪をひきやすい means you catch colds easily. This is common for things that happen on their own, like breaking or getting tired.
にくい often softens a request or a hard topic: 言いにくいんですが (this is hard to say, but). It is polite and very common at work.
These are neutral in register. They work in casual chat, polite speech and writing. A close alternative is づらい, which stresses that something is physically or emotionally hard for the person.

examples.context: Trying a pen in a shop
examples.romaji: Kono pen wa kakiyasui desu.
examples.en: This pen is easy to write with.

examples.romaji: Kare no ji wa yominikui.
examples.en: His handwriting is hard to read.

examples.romaji: Sensei no setsumei wa wakariyasukatta.
examples.en: The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.

examples.context: Asking your manager for a day off
examples.romaji: Iinikui n desu ga, ashita yasunde mo ii desu ka.
examples.en: This is hard to say, but may I take tomorrow off?

compare.note: 安い (yasui) means cheap and stands alone. The やすい in 書きやすい is a different word that attaches to a verb stem.
づらい also means hard to do, but focuses on physical or emotional difficulty for the person: 言いづらい, 歩きづらい. にくい is more objective.

mistakes: Attaching to the dictionary form: 読むやすい is wrong. Say 読みやすい.
Conjugating like a verb: わかりやすいでした is wrong. Say わかりやすかったです.

faq.q: What is the difference between にくい and づらい?
faq.a: Both mean hard to do. にくい often describes the thing itself (読みにくい字). づらい focuses on the person's discomfort (言いづらい, hard for me to say). They overlap a lot.

faq.q: Is やすい here the same as 安い (cheap)?
faq.a: No. 安い means cheap. The やすい that attaches to a verb stem means easy to do, and it is usually written in hiragana.

intro: はじめる (hajimeru) means "start doing" and おわる (owaru) means "finish doing". You attach them to the ます-stem of a verb: 読む becomes 読み始める (start reading) or 読み終わる (finish reading). They are usually written 始める and 終わる.

formation.rule: ます-stem + 始める / 終わる
formation.example: 読む → 読み始める, 書く → 書き終わる

formation.rule: ます-stem + 始める / 終わる
formation.example: 食べる → 食べ始める, 食べ終わる

formation.rule: し / 来 + 始める / 終わる
formation.example: 勉強する → 勉強し始める, 来る → 来始める
読み終わった, 降り始めました

usage: The helper verb carries the tense and politeness: 読み終わった (finished reading), 降り始めました (started falling). Both 始める and 終わる conjugate as normal verbs.
始める works with actions you do and with things that happen by themselves, like rain or cherry blossoms: 雨が降り始めた. 終わる is mainly used for actions with a clear end, like reading a book or eating a meal.
終える is a more formal, written version of 終わる: 作業を終える. In everyday speech, 終わる is the normal choice after a verb stem.
For a sudden or unexpected start, Japanese often uses 出す instead: 急に泣き出した (suddenly burst into tears). To keep going, use 続ける: 読み続ける.

examples.context: Introducing yourself at a language exchange
examples.romaji: Kyonen kara nihongo o benkyou shihajimemashita.
examples.en: I started studying Japanese last year.

examples.context: Telling a friend about a long novel
examples.romaji: Kono hon, yatto yomiowatta.
examples.en: I finally finished reading this book.

examples.romaji: Ame ga furihajimeta ne.
examples.en: It started raining, huh.

examples.context: A parent at the dinner table
examples.romaji: Tabeowattara, osara o aratte ne.
examples.en: When you finish eating, wash your plate, OK?

compare.note: 出す also means start, but suggests a sudden start: 笑い出した (burst out laughing). 始める is neutral.
終える means finish, like 終わる, but sounds more formal and written. It is common in reports and announcements.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 読むはじめる is wrong. Say 読み始める.
Using a separate verb phrase where the compound is natural: 読むのを終わった sounds odd. Say 読み終わった.

faq.q: Is it 終わる or 終える after a verb?
faq.a: Both are correct. 読み終わる is the everyday choice. 読み終える sounds more formal and is common in writing.

faq.q: What is the difference between 始める and 出す?
faq.a: 始める is a neutral start. 出す adds that the start was sudden or unexpected, like 急に泣き出した.

intro: から (kara) after a clause means "because" or "so": the reason comes first, then から, then the result. It attaches to plain or polite forms, as in 雨だから (because it's raining) or 眠いから (because I'm sleepy).

formation.rule: plain or polite form + から
formation.example: 行く → 行くから, 行きます → 行きますから
眠い → 眠いから, 高かった → 高かったから

formation.rule: stem + だから / ですから
formation.example: 暇 → 暇だから

formation.rule: noun + だから / ですから
formation.example: 雨 → 雨だから, 学生 → 学生だから

usage: Reason first, result second: 時間がないから、急いで means there's no time, so hurry. This is the reverse of English "because", which can come either before or after.
から is direct and very common in speech. It is the natural choice when your reason leads to a request, command, invitation or opinion: 寒いから窓を閉めて (it's cold, so close the window).
You can end a sentence with から to give a reason by itself: どうして来なかったの? 忙しかったから. With polite speech, use ですから or ますから.
Do not confuse it with から meaning "from" (駅から). The "because" から follows a full clause, while "from" から follows a noun of place or time.

examples.context: Explaining your plans on a rainy day
examples.romaji: Ame da kara, ie ni imasu.
examples.en: It's raining, so I'm staying home.

examples.romaji: Nemui kara, mou neru ne.
examples.en: I'm sleepy, so I'm going to bed now.

examples.context: Rushing a friend out the door
examples.romaji: Jikan ga nai kara, isoide!
examples.en: There's no time, so hurry!

examples.romaji: Ashita wa hayai desu kara, kyou wa kaerimasu.
examples.en: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'll head home today.

compare.note: ので also means because but sounds softer and more objective, so it is preferred for polite excuses and apologies. から is more direct and personal.
After a noun, から means from: 東京から来ました. After a clause, it means because.

mistakes: Leaving out だ after a noun or な-adjective: 雨から means from the rain. Say 雨だから for because it's raining.
Using から for a polite apology to a boss: 電車が遅れたから遅刻しました can sound like you are making excuses. 電車が遅れたので遅刻しました is softer.

faq.q: What is the difference between から and ので?
faq.a: Both mean because. から is more direct and common in casual speech and with requests. ので sounds softer and more objective, so it is better for polite explanations and excuses.

faq.q: Is から rude?
faq.a: No, but in formal situations a bare から can sound like you are pushing your reason. ですから or ので feel more polite when apologizing or explaining to a superior.

intro: ので (node) means "because" or "since", and it sounds softer and more objective than から. It attaches to the plain form, with な before nouns and な-adjectives: 痛いので (because it hurts), 雨なので (because it's raining).

formation.example: 遅れる → 遅れるので, 遅れた → 遅れたので
痛い → 痛いので, 寒かった → 寒かったので
静か → 静かなので, 暇 → 暇なので
雨 → 雨なので, 休み → 休みなので

usage: ので presents the reason as a natural cause or a fact, not as your personal argument. That makes it the standard choice for polite explanations, excuses and apologies: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました.
It is common at work, in shops, with teachers and in announcements. In polite speech you can put the polite form before it, as in 遅れますので, which sounds very formal and is common in business.
In casual speech, ので often shortens to んで: 疲れたんで、帰るね. This sounds relaxed but still a little softer than から.
You can end a sentence with ので to leave the request unspoken: 用事があるので... This politely hints at what you mean without saying it.

examples.romaji: Atama ga itai node, kyou wa yasumimasu.
examples.en: I have a headache, so I'll take today off.

examples.context: An announcement at a sports ground
examples.romaji: Ame na node shiai wa chuushi desu.
examples.en: Because of the rain, the game is canceled.

examples.romaji: Densha ga okureta node, chikoku shimashita.
examples.en: The train was late, so I was late.

examples.romaji: Mou osoi node, shitsurei shimasu.
examples.en: It's getting late, so I'll be going.

compare.note: から is more direct and personal, and common in casual speech. ので sounds softer and more objective, so it fits polite excuses better.
のに looks similar but means the opposite kind of link: even though. 雨なので行かない (because it rains, I won't go) vs 雨なのに行く (I'll go even though it rains).

mistakes: Using だ before ので: 雨だので is wrong. Say 雨なので.
Mixing up ので and のに: 勉強したので落ちた means I failed because I studied. You probably mean 勉強したのに落ちた (I failed even though I studied).

faq.q: What is the difference between ので and から?
faq.a: Both mean because. ので sounds softer and presents the reason as a fact, so it is preferred in polite and formal speech. から is more direct and natural with commands and strong opinions.

faq.q: Is ので formal?
faq.a: It is neutral to polite. It works with friends too, but in casual speech people often shorten it to んで or just use から.

intro: のに (noni) means "even though" or "despite", usually with surprise, disappointment or frustration about the result. It attaches to the plain form, with な before nouns and な-adjectives: 勉強したのに (even though I studied), 日曜日なのに (even though it's Sunday).

formation.example: する → するのに, した → したのに
高い → 高いのに, 寒かった → 寒かったのに
元気 → 元気なのに
日曜日 → 日曜日なのに

usage: のに shows that the result goes against what you expected, and that you feel something about it: annoyance, disappointment or surprise. 約束したのに来なかった means he promised, but he didn't come, and you are upset.
At the end of a sentence, のに expresses regret or a complaint: 早く言ってくれればよかったのに (you should have told me sooner). This use is very common in conversation.
Because it carries emotion, のに is not used for neutral contrasts. For a plain "but", use けど or が.
The second half cannot be a request, command or invitation. 雨なのに行こう is wrong. Use ても or けど for those: 雨でも行こう.

examples.romaji: Isshoukenmei benkyou shita noni, shiken ni ochita.
examples.en: I studied so hard, and I still failed the exam.

examples.romaji: Nichiyoubi na noni, shigoto ni ikanakya.
examples.en: Even though it's Sunday, I have to go to work.

examples.romaji: Yakusoku shita noni, kare wa konakatta.
examples.en: He promised, but he didn't come.

examples.context: Finding out about a problem too late
examples.romaji: Hayaku itte kurereba yokatta noni.
examples.en: You should have told me sooner.

compare.note: けど and が are a neutral but. のに adds surprise or frustration that the result went against expectations.
ても means even if and works for hypothetical cases and with requests: 雨でも行こう. のに is about facts that already happened or are true.
ので means because and looks similar, but gives a reason, not a contrast.

mistakes: Using だ before のに: 日曜日だのに is wrong. Say 日曜日なのに.
Following のに with a request: 寒いのに窓を開けてください is wrong. Say 寒いけど窓を開けてください, or rethink the sentence.

faq.q: What is the difference between のに and けど?
faq.a: けど is a neutral but. のに means even though and adds feelings like disappointment or surprise. のに also cannot be followed by a request or invitation.

faq.q: What does のに mean at the end of a sentence?
faq.a: It shows regret or a complaint about something that did not happen: 来ればよかったのに means you should have come, it's a shame you didn't.

intro: けど (kedo) and が (ga) both mean "but" or "although" when they join two clauses. けど is casual and が is more polite or written, and both attach to the end of a plain or polite clause: 高いけど (it's expensive, but), 難しいですが (it's difficult, but).

formation.rule: plain or polite form + けど / が
formation.example: 行きたい → 行きたいけど, 行きます → 行きますが

formation.rule: い-adjective + けど / ですが
formation.example: 高い → 高いけど, 高いですが

formation.rule: stem + だけど / ですが
formation.example: 静か → 静かだけど, 静かですが

formation.rule: noun + だけど / ですが
formation.example: 学生 → 学生だけど, 学生ですが

usage: けど is the everyday spoken form. けれど and けれども are longer, slightly more formal versions. が after です or ます is the polite and written choice, common at work and in emails.
Both are often used as softeners, not as a real "but". すみません、ちょっと聞きたいんですが opens a request politely. The sentence often trails off and the listener understands the rest.
At the end of a sentence, けど makes a statement softer or less direct: 明日はちょっと忙しいんだけど... hints that you can't make it without saying no.
This が is different from the subject marker が. The "but" が comes after a full clause, usually after です, ます or a plain verb.

examples.context: Recommending a restaurant to a friend
examples.romaji: Kono mise, takai kedo oishii yo.
examples.en: This place is pricey, but it's good.

examples.romaji: Sumimasen, chotto kikitai n desu ga.
examples.en: Excuse me, I'd like to ask you something.

examples.romaji: Ikitai kedo, jikan ga nai.
examples.en: I want to go, but I don't have time.

examples.context: Talking about your studies in an interview
examples.romaji: Nihongo wa muzukashii desu ga, omoshiroi desu.
examples.en: Japanese is difficult, but it's interesting.

compare.note: でも at the start of a new sentence means but: 高い。でも、おいしい. けど and が join the two ideas in one sentence.
のに also contrasts two facts but adds frustration or surprise. けど is neutral.

mistakes: Leaving out だ after a noun or な-adjective in casual speech: 学生けど is wrong. Say 学生だけど.
Mixing registers: 高いだけど is wrong because い-adjectives don't take だ. Say 高いけど.

faq.q: What is the difference between けど and が?
faq.a: They mean the same. けど is casual and spoken. が is more formal, used after です and ます and in writing. けれども sits in between.

faq.q: Why do Japanese people end sentences with けど?
faq.a: It softens what you say and leaves room for the listener. 今ちょっと忙しいんだけど... politely hints at a problem without stating it directly.

intro: ながら (nagara) means "while": the same person does two things at the same time, like eating while watching TV. You attach it to the ます-stem of a verb, so 食べます becomes 食べながら.

formation.example: 聞く → 聞きながら, 歩く → 歩きながら
食べる → 食べながら, 見る → 見ながら
する → しながら, 来る → 来ながら

usage: The main action goes at the end of the sentence, and the side action takes ながら. 音楽を聞きながら勉強します means you are studying, with music on in the background.
Both actions must be done by the same person. For two people doing different things at the same time, use あいだ or とき instead.
With some words, ながら means "although" instead of "while", as in 残念ながら (unfortunately) or 知っていながら (even though I knew). This use is more written and more advanced.

examples.romaji: Ongaku o kikinagara benkyou shimasu.
examples.en: I study while listening to music.

examples.context: A parent scolding a child at dinner
examples.romaji: Terebi o minagara tabenaide!
examples.en: Don't eat while watching TV!

examples.romaji: Kare wa warainagara hanashita.
examples.en: He talked while laughing.

examples.romaji: Zannen nagara sanka dekimasen.
examples.en: Unfortunately, I can't attend.

compare.note: あいだ is for a stretch of time and works with two different people: 私が寝ているあいだ、弟はゲームをしていた. ながら needs one person doing both.
とき marks the moment something happened during another action. ながら describes two actions running side by side.

mistakes: Attaching ながら to the dictionary form: 聞くながら is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 聞きながら.
Using it for two different people: 母が料理しながら私はテレビを見た sounds wrong. Say 母が料理しているあいだ、私はテレビを見た.

faq.q: What is the difference between ながら and ている間?
faq.a: ながら joins two actions by the same person at the same time. ている間 (あいだ) marks a period of time, and the other action can be done by someone else.

faq.q: Does ながら always mean while?
faq.a: Mostly. With a few words, like 残念ながら or 知っていながら, it means although. That use is more formal.

intro: たら (tara) means "if" or "when": once the first thing happens, the second follows. You make it by adding ら to the past (た) form, so 着いた becomes 着いたら (when you arrive) and 安かった becomes 安かったら (if it's cheap).

formation.example: 行く → 行ったら, 食べる → 食べたら, する → したら
安い → 安かったら, いい → よかったら
暇 → 暇だったら, 雨 → 雨だったら
行かない → 行かなかったら

usage: たら is the most flexible conditional and the most common in conversation. It works for both "if" (雨だったら、行かない) and "when, once" (駅に着いたら、電話して). If you are unsure which conditional to use, たら is usually safe.
Unlike と and ば, the second half can be a request, invitation, plan or command: 終わったら、帰っていいよ. This makes it very useful in daily speech.
