With a past result, たら can show discovery: 窓を開けたら、雪が降っていた (when I opened the window, it was snowing). The second event was something you found, not something you did.
Common set phrases include よかったら (if you like), どうしたら (what should I do), and もし〜たら (if by any chance). たら is casual to polite, depending on the rest of the sentence.

examples.romaji: Eki ni tsuitara, denwa shite ne.
examples.en: Give me a call when you get to the station.

examples.romaji: Ame dattara, ikimasen.
examples.en: If it rains, I won't go.

examples.romaji: Yasukattara kau.
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

examples.romaji: Mado o aketara, yuki ga futte ita.
examples.en: When I opened the window, it was snowing.

compare.note: ば focuses on the condition itself and is common in set phrases like どうすればいい. たら is more general and works better for one-time events and requests.
と is for natural or automatic results (押すと開く). It cannot be followed by a request. たら can.
なら picks up a topic or plan someone mentioned: 行くなら (if you're going). The order of events can be reversed with なら, but not with たら.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 行くたら is wrong. Use the た-form: 行ったら.
Forgetting だった with nouns: 雨たら is wrong. Say 雨だったら.

faq.q: What is the difference between たら and ば?
faq.a: Both mean if. たら is more conversational and can mean when, once. ば stresses the condition and is common in advice like どうすればいい. In many sentences either works.

faq.q: Can たら mean when instead of if?
faq.a: Yes. For something sure to happen, たら means when or once: 家に帰ったら、連絡するね (I'll message you when I get home).

intro: ば (ba) is the conditional form meaning "if": if the condition is met, the result follows. You change the last -u of a verb to -e and add ば (行く → 行けば), and い-adjectives change い to ければ (安い → 安ければ).

formation.example: 行く → 行けば, 急ぐ → 急げば, ある → あれば
食べる → 食べれば, 見る → 見れば
する → すれば, 来る → 来れば (くれば)

formation.rule: い → ければ, ない → なければ
formation.example: 安い → 安ければ, 行かない → 行かなければ
暇 → 暇なら, 学生 → 学生であれば

usage: ば focuses on the condition: as long as this is true, the result happens. 急げば間に合う means if you hurry, you'll make it. It is common in advice and general statements.
Many set phrases use ば: どうすればいい? (what should I do?), 〜ばよかった (I should have), and 〜ば〜ほど (the more ... the more). These are very common in daily speech.

When the first half is about a state (ある, いる, adjectives) or the subjects differ, the second half can be a request or invitation: 時間があれば、一緒に行こう. With an action verb and the same subject, a request after ば sounds odd. Use たら instead.
ば sounds a little more neutral and written than たら. In casual speech, ければ often shortens to きゃ (行かなければ → 行かなきゃ) and れば can become りゃ.

examples.context: Encouraging a friend before the train leaves
examples.romaji: Isogeba, maniaimasu yo.
examples.en: If you hurry, you'll make it.

examples.context: Thinking about buying a used bike
examples.romaji: Yasukereba kaimasu.
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

examples.romaji: Dou sureba ii desu ka.
examples.en: What should I do?

examples.context: Inviting a friend to a festival
examples.romaji: Jikan ga areba, issho ni ikou.
examples.en: If you have time, let's go together.

compare.note: たら is more conversational and works freely with requests and one-time events. ば stresses the condition and fits advice and set phrases.
と is for automatic, always-true results. ば also works for general truths but can carry a hint of hope or advice.

mistakes: Using ば with a noun directly: 雨ば is wrong. Say 雨なら or 雨であれば.
Following an action verb ば with a request: 駅に着けば、電話してください sounds odd. Say 駅に着いたら、電話してください.

faq.q: What is the difference between ば and たら?
faq.a: Both mean if. ば puts the focus on the condition and is common in advice and fixed phrases. たら is more general, often means when or once, and can easily take a request.

faq.q: What does なければ mean?
faq.a: It is the ば form of ない, meaning if not: 行かなければ means if I don't go. It is also the first half of なければならない (must).

intro: と (to) after a verb or adjective means "when", "whenever" or "if" for a natural, automatic result: every time A happens, B follows. It attaches to the dictionary form or the ない-form, as in 押すと (when you press it) or 行かないと (if you don't go).

formation.example: 押す → 押すと, なる → なると
行かない → 行かないと
寒い → 寒いと
静か → 静かだと, 雨 → 雨だと

usage: と is used for results that always or naturally follow: laws of nature, how machines work, habits and directions. このボタンを押すと、ドアが開きます means the door opens whenever you press the button.
It is very common for giving directions: 右に曲がると、駅があります (if you turn right, there's the station).
The second half cannot be a request, invitation, wish or command. 駅に着くと電話してください is wrong. Use たら for that: 駅に着いたら電話してください.
〜ないと at the end of a sentence is short for ないといけない (have to): もう行かないと means I have to go now. With a past second half, と can show discovery: 家に帰ると、荷物が届いていた.

examples.romaji: Haru ni naru to, sakura ga sakimasu.
examples.en: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.context: Explaining a machine to a new coworker
examples.romaji: Kono botan o osu to, doa ga akimasu.
examples.en: When you press this button, the door opens.

examples.romaji: Migi ni magaru to, eki ga arimasu.
examples.en: If you turn right, you'll see the station.

examples.romaji: Hayaku ikanai to, okureru yo.
examples.en: If we don't hurry, we'll be late.

compare.note: たら can be followed by requests and plans. と cannot, and is limited to natural or habitual results.
After a noun, と means and or with: 友達と行く. After a verb or adjective, it means when or if.

mistakes: Following と with a request: 家に着くと連絡して is wrong. Say 家に着いたら連絡して.
Using the past before と: 押したと開く is wrong. Use the dictionary form: 押すと開く.

faq.q: What is the difference between と and たら?
faq.a: と is for automatic, always-true results and cannot take a request or invitation after it. たら is more flexible and works for one-time events, plans and requests.

faq.q: What does ないと mean at the end of a sentence?
faq.a: It is short for ないといけない, meaning I have to: 勉強しないと means I have to study.

meaning: if, if it's the case that, as for
intro: なら (nara) means "if" or "if that's the case": you take up a topic or situation, often one the other person just mentioned, and then give advice or an opinion about it. It attaches directly to nouns and な-adjectives (寿司なら, 暇なら) and to the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives (行くなら).

formation.example: 行く → 行くなら, 行った → 行ったなら
高い → 高いなら
暇 → 暇なら, 好き → 好きなら
寿司 → 寿司なら, 明日 → 明日なら

usage: なら often responds to what someone said: if that's the case, then here's my advice. A: 京都に行きたい. B: 京都に行くなら、秋がいいよ. It is the go-to form for recommendations.
With nouns, なら works like "as for" or "if it's about": 寿司なら、あの店がおすすめ means if it's sushi you want, I recommend that place.
なら can reverse the order of events. 京都に行くなら、新幹線で行ったほうがいい gives advice for before the trip. たら cannot do this because たら means after the first thing happens.
The second half can be a request, opinion or invitation: 暇なら手伝って. なら is common in casual and polite speech alike. なら(ば) and であれば are more formal variants.

examples.romaji: Kyouto ni iku nara, aki ga ii desu yo.
examples.en: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a great time.

examples.romaji: Sushi nara, ano mise ga osusume desu.
examples.en: If it's sushi you want, I recommend that place.

examples.romaji: Hima nara, tetsudatte kurenai?
examples.en: If you're free, can you help me?

examples.romaji: Kimi ga sou iu nara, shinjiru yo.
examples.en: If you say so, I'll believe you.

compare.note: たら means once A happens, then B. なら takes up A as a topic or premise, and B can come before A in time.
ば focuses on the condition being met. なら is used to react to something said and give advice about it.

mistakes: Adding だ before なら: 暇だなら is wrong. Say 暇なら.
Using たら for advice before an event: 京都に行ったら、新幹線を予約して sounds like you book it after arriving. Say 京都に行くなら、新幹線を予約して.

faq.q: What is the difference between なら and たら?
faq.a: たら means when or after A happens. なら means if that's the case, and it often responds to what someone just said. With なら, the advice can be for something before A.

faq.q: Is なら casual?
faq.a: No, it is neutral. なら works with friends and in polite speech. The second half sets the politeness: 秋がいいよ vs 秋がいいですよ.

intro: ても (temo) means "even if" or "even though": the result is the same no matter what the first part says. You add も to the て-form, so 降って becomes 降っても (even if it rains), and nouns and な-adjectives take でも (子供でも).

formation.example: 降る → 降っても, 食べる → 食べても, する → しても
高い → 高くても, いい → よくても
静か → 静かでも, 子供 → 子供でも
行かない → 行かなくても

usage: ても shows that the second half happens anyway: 雨が降っても、行きます means I'll go whether it rains or not. It works for both hypothetical and real situations.
With question words it means "no matter": いくら食べても (no matter how much I eat), 何を言っても (no matter what you say), どこに行っても (wherever you go).
Unlike のに, ても can be followed by a request, invitation or plan: 雨でも行こう (let's go even if it rains).
ても is also the base of other patterns: てもいい (it's OK to), なくてもいい (you don't have to). In casual speech, ても sometimes becomes たって: 言ったって (even if you say).

examples.romaji: Ame ga futte mo, ikimasu.
examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.

examples.romaji: Ikura tabete mo futoranai.
examples.en: No matter how much I eat, I don't gain weight.

examples.romaji: Takakute mo kaitai.
examples.en: I want to buy it even if it's expensive.

examples.romaji: Kodomo demo wakarimasu yo.
examples.en: Even a child can understand it.

compare.note: のに is about real facts and adds frustration or surprise, and it cannot take a request. ても is neutral, works for hypotheticals, and can take a request.
けど is a simple but between two facts. ても means the result holds whatever the condition is.

mistakes: Adding も to the dictionary form: 降るも is wrong. Use the て-form: 降っても.
Using くても with な-adjectives: 静かくても is wrong. Say 静かでも.

faq.q: What is the difference between ても and のに?
faq.a: ても means even if and is neutral, for real or imagined cases. のに means even though, only for real facts, and shows frustration or surprise.

faq.q: Is でも the same as ても?
faq.a: After a noun or な-adjective, でも is just ても with those words: 子供でも. At the start of a sentence, でも means but.

intro: てから (te kara) means "after doing A, then B". It puts two actions in a clear order and stresses that A comes first. You attach から to the て-form of a verb, so 食べる becomes 食べてから.

formation.example: 書く → 書いてから, 飲む → 飲んでから
食べる → 食べてから, 見る → 見てから

formation.rule: して / 来て + から
formation.example: する → してから, 来る → 来てから

formation.rule: て-form + から + time + になる / です
formation.example: 日本に来てから三年になります

usage: A てから B means you do A first and then B. It often suggests that A has to be finished before B can start: 手を洗ってから食べてね (wash your hands first, then eat).
With an amount of time after it, てから means "since": 日本に来てから三年になります means it has been three years since I came to Japan.
The tense of the whole sentence comes from the last verb. てから itself never changes, so it works for past, present and future: 宿題をしてから遊んだ / 宿題をしてから遊ぶ.
It is neutral in register. You hear it in casual talk with friends, in polite speech with ます, and in instructions and manuals.

examples.context: A parent to a child before dinner
examples.romaji: Te o aratte kara, tabete ne.
examples.en: Wash your hands, then eat, okay?

examples.context: Telling a friend your evening plan
examples.romaji: Shukudai o shite kara, geemu o shimasu.
examples.en: I'll play games after I do my homework.

examples.romaji: Nihon ni kite kara, mou sannen ni narimasu.
examples.en: It's already been three years since I came to Japan.

examples.context: Answering a friend who wants a quick decision
examples.romaji: Chotto kangaete kara kimeru.
examples.en: I'll think about it a bit, then decide.

compare.note: 食べたあとで also means "after eating", but it only marks time. てから puts more weight on doing A first, and only てから can mean "since".
Plain form + から means "because": 来るから (because they are coming). て-form + から means "after": 来てから (after they come).

mistakes: Using the past form: 食べたから means "because I ate". For "after eating", say 食べてから.
Using the dictionary or ます form: 食べるから and 食べますから mean "because". The "after" meaning needs the て-form: 食べてから.
Mixing up the reading of 来てから: it is きてから, not くてから.

faq.q: What is the difference between てから and たあとで?
faq.a: Both mean "after". てから stresses the order, often with a sense that A must come first. たあとで simply says B happens later than A. Only てから can mean "since" with a length of time.

faq.q: Can てから mean since?
faq.a: Yes. Followed by a length of time, it means "since": 結婚してから五年です (it has been five years since we got married).

intro: あとで (ato de) means "after" or, on its own, "later". After a verb, use the past た-form: 食べたあとで (after eating). After a noun, add の: 授業のあとで (after class). It is often written 後で.

formation.example: 食べる → 食べたあとで, 見る → 見たあとで

formation.rule: した / 来た + あとで
formation.example: する → したあとで, 来る → 来たあとで
授業 → 授業のあとで, 食事 → 食事のあとで
あとで電話する (I'll call later)

usage: A たあとで B means B happens after A. The verb before あとで is always in the た-form, even when you talk about the future: ご飯を食べたあとで薬を飲みます.
On its own, あとで means "later": あとでね (see you later, talk later). This is one of the most common uses in daily conversation.
You can also say あと without で (食べたあと、散歩した) or あとに. あとで is the most common choice when the second part is a single action.
It is neutral and used everywhere. In business, people often replace あとで with the more polite 後ほど (のちほど): 後ほどご連絡します.

examples.context: Ending a phone call in a hurry
examples.romaji: Ato de denwa suru ne.
examples.en: I'll call you later, okay?

examples.romaji: Jugyou no ato de, toshokan ni ikimasu.
examples.en: After class, I'm going to the library.

examples.romaji: Gohan o tabeta ato de, kusuri o nonde kudasai.
examples.en: Please take the medicine after eating.

examples.context: Telling a friend about a date
examples.romaji: Eiga o mita ato de, kafe de hanashita.
examples.en: After the movie, we talked at a café.

compare.note: 食べてから also means "after eating" but stresses doing A first. あとで simply places B later in time. あとで alone can mean "later", てから cannot.
The opposite: 寝るまえに (before sleeping) uses the dictionary form, while 寝たあとで (after sleeping) uses the た-form.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 食べるあとで is wrong. Use the た-form: 食べたあとで.
Leaving out の after a noun: 授業あとで is wrong. Say 授業のあとで.

faq.q: What is the difference between あとで and てから?
faq.a: Both can mean "after". てから focuses on the order of two actions, and A often has to come first. あとで just says B comes later. あとで can also stand alone to mean "later".

faq.q: Is あとで polite?
faq.a: It is neutral. With customers or in business emails, people usually say 後ほど (のちほど) instead, as in 後ほどお電話します.

intro: まえに (mae ni) means "before". After a verb, use the dictionary form: 寝るまえに (before going to bed). After a noun, add の: 食事のまえに (before the meal). It is usually written 前に.

formation.example: 寝る → 寝るまえに, 行く → 行くまえに

formation.rule: する / 来る + まえに
formation.example: する → するまえに, 来る → 来るまえに
食事 → 食事のまえに, 試験 → 試験のまえに
三年まえに (three years ago)

usage: A まえに B means you do B before A. The verb before まえに stays in the dictionary form even when the whole sentence is in the past: 日本に来る前に日本語を勉強しました.
After a length of time, 前に means "ago": 三年前に東京に引っ越した (I moved to Tokyo three years ago).
It is neutral and used in every register. With ます at the end of the sentence it is polite, and with plain forms it is casual.
Do not confuse it with 前に as a place, "in front of": 駅の前に銀行があります means there is a bank in front of the station.

examples.romaji: Neru mae ni, ha o migaite ne.
examples.en: Brush your teeth before bed, okay?

examples.romaji: Nihon ni kuru mae ni, sukoshi nihongo o benkyou shimashita.
examples.en: Before coming to Japan, I studied a little Japanese.

examples.context: A teacher to the class before lunch
examples.romaji: Shokuji no mae ni, te o araimashou.
examples.en: Let's wash our hands before we eat.

examples.romaji: Sannen mae ni Toukyou ni hikkoshita.
examples.en: I moved to Tokyo three years ago.

compare.note: The opposite: 食べたあとで (after eating) uses the た-form. まえに always takes the dictionary form.
までに means "by" a deadline: 五時までに帰る (be home by five). まえに just means "earlier than": 五時前に帰る (be home before five).
暗くならないうちに also means "before it gets dark", but it adds urgency: do it while you still can. 暗くなる前に is neutral.

mistakes: Using the past form: 日本に来たまえに is wrong, even for past events. Say 日本に来るまえに.
Using the ます form: 寝ますまえに is wrong. Say 寝るまえに, and put ます at the end of the sentence.
Using 前に for a place where an action happens: 駅の前に待っています is wrong. For the place of an action use で: 駅の前で待っています.

faq.q: Why does まえに use the dictionary form even in the past?
faq.a: At the time of A, A has not happened yet, so Japanese uses the non-past form. The tense of the sentence is shown by the last verb: 寝る前に本を読みました.

faq.q: What is the difference between 前に and までに?
faq.a: 前に means "before" with no deadline. までに means "by" a time, so the action must be done no later than that point.

meaning: in order to; for the sake of
intro: ために (tame ni) means "in order to" after a verb and "for" (someone or something) after a noun. Use the dictionary form of a verb, 働くために, or noun + の, 家族のために. In formal writing it can also mean "because of".

formation.example: 働く → 働くために, 買う → 買うために

formation.rule: する / 来る + ために
formation.example: 留学する → 留学するために
家族 → 家族のために, 健康 → 健康のために

formation.rule: noun + の + ために / ため
formation.example: 台風のために電車が止まった

usage: For purpose, ために goes with actions you choose to do, and both parts have the same subject: 車を買うために、お金を貯めている (I am saving money so that I can buy a car).
After a noun it means "for the benefit of": 家族のために頑張る (I work hard for my family). 健康のために走る means running for your health.
In news, announcements and formal writing, noun + のため(に) means "because of": 台風のため、電車が止まりました. In this use, に is often dropped.
For verbs that are not chosen actions, like なる, わかる, 見える or potential forms, Japanese normally uses ように instead of ために.

examples.romaji: Nihon de hataraku tame ni, nihongo o benkyou shite imasu.
examples.en: I'm studying Japanese in order to work in Japan.

examples.context: Talking about why you work so hard
examples.romaji: Kazoku no tame ni ganbaru.
examples.en: I work hard for my family.

examples.context: Telling a friend why you are saving
examples.romaji: Kuruma o kau tame ni, okane o tamete iru.
examples.en: I'm saving money to buy a car.

examples.romaji: Taifuu no tame ni, densha ga tomarimashita.
examples.en: The trains stopped because of the typhoon.

compare.note: ように is for goals you cannot directly choose: potential forms, ない-forms and verbs like なる or 見える. 話せるように練習する, but 留学するために勉強する.
から and ので are the everyday ways to say "because". ため(に) for a cause is formal and mostly written or announced.

mistakes: Using ために with a potential form: 日本語が話せるために練習する sounds wrong. Say 日本語が話せるように練習する.
Leaving out の after a noun: 家族ために is wrong. Say 家族のために.
Using different subjects for purpose: 子供が読めるために is wrong. Use ように: 子供が読めるように、大きく書いた.

faq.q: What is the difference between ために and ように?
faq.a: ために follows actions the subject chooses to do (買う, 行く, 勉強する). ように follows things that just happen or abilities (なる, 見える, 話せる, 忘れない). Both can be translated as "so that" or "in order to".

faq.q: Can ために mean because?
faq.a: Yes, in formal Japanese. 事故のため、遅れました means "we were delayed because of an accident". In conversation, people usually say から or ので.

meaning: so that; in order to (be able to)
intro: ように (you ni) means "so that" when the goal is a state or ability you cannot simply choose to do. It follows the dictionary form, the potential form or the ない-form of a verb: 話せるように, 忘れないように.

formation.example: 話す → 話せるように, 読む → 読めるように
見える → 見えるように, 治る → 治るように
忘れる → 忘れないように, 遅れる → 遅れないように
合格します → 合格しますように

usage: A ように B means you do B so that A will happen or become possible. A is usually not something you control directly: 風邪をひかないように、早く寝る (I go to bed early so I won't catch a cold).
With the ない-form it is very common for avoiding something: 忘れないように, 遅れないように, 落とさないように. This is one of the most frequent patterns in daily life.
ますように at the end of a sentence is a wish or prayer: 合格しますように (I hope I pass). You see it on shrine prayer tablets and in birthday messages.
ように also appears in indirect commands (早く寝るように言われた, I was told to go to bed early) and in the separate patterns ようになる and ようにする.

examples.romaji: Wasurenai you ni, memo shite okimasu.
examples.en: I'll write it down so I don't forget.

examples.romaji: Ushiro no hito ni mo mieru you ni, ji o ookiku kaite kudasai.
examples.en: Please write big so the people in the back can see too.

examples.romaji: Nihongo ga hanaseru you ni, mainichi renshuu shite iru.
examples.en: I practice every day so I can speak Japanese.

examples.context: Praying at a shrine before an exam
examples.romaji: Goukaku shimasu you ni.
examples.en: Please let me pass.

compare.note: ために follows actions you choose to do: 留学するために貯金する. ように follows abilities and states: 留学できるように貯金する.
ようになる describes a change: 話せるようになった (I became able to speak). ように alone gives the purpose of another action.
ようだ means "it seems": 雨が降ったようだ. It looks similar but has nothing to do with purpose.

mistakes: Using ように with a chosen action and the same subject: 日本に行くように貯金する sounds odd. Say 日本に行くために貯金する.
Using 見る instead of 見える: 後ろの人も見るように is wrong. The goal is being visible, so say 見えるように.

faq.q: What is the difference between ために and ように?
faq.a: Use ために when the goal is an action you choose (行く, 買う). Use ように when the goal is a state, an ability, or something to avoid (話せる, 見える, 忘れない).

faq.q: What does ますように mean?
faq.a: It is a wish: "I hope" or "may it happen". 元気でいられますように means "I hope you stay well". It is common in prayers, cards and song lyrics.

intro: し (shi) lists reasons or points, like "and what's more". It suggests there could be more reasons than the ones you say. It goes after plain or polite forms: 安いし, 静かだし, 近いですし.

formation.example: 降る → 降るし, 行った → 行ったし
安い → 安いし, 遠くない → 遠くないし
静か → 静かだし, 便利 → 便利だし
学生 → 学生だし, 雨 → 雨だし
近いですし, ありますし

usage: A し、B し、C lists reasons that lead to a conclusion: 安いし、おいしいし、よく来る (it's cheap and tasty, so I come often). The particle も often appears with it: 雨も降っているし.
A single し is very common. It gives one reason and hints that there are others, which makes it sound softer than から: もう遅いし、帰るね.
It is mostly used in conversation. With ですし or ますし it is fine in polite speech, for example with a customer or colleague.
し can also list facts without a clear conclusion, often to praise or complain: 彼は優しいし、頭もいい (he's kind, and smart too).

examples.context: Recommending a restaurant to a friend
examples.romaji: Kono mise wa yasui shi, oishii shi, yoku kuru n da.
examples.en: This place is cheap and tasty, so I come here a lot.

examples.romaji: Ame mo futte iru shi, kyou wa ie ni iyou.
examples.en: It's raining, so let's stay home today.

examples.context: A real estate agent showing an apartment
examples.romaji: Eki kara chikai desu shi, benri desu yo.
examples.en: It's close to the station, so it's convenient.

examples.romaji: Mou osoi shi, kaeru ne.
examples.en: It's getting late, so I'll head home.

compare.note: から gives one direct reason. し gives a reason and hints at others, so it sounds softer and less like an excuse.
たり lists actions as examples (映画を見たり、買い物をしたり). し lists reasons or facts that support a point.
安くて、おいしい just joins two descriptions. 安いし、おいしいし presents them as reasons for something.

mistakes: Dropping だ after な-adjectives and nouns: 静かし and 学生し are wrong. Say 静かだし and 学生だし.
Using the stem of an い-adjective: 安し is wrong (it is old written style). Say 安いし.

faq.q: Is し casual?
faq.a: Plain form + し is casual and very common in conversation. ですし and ますし are polite and fine at work. In formal writing, people use other connectors.

faq.q: Can I use only one し?
faq.a: Yes. One し is natural and very common: 疲れたし、もう寝る. It gives one reason and suggests there are more.

meaning: doing things like A and B
intro: たり〜たり (tari tari suru) lists actions as examples, like "doing things like A and B". Make the past た-form, add り, and finish with する: 見たり、買い物をしたりする.

formation.example: 読む → 読んだり, 書く → 書いたり, 行く → 行ったり
食べる → 食べたり, 見る → 見たり
する → したり, 来る → 来たり

formation.rule: かった / だった + り
formation.example: 暑い → 暑かったり, 静か → 静かだったり
見たり買ったりします, 見たり買ったりした

usage: A たり B たりする means you do things such as A and B. The list is not complete and not in any order. It is the standard way to talk about what you do on weekends or holidays.
The tense and politeness go on the final する: したりします (polite), したりした (past), したりしたい (want to).
With opposites, it shows going back and forth or changing: 行ったり来たりする (go back and forth), 暑かったり寒かったりする (hot one day, cold the next).
A single たり is also common. It gives one example and hints at others: 週末は映画を見たりします (I do things like watch movies).

examples.context: Answering "What do you do on weekends?"
examples.romaji: Shuumatsu wa eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shimasu.
examples.en: On weekends I watch movies, go shopping, and so on.

examples.context: Telling a friend about summer break
examples.romaji: Natsuyasumi wa umi de oyoidari, tomodachi to asondari shita.
examples.en: Over summer break I swam in the sea, hung out with friends, and so on.

examples.romaji: Saikin, atsukattari samukattari shimasu ne.
examples.en: Lately it's hot one day and cold the next, isn't it?

examples.romaji: Heya no naka o ittari kitari shinaide.
examples.en: Stop pacing back and forth in the room.

compare.note: 見て、買い物をして、帰った lists every action in order. 見たり、買い物をしたり gives a few examples in no order.
し lists reasons that support a point. たり lists sample actions.
とか is a casual way to give examples, mostly with nouns: 映画とか買い物とか. たり is the standard pattern for actions.

mistakes: Using たり only on the first verb: 映画を見たり、買い物をします is incorrect in standard Japanese. Say 映画を見たり、買い物をしたりします.
Forgetting する at the end: 映画を見たり、買い物をしたり。 can be heard in casual talk, but in normal sentences finish with する: 見たり、買い物をしたりする.
Using the dictionary form: 食べるり is wrong. Build it from the た-form: 食べたり.

faq.q: Can I use just one たり?
faq.a: Yes. 日曜日は掃除をしたりします means "On Sundays I do things like cleaning". It gives one example and hints at others.

faq.q: What is the difference between たり and て?
faq.a: て joins actions in order and implies that is everything you did. たり picks a few examples, in no particular order.

intro: ないで (naide) means "without doing" or "instead of doing". Add で to the ない-form of a verb: 食べない becomes 食べないで, as in 朝ご飯を食べないで出かけた (I went out without eating breakfast).

formation.example: 持つ → 持たないで, 使う → 使わないで
食べる → 食べないで, 寝る → 寝ないで

formation.rule: しない / 来ない + で
formation.example: する → しないで, 来る → 来ないで (こないで)

usage: A ないで B means you do B without doing A: 傘を持たないで出かけた (I went out without an umbrella). Both actions have the same subject.
It also means "instead of": バスに乗らないで、歩いて帰った (I walked home instead of taking the bus).
At the end of a sentence, ないで is a casual "don't": 行かないで (don't go). The polite version is ないでください, which has its own page.
In writing and formal speech, ずに means the same as ないで: 食べずに出かけた. ないで is the normal choice in conversation.

examples.romaji: Asagohan o tabenaide, ie o deta.
examples.en: I left the house without eating breakfast.

examples.romaji: Kasa o motanaide dekakete shimatta.
examples.en: I went out without my umbrella.

examples.romaji: Kyou wa basu ni noranaide, aruite kaerimasu.
examples.en: Today I'll walk home instead of taking the bus.

examples.romaji: Jisho o tsukawanaide, kono bun o yonde mite kudasai.
examples.en: Try reading this sentence without a dictionary.

compare.note: なくて gives a reason or cause: 会えなくて寂しい (I'm lonely because I can't see you). ないで describes how an action is done: 寝ないで勉強した (I studied without sleeping).
ずに means the same as ないで but is more written and formal: 何も言わずに帰った. する becomes せずに.
ないでください is a polite request not to do something: 触らないでください. ないで in the middle of a sentence means "without".

mistakes: Using なくて for "without": 朝ご飯を食べなくて学校に行った sounds wrong. Say 食べないで学校に行った.
Misreading 来ないで: it is こないで, not きないで or くないで.

faq.q: What is the difference between ないで and なくて?
faq.a: ないで means "without" or "instead of" and links two actions by the same person. なくて gives a reason: 宿題が終わらなくて、寝られなかった (my homework wasn't done, so I couldn't sleep).

faq.q: What is the difference between ないで and ずに?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. ずに is more formal and common in writing. ないで is the everyday form.

intro: とき (toki) means "when" or "at the time". It works like a noun, so it follows the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, な-adjective + な, or noun + の: 行くとき, 寒いとき, 暇なとき, 子供のとき. It can also be written 時.

formation.example: 行く → 行くとき, 行った → 行ったとき, 行かない → 行かないとき
寒い → 寒いとき, 若い → 若いとき
暇 → 暇なとき, 元気 → 元気なとき
子供 → 子供のとき, 雨 → 雨のとき

usage: A とき、B means B happens at the time of A. It is used for habits (暇なとき、本を読む), single events (日本に行ったとき) and instructions (出るとき、電気を消して).
The tense before とき shows the order. 日本に行くとき、カメラを買った means I bought a camera before or on the way to Japan. 日本に行ったとき、カメラを買った means I bought it in Japan.
ときは and ときに are also common. ときは sets the topic (困ったときは連絡して), and ときに points to a specific moment.
とき is neutral and works in casual and polite speech. It is usually written in kana when it means "when" in a sentence like this.

examples.romaji: Hima na toki, nani o shite imasu ka.
examples.en: What do you do when you're free?

examples.romaji: Kodomo no toki, yoku kono kouen de asonda.
examples.en: When I was a kid, I often played in this park.

examples.romaji: Ie o deru toki, denki o keshite ne.
examples.en: Turn off the lights when you leave, okay?

examples.romaji: Nihon ni itta toki, tomodachi ni aimashita.
examples.en: When I went to Japan, I met up with a friend.

compare.note: たら often means "once A happens, then B" and can be a condition: 駅に着いたら電話して. とき just marks the time, with no sense of condition.
あいだ covers a whole period: 夏休みのあいだ、ずっと家にいた. とき points to a time or occasion.

mistakes: Dropping な or の: 暇とき and 子供とき are wrong. Say 暇なとき and 子供のとき.
Getting the tense wrong: 家に帰るとき、「ただいま」と言います sounds like you say it on the way. Since you say it after arriving, say 家に帰ったとき.

faq.q: What is the difference between とき and たら?
faq.a: とき marks the time something happens. たら adds the idea of "once" or "if", and the second part often happens as a result. For a sure future event like arriving, both can work, but たら is more natural for instructions: 着いたら教えて.

faq.q: What is the difference between 行くとき and 行ったとき?
faq.a: 行くとき means before you get there or on the way. 行ったとき means after you arrived. The tense before とき shows which happens first.

intro: あいだ (aida) means "while" or "during" a whole period, and あいだに (aida ni) means "at some point during" it. It follows ている, noun + の, or an adjective: 寝ているあいだ, 夏休みのあいだ. It is also written 間.

formation.example: 寝る → 寝ているあいだ, 待つ → 待っているあいだに
夏休み → 夏休みのあいだ, 留守 → 留守のあいだに
若い → 若いあいだに

formation.rule: な-adjective + な + あいだ(に)
formation.example: 静か → 静かなあいだに

usage: A あいだ、B means B goes on for the whole time A goes on. The second part is usually something continuous, often with ずっと or ている: 夏休みのあいだ、ずっと実家にいた.
A あいだに、B means B happens once at some point during A: 寝ているあいだに地震があった (an earthquake happened while I was asleep).
The two parts can have different subjects: 私が料理しているあいだ、子供たちはテレビを見ていた. This is a key difference from ながら.
あいだ is neutral and fits both casual and polite speech. It is written either in kana or as 間, and both are common.

examples.romaji: Natsuyasumi no aida, zutto jikka ni imashita.
examples.en: I was at my parents' home the whole summer break.

examples.context: Reading the news in the morning
examples.romaji: Nete iru aida ni, jishin ga atta rashii.
examples.en: Apparently there was an earthquake while I was asleep.

examples.romaji: Watashi ga ryouri shite iru aida, kodomotachi wa terebi o mite ita.
examples.en: While I was cooking, the kids were watching TV.

examples.romaji: Rusu no aida ni, nimotsu ga todoite imashita.
examples.en: A package had arrived while I was away.

compare.note: ながら is one person doing two things at once: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する. あいだ can link two different people: 母が寝ているあいだ、私は勉強した.
うちに adds "while you still can" or "before it changes": 熱いうちに食べて. あいだに is neutral about time.
とき points to a time or occasion. あいだ stresses the whole stretch of time.

mistakes: Using あいだ for a one-time event: 寝ているあいだ、電話が鳴った sounds odd. Use あいだに: 寝ているあいだに電話が鳴った.
Leaving out の after a noun: 夏休みあいだ is wrong. Say 夏休みのあいだ.

faq.q: What is the difference between あいだ and あいだに?
faq.a: あいだ means B lasts for the whole period. あいだに means B happens once inside the period. Think "throughout" versus "at some point during".

faq.q: What is the difference between あいだ and ながら?
faq.a: ながら needs one person doing both actions. あいだ marks a period of time, and someone else can do the other action.

intro: うちに (uchi ni) means "while something is still true", so do it before the situation changes: 熱いうちに食べて (eat it while it's hot). It follows adjectives, ている, ない-forms, or noun + の.

formation.example: 熱い → 熱いうちに, 若い → 若いうちに
元気 → 元気なうちに, 静か → 静かなうちに
学生 → 学生のうちに, 午前 → 午前のうちに
暗くなる → 暗くならないうちに, 忘れる → 忘れないうちに
聞く → 聞いているうちに

usage: A うちに B means do B while A still holds, because A will not last. It carries a sense of "now, while you can": 若いうちに旅行したい (I want to travel while I'm young).
With a negative, it means "before": 暗くならないうちに帰ろう (let's go home before it gets dark). This sounds more urgent than 暗くなる前に.
With ている, it describes a change that happens gradually or without noticing during an activity: 話しているうちに仲良くなった (as we talked, we became friends).
It is common in conversation and in writing, and it works with both casual and polite endings.

examples.romaji: Atsui uchi ni tabete kudasai.
examples.en: Please eat it while it's hot.

examples.romaji: Gakusei no uchi ni, iroiro na kuni e ikitai.
examples.en: I want to visit lots of countries while I'm still a student.

examples.context: Friends hiking in the late afternoon
examples.romaji: Kuraku naranai uchi ni, kaerou.
examples.en: Let's head back before it gets dark.

examples.romaji: Nando mo kiite iru uchi ni, kashi o oboeta.
examples.en: After listening to it over and over, I learned the lyrics.

compare.note: あいだに just says something happens during a period. うちに adds that the period will end, so act now.
暗くなる前に is a neutral "before it gets dark". 暗くならないうちに has the same meaning with more urgency.

mistakes: Using the positive form for "before": 暗くなるうちに is wrong. Say 暗くならないうちに or 暗くなる前に.
Leaving out の or な: 学生うちに and 元気うちに are wrong. Say 学生のうちに and 元気なうちに.

faq.q: What is the difference between うちに and あいだに?
faq.a: Both mean "during". うちに suggests the situation will change, so you should act while you can. あいだに is a neutral time frame.

faq.q: Why does ないうちに mean before?
faq.a: 暗くならないうちに literally means "while it has not yet become dark". In natural English this is "before it gets dark".

meaning: about to; in the middle of; just did
intro: ところ (tokoro) marks exactly where you are in an action: about to do it, in the middle of it, or just finished. Dictionary form + ところ is "about to", ている + ところ is "in the middle of", and た-form + ところ is "just did". It is usually followed by だ or です.

formation.example: 出る → 出るところ, 寝る → 寝るところ
食べる → 食べているところ
着く → 着いたところ, 起きる → 起きたところ

formation.rule: する / している / した + ところ
formation.example: 確認するところ, 確認しているところ, 確認したところ

usage: ところ literally means "place", and here it is the point in time of an action. The verb form tells you which point: 出るところ (about to leave), 出ているところ (doing it now), 出たところ (just left).
It is very common when answering "Where are you?" or "Are you busy?": 今、駅に着いたところ (I just got to the station). 今から and ちょうど often come with it.
たところ means something finished a moment ago. For something that happened some time ago but still feels recent, use たばかり instead.
It is neutral. With です it is polite and common at work: 今、確認しているところです (I'm checking it now).

examples.context: A friend calls as you put your shoes on
examples.romaji: Ima kara dekakeru tokoro desu.
examples.en: I'm just about to head out.

examples.romaji: Gomen, ima gohan o tabete iru tokoro.
examples.en: Sorry, I'm in the middle of eating.

examples.romaji: Choudo eki ni tsuita tokoro da yo.
examples.en: I just got to the station.

examples.context: A boss asks about a report
examples.romaji: Ima, shiryou o kakunin shite iru tokoro desu.
examples.en: I'm checking the documents right now.

compare.note: 着いたところ means you arrived a moment ago. 着いたばかり also works for a longer stretch that still feels recent: 先月日本に来たばかりです.
食べている says you are eating. 食べているところ says you are right in the middle of it at this moment, often as a reason you can't do something else.

mistakes: Using たところ for something days ago: 先週日本に来たところです sounds wrong. Say 先週日本に来たばかりです.
Mixing up the forms: 出たところ means "just left", not "about to leave". For "about to", use 出るところ.

faq.q: What is the difference between たところ and たばかり?
faq.a: たところ is for an action finished just a moment ago. たばかり is for something that feels recent to the speaker, even if it was days or weeks ago.

faq.q: Doesn't ところ mean place?
faq.a: Yes, 所 means "place". In this grammar it marks a point in time within an action, and it is usually written in kana.

intro: たい (tai) means "want to" do something. Attach it to the ます-stem of a verb: 行きます becomes 行きたい (I want to go). The result works like an い-adjective, so the negative is 行きたくない and the past is 行きたかった.

formation.example: 行く → 行きたい, 飲む → 飲みたい
食べる → 食べたい, 見る → 見たい
する → したい, 来る → 来たい (きたい)

formation.rule: たくない / たかった / たくなかった
formation.example: 行きたくない, 行きたかった, 行きたくなかった
行きたいです, 行きたくないです

usage: たい expresses the speaker's own wish: 日本に行きたい. In questions, it asks about the listener's wish: 何が食べたい?
For other people, Japanese avoids stating their feelings directly. Use たがっている (弟は犬を飼いたがっている), たいと言っていた, or たいそうだ.
The object can take を or が: 水を飲みたい and 水が飲みたい are both correct. が puts a little more focus on the thing you want.
Asking a superior 〜たいですか can sound too direct. With a teacher or customer, offers like いかがですか are better. To make a polite request, people often say 〜たいんですが (I'd like to...).

examples.romaji: Nihon ni ikitai!
examples.en: I want to go to Japan!

examples.context: A host asking a friend about dinner
examples.romaji: Kyou wa nani ga tabetai desu ka.
examples.en: What do you want to eat today?

examples.romaji: Tsukareta kara, kyou wa dekaketakunai.
examples.en: I'm tired, so I don't want to go out today.

examples.context: Asking your manager for time off
examples.romaji: Raishuu, yasumi o toritai n desu ga.
examples.en: I'd like to take a day off next week...

compare.note: ほしい is for wanting a thing: 車がほしい. たい is for wanting to do an action: 車を買いたい.
たがる describes someone else's wish as it shows: 子供が遊びたがっている. たい is for your own wish or a question to the listener.
つもり is a plan or intention: 来年留学するつもりです. たい is a wish, which may never happen.

mistakes: Attaching たい to the dictionary form: 食べるたい is wrong. Use the ます-stem: 食べたい.
Using たい for another person: 彼は行きたいです sounds unnatural. Say 彼は行きたがっています or 彼は行きたいと言っていました.
Making the negative like a verb: 行きたいない is wrong. たい works like an い-adjective, so say 行きたくない.

faq.q: What is the difference between たい and ほしい?
faq.a: たい attaches to verbs and means "want to do". ほしい follows a noun with が and means "want something". 時計がほしい, but 時計を買いたい.

faq.q: Should I use を or が with たい?
faq.a: Both are correct. 水が飲みたい and 水を飲みたい mean the same. を is more common when the sentence is long or there are words between the object and the verb.

faq.q: Is たいです polite?
faq.a: Yes, 行きたいです is polite. Still, telling a superior what you want directly can feel strong, so people soften it: 行きたいんですが or 行かせていただきたいのですが.

intro: ほしい (hoshii) means "want" a thing. Put the thing before it with が: 車がほしい (I want a car). After a て-form, it means "want someone to do": 来てほしい (I want you to come). It is often written 欲しい.

formation.example: 車 → 車がほしい, 時間 → 時間がほしい
来る → 来てほしい, 手伝う → 手伝ってほしい

formation.rule: ほしくない / ほしかった
formation.example: ほしくない, ほしかった, ほしくなかった
ほしいです, ほしかったです

usage: ほしい is an い-adjective, so it conjugates like one: ほしくない (don't want), ほしかった (wanted). The thing you want is marked with が.
て-form + ほしい means you want someone else to do something: もっと話してほしい (I want you to talk more). The person can be marked with に: 彼に来てほしい.
Like たい, it describes the speaker's own feeling. For someone else, use ほしがっている: 妹が新しいスマホをほしがっている.
てほしい can sound direct when said to a superior. In polite situations, people use ていただきたい or ていただけませんか instead.

examples.context: Looking at phones in a shop
examples.romaji: Atarashii sumaho ga hoshii.
examples.en: I want a new smartphone.

examples.context: Asking a friend before their birthday
examples.romaji: Tanjoubi ni nani ga hoshii?
examples.en: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.context: Asking a roommate for a favor
examples.romaji: Chotto tetsudatte hoshii n da kedo.
examples.en: I'd like you to help me for a sec...

examples.romaji: Kodomo no koro wa, inu ga hoshikatta desu.
examples.en: When I was a kid, I wanted a dog.

compare.note: たい is for actions you want to do: 旅行したい. ほしい is for things you want: お金がほしい.
手伝ってもらいたい means the same as 手伝ってほしい. The もらいたい version is a little softer, and ていただきたい is the polite form.

mistakes: Using ほしい after a verb: 行くがほしい is wrong. For actions use たい: 行きたい.
Using を in standard sentences: 水をほしい is heard sometimes but is not standard. Say 水がほしい.
Using ほしい for someone else: 彼は車がほしいです sounds unnatural. Say 彼は車をほしがっています.

faq.q: What is the difference between ほしい and たい?
faq.a: ほしい follows a noun and means "want something". たい attaches to a verb stem and means "want to do". 本がほしい, but 本を読みたい.

faq.q: Is てほしい rude?
faq.a: Not with friends or family. To a boss or a customer it can sound demanding, so use ていただきたいのですが or ていただけませんか.

intro: ほうがいい (hou ga ii) means "you had better" or "you should" and is the most common way to give advice in Japanese. For positive advice it usually follows the past た-form of a verb (行ったほうがいい), and for negative advice it follows the ない-form (行かないほうがいい).

formation.example: 行く → 行ったほうがいい, 寝る → 寝たほうがいい
飲む → 飲まないほうがいい, 言う → 言わないほうがいい
安い → 安いほうがいい

formation.rule: stem + な + ほうがいい
formation.example: 静か → 静かなほうがいい

formation.rule: noun + の + ほうがいい
formation.example: こっち → こっちのほうがいい

usage: ほう means "side" or "direction", so the phrase literally says "that side is good". In practice it is a recommendation: 薬を飲んだほうがいい means "you should take some medicine."

With positive advice, the た-form is the normal choice and sounds like clear, practical advice. The dictionary form (行くほうがいい) is also possible, but it sounds more like a general comparison than advice to one person. Negative advice always uses ない, never なかった.

Advice with ほうがいい is fairly direct. It is fine with friends, family and people below you. To a teacher or boss it can sound like you are telling them what to do, so people soften it with と思います, or use a question like 〜たほうがいいですか to ask for advice instead.
With adjectives and nouns, ほうがいい usually means "is better" in a choice: 部屋は広いほうがいい (I'd rather have a big room), 私はこっちのほうがいい (I prefer this one).

examples.romaji: Kyou wa hayaku neta hou ga ii yo.
examples.en: You should go to bed early today.

examples.context: A doctor talking to a patient
examples.romaji: Osake wa amari nomanai hou ga ii desu ne.
examples.en: You'd better not drink too much alcohol.

examples.context: Asking a coworker about a popular restaurant
examples.romaji: Yoyaku shita hou ga ii desu ka.
examples.en: Should I make a reservation?

examples.context: Looking at the sky before going out
examples.romaji: Kasa o motte itta hou ga ii to omoimasu.
examples.en: I think you should take an umbrella.

compare.note: 〜たらいい and 〜ばいい suggest what would work: どうしたらいい？ (what should I do?). ほうがいい is stronger and compares one choice against the other.
なければならない means you must, as a rule or duty. ほうがいい is only advice, and the listener can ignore it.

mistakes: Using the past tense for negative advice: 行かなかったほうがいい is wrong. Use 行かないほうがいい.
Giving direct advice to a superior: 部長、休んだほうがいいです can sound pushy. Soften it: 少し休まれたほうがいいと思います.

faq.q: Why does ほうがいい use the past tense?
faq.a: It does not refer to the past here. The た-form with ほうがいい is simply the standard pattern for positive advice. 行ったほうがいい means "you should go", now or in the future.

faq.q: Is ほうがいい rude?
faq.a: It is not rude, but it is direct. With friends it is normal. With a boss or teacher, add と思います or rephrase so you do not sound like you are giving orders.

faq.q: What is the difference between ほうがいい and なければならない?
faq.a: ほうがいい is a recommendation. なければならない is an obligation that you have to follow.

intro: と思う (to omou) means "I think (that)". You put the plain form of a sentence before と, then add 思う, or 思います in polite speech. Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before と: 学生だと思う.

formation.example: 降る → 降ると思う, 来ない → 来ないと思う, 行った → 行ったと思う
おいしい → おいしいと思う
静か → 静かだと思う, 学生 → 学生だと思う

formation.rule: volitional + と思う (I'm thinking of doing)
formation.example: 行く → 行こうと思う, 食べる → 食べようと思う
彼は無理だと思っている

usage: と思う is how you give an opinion or a guess in Japanese. Japanese speakers add it often, even to things they are fairly sure about, because it softens a statement and makes it sound less pushy.
と思う on its own is for the speaker's own thoughts. For what someone else thinks, use と思っている (彼は私が悪いと思っている), or a softer form like と思っているみたい.
With the volitional form, と思う means "I'm thinking of doing": 日本に行こうと思う. と思っています makes it a plan you have been holding for a while.
In negatives, Japanese usually puts the negative inside the quote: 来ないと思う (I think he won't come). 来るとは思わない (I don't think he'll come) also exists but sounds stronger.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furu to omou.
examples.en: I think it will rain tomorrow.

examples.context: Recommending a place to a coworker
examples.romaji: Kono mise no raamen wa oishii to omoimasu.
examples.en: I think the ramen at this shop is good.

examples.context: Waiting for a friend who is always late
examples.romaji: Kare wa tabun konai to omou yo.
examples.en: I don't think he's coming.

examples.romaji: Natsuyasumi ni Nihon e ikou to omotte imasu.
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to Japan over summer vacation.

compare.note: と思う is the speaker's thought right now. と思っている is a thought held over time, and it is the usual form for someone else's opinion.
と考える is more logical and formal, used for reasoned opinions in essays and meetings. と思う is the everyday word.
でしょう also makes a guess, but it sounds more like a prediction. と思う puts the focus on it being your own opinion.

mistakes: Dropping だ after a noun: 学生と思う is wrong. Say 学生だと思う.
Using と思う for another person: 彼はおいしいと思う sounds like your opinion. For his opinion, say 彼はおいしいと思っている.

faq.q: What is the difference between と思う and と思っている?
faq.a: と思う is what you think at this moment, usually about yourself. と思っている is an ongoing thought, and you use it to say what other people think.

faq.q: Is と思う polite?
faq.a: と思う is plain. と思います is the polite version. Both are very common, and adding them to a statement makes you sound softer, not ruder.

intro: かもしれない (kamoshirenai) means "might" or "maybe". It follows the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, or directly follows a noun or な-adjective stem with no だ: 雨かもしれない. The polite form is かもしれません, and in casual speech it is often shortened to かも.

formation.rule: plain form + かもしれない
formation.example: 降る → 降るかもしれない, 来ない → 来ないかもしれない, 忘れた → 忘れたかもしれない

formation.rule: plain form + かもしれない
formation.example: 高い → 高いかもしれない

formation.rule: stem + かもしれない (no だ)
formation.example: 静か → 静かかもしれない

formation.rule: noun + かもしれない (no だ)
formation.example: 風邪 → 風邪かもしれない

usage: かもしれない shows that something is possible, but you are not sure. It is weaker than でしょう, which sounds more confident. Think of it as about a 50/50 guess.
The polite form かもしれません is common at work and with people you don't know well. It is also a soft way to give bad news or refuse: 少し遅れるかもしれません (I might be a bit late).
In casual speech, people shorten it to かも: 本当かも (that might be true). かも is very casual, so avoid it in polite speech and writing.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa yuki ga furu kamoshirenai.
examples.en: It might snow tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Sukoshi okureru kamoshiremasen.
examples.en: I might be a little late.

examples.context: Searching your pockets at a store
examples.romaji: Saifu o ie ni wasureta kamoshirenai.
examples.en: I might have left my wallet at home.

examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa kaze kamoshirenai ne.
examples.en: Tanaka might have a cold.

compare.note: でしょう is a more confident guess (probably). かもしれない is weaker (maybe).
はず means you expect something based on clear reasons. かもしれない is just a possibility.
かな is wondering out loud: 来るかな (I wonder if he'll come). かもしれない states the possibility.

mistakes: Adding だ after a noun or な-adjective: 学生だかもしれない is wrong. Say 学生かもしれない.
Using かも in polite speech: 遅れるかもです sounds too casual to a client. Use 遅れるかもしれません.

faq.q: Is かも casual?
faq.a: Yes. かも is the casual short form of かもしれない. Use it with friends, and use かもしれません in polite situations.

faq.q: What is the difference between かもしれない and でしょう?
faq.a: でしょう means probably and shows more confidence. かもしれない means maybe, and the speaker is less sure.

intro: はず (hazu) means "should" in the sense of "I expect so": the speaker is fairly sure something is true because of what they know. It follows the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, な + a な-adjective, or の + a noun, and is usually followed by だ or です.

formation.example: 届く → 届くはずだ, 来ない → 来ないはずだ, 入れた → 入れたはずだ
安い → 安いはずだ
静か → 静かなはずだ
休み → 休みのはずだ
言う → 言うはずがない (there's no way)

usage: はず is a conclusion based on facts, a schedule or logic: 荷物は明日届くはずです (the package should arrive tomorrow, because the tracking says so). It sounds more certain than かもしれない or でしょう.
English "should" also means advice or duty, but はず never does. For advice use ほうがいい, and for duty use べき or なければならない.
はずだった means something was expected but did not happen: 来るはずだったのに (he was supposed to come, but...). はずがない means "there's no way" and is a strong denial.
はず is neutral in register. はずです is polite, はずだ is plain, and in conversation people often say はずなんだけど when reality doesn't match what they expected.

examples.romaji: Nimotsu wa ashita todoku hazu desu.
examples.en: The package should arrive tomorrow.

examples.context: Searching your bag for the key
examples.romaji: Kagi wa kaban ni ireta hazu nan da kedo.
examples.en: I'm sure I put the key in my bag, though.

examples.romaji: Kare ga sonna koto o iu hazu ga nai.
examples.en: There's no way he would say something like that.

examples.context: Someone asks where a coworker is
examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa kyou yasumi no hazu da yo.
examples.en: Tanaka should be off today.

compare.note: べき is about what someone ought to do (duty or advice). はず is about what you expect to be true.
かもしれない is only a possibility. はず is a confident expectation with a reason behind it.
つもり is your own intention. はず is your expectation about a fact or event.

mistakes: Using はず for advice: もっと勉強するはずです does not mean "you should study more". Say もっと勉強したほうがいいです.
Leaving out の after a noun: 休みはずだ is wrong. Say 休みのはずだ.

faq.q: What is the difference between はずがない and ないはず?
faq.a: はずがない means "there's no way" and is a strong denial. ないはず means "I expect it isn't" and is a calmer guess.

faq.q: What is the difference between はず and べき?
faq.a: はず is an expectation about facts: he should be home by now. べき is a duty or advice: you should apologize.

intro: らしい (rashii) has two uses. After a plain verb, adjective or noun it means "apparently" or "I hear that", based on information you got from somewhere else. After a noun it can also mean "typical of" or "like a real": 春らしい天気 (real spring weather).

formation.example: 来る → 来るらしい, 閉店した → 閉店したらしい
高い → 高いらしい
静か → 静からしい
雨 → 雨らしい

formation.rule: noun + らしい, used like an い-adjective
formation.example: 春 → 春らしい天気, 彼 → 彼らしい

usage: As "apparently", らしい passes on something you heard or read, often without naming the source. The speaker keeps some distance from the information and doesn't take full responsibility for it: 来週テストがあるらしい (I hear there's a test next week).
It can also be a guess from indirect evidence: 誰もいないらしい (it looks like nobody is home). The feeling is less direct than みたい or ようだ, which come more from what you saw yourself.

As "typical of", noun + らしい says something has the qualities you expect: 男らしい (manly), 子供らしい (childlike, in a good way), 彼らしい (just like him). This らしい conjugates like an い-adjective: らしくない (not like).
らしい is fine in conversation, and らしいです is the polite form. In writing and the news it is also common for reporting uncertain information.

examples.romaji: Raishuu, atarashii sensei ga kuru rashii yo.
examples.en: Apparently a new teacher is coming next week.

examples.context: Telling a coworker about a shop
examples.romaji: Ano mise, heiten shita rashii desu.
examples.en: Apparently that shop has closed down.

examples.context: Small talk on a warm day
examples.romaji: Kyou wa haru rashii tenki desu ne.
examples.en: It's real spring weather today.

examples.romaji: Kare rashii kotae da ne.
examples.en: That's such a typical answer from him.

compare.note: そうだ reports what you heard more directly, often with a clear source. らしい can be hearsay or a guess, and is vaguer.
みたい is usually your own impression from what you see. らしい leans toward information from other people.
っぽい also means "-ish" but often in a negative way: 子供っぽい (childish). 子供らしい is positive (childlike, as a child should be).

mistakes: Adding だ: 静かだらしい is wrong. Say 静からしい.
Mixing up 子供らしい and 子供っぽい: calling an adult 子供らしい sounds odd. For an adult acting childish, say 子供っぽい.

faq.q: What is the difference between らしい and そうだ?
faq.a: Both can mean "I heard". そうだ is a direct report of what you were told. らしい is vaguer and can also be a guess from indirect evidence.

faq.q: What is the difference between らしい and みたい?
faq.a: みたい is a casual impression, often from what you see yourself. らしい leans toward what you heard, and also has the "typical of" meaning.

intro: みたい (mitai) means "it seems" or "it looks like", and it also means "like" for comparisons: 夢みたい (like a dream). It follows the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, or a noun or な-adjective stem directly, with no だ. It is the casual version of ようだ.

formation.example: 降る → 降るみたい, 降ってる → 降ってるみたい, 来た → 来たみたい
忙しい → 忙しいみたい
静か → 静かみたい
子供 → 子供みたい

formation.rule: みたいな + noun, みたいに + verb
formation.example: 夢みたいな話, 子供みたいに泣く

usage: As "it seems", みたい is a guess based on what you see, hear or notice: 外、雨みたい (it looks like rain outside). Polite speech uses みたいです.
As "like", みたい compares two things: 夢みたい (like a dream), 猫みたいな人 (a person like a cat). Use みたいな before a noun and みたいに before a verb or adjective.
みたい is conversational. In writing, speeches or formal situations, ようだ (ようです) is used instead. Both have the same meanings.
みたい conjugates like a な-adjective: みたいだ, みたいじゃない, みたいだった. Casual speakers often drop the final だ.

examples.romaji: Soto, ame ga futteru mitai.
examples.en: It looks like it's raining outside.

examples.context: Telling your manager about a colleague
examples.romaji: Tanaka-san, kyou wa isogashii mitai desu.
examples.en: Tanaka seems busy today.

examples.romaji: Yume mitai na hanashi da ne.
examples.en: That's like something out of a dream.

examples.romaji: Kodomo mitai ni nakanaide.
examples.en: Don't cry like a child.

compare.note: ようだ has the same meanings but is more formal and written. ようだ needs な or の (静かなようだ, 雨のようだ), while みたい does not.
らしい leans toward information you heard from others. みたい is more your own impression.
そう attaches to stems and is about how something looks right now: おいしそう. みたい attaches to full forms and is a more general guess.

mistakes: Adding な or だ before みたい: 静かなみたい and 学生だみたい are wrong. Say 静かみたい and 学生みたい.
Confusing it with 見たい (want to see). 映画が見たい means "I want to see a movie". みたい after a noun or plain form means "seems" or "like".

faq.q: Is みたい casual?
faq.a: Yes, みたい is conversational. みたいです is fine in polite talk, but in writing or very formal speech use ようです.

faq.q: What is the difference between みたい and らしい?
faq.a: みたい is usually your own impression from what you see or notice. らしい is more for things you heard from others, and it also means "typical of".

intro: そうだ (sou da) after a plain-form sentence means "I heard that" or "they say": it reports information you got from someone else. It follows the full plain form, including だ for nouns and な-adjectives (学生だそうだ), and the polite form is そうです.

formation.example: 降る → 降るそうだ, 降らない → 降らないそうだ, 結婚した → 結婚したそうだ
高い → 高いそうだ
簡単 → 簡単だそうだ, 簡単だった → 簡単だったそうだ
学生 → 学生だそうだ

formation.rule: source + によると / では + 〜そうだ
formation.example: ニュースによると、〜そうです

usage: Hearsay そうだ passes on information without adding your own judgment. It is common with a source: 天気予報によると (according to the forecast), 先生の話では (from what the teacher said).
そうです is the polite form and is very common. In casual speech, people more often use って or らしい: 明日雨だって (they say it'll rain tomorrow).
This そうだ does not change. You cannot make it negative or past: そうではない and そうだった do not work as "I didn't hear" or "I heard". Change the sentence before it instead: 来ないそうだ, 来たそうだ.

examples.romaji: Tenki yohou ni yoru to, ashita wa yuki ga furu sou desu.
examples.en: According to the forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa raigetsu kekkon suru sou desu.
examples.en: I heard Tanaka is getting married next month.

examples.romaji: Ano resutoran, sugoku takai sou da yo.
examples.en: I heard that restaurant is really expensive.

examples.romaji: Kinou no shiken wa kantan datta sou da.
examples.en: I heard yesterday's exam was easy.

compare.note: Looks-like そう attaches to the stem: 降りそう (looks like it'll rain). Hearsay そうだ follows the full plain form: 降るそうだ (I heard it'll rain).
らしい can be hearsay or a guess and sounds vaguer. そうだ is a direct report of what you were told.
って is the casual spoken way to report hearsay: 雨だって. そうだ is neutral to polite.

mistakes: Mixing up the two そう: 雨が降りそうです means "it looks like rain". For "I heard it will rain", say 雨が降るそうです.
Dropping だ with nouns and な-adjectives: 学生そうです is wrong for hearsay. Say 学生だそうです.

faq.q: What is the difference between そうだ (I heard) and そう (looks like)?
faq.a: Hearsay そうだ follows a full plain sentence and reports what you heard: おいしいそうだ (I heard it's good). Looks-like そう attaches to a stem and describes appearance: おいしそう (it looks good).

faq.q: Is そうです polite?
faq.a: Yes. そうです is the polite form and is natural at work. With friends, って or らしい is more common.

intro: そう (sou) attached to a stem means "looks" or "seems": おいしそう (looks delicious), 雨が降りそう (looks like it's going to rain). It attaches to the ます-stem of a verb or the stem of an adjective, and the exception is いい, which becomes よさそう.

formation.example: 降る → 降りそう, 落ちる → 落ちそう

formation.rule: drop い + そう (いい → よさそう)
formation.example: おいしい → おいしそう, 高い → 高そう, いい → よさそう
元気 → 元気そう, 便利 → 便利そう

formation.rule: ない → なさそう; verb also そうにない
formation.example: おいしくない → おいしくなさそう, 降る → 降りそうにない

formation.rule: そうな + noun, そうに + verb
formation.example: おいしそうなケーキ, 楽しそうに笑う

usage: This そう is a judgment based on how something looks right now. With adjectives it describes appearance: 高そう (looks expensive). With verbs it often means something is about to happen: 落ちそう (it's about to fall).
It is used for things you can't confirm just by looking. You don't say きれいそう about someone who is clearly beautiful, because you can already see it. Just say きれい.
そう does not attach to nouns. For "looks like a student", use みたい or らしい: 学生みたい.
そう is neutral. Use そうです in polite speech, and in casual speech it often stands alone: わあ、おいしそう！

examples.context: Seeing food arrive at the table
examples.romaji: Waa, oishisou!
examples.en: Wow, that looks delicious!

examples.romaji: Ame ga furisou desu ne.
examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.romaji: Kanojo wa tanoshisou ni waratte ita.
examples.en: She was laughing and looked like she was having fun.

examples.context: Meeting a friend after a long time
examples.romaji: Genki sou de yokatta.
examples.en: I'm glad you look well.

compare.note: Hearsay そうだ follows the full plain form: 降るそうだ (I heard it will rain). Looks-like そう attaches to the stem: 降りそう.
みたい and ようだ are guesses from any kind of evidence and work with nouns. そう is about visible appearance or an event about to happen.

mistakes: Saying いいそう for "looks good": いいそう is the hearsay form (I heard it's good). For "looks good", say よさそう.
Using そう with nouns: 学生そう is wrong. Say 学生みたい or 学生らしい.
Using it for what is obvious: その花はきれいそう sounds odd when you are looking at the flower. Say きれいですね.

faq.q: Does かわいそう mean "looks cute"?
faq.a: No. かわいそう is its own word and means "poor thing" or "pitiful". To say something looks cute, just say かわいい.

faq.q: What is the difference between そう (looks like) and そうだ (I heard)?
faq.a: Looks-like そう uses the stem and is your own judgment from appearance: おいしそう. Hearsay そうだ uses the full plain form and reports what you heard: おいしいそうだ.

intro: ようだ (you da) means "it seems" or "it appears", and also "like" in comparisons: 夢のようだ (it's like a dream). It follows the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, な after a な-adjective, and の after a noun. It is the more formal version of みたい.

formation.example: 来る → 来るようだ, 来た → 来たようだ, 疲れている → 疲れているようだ
高い → 高いようだ
静か → 静かなようだ
風邪 → 風邪のようだ, 人形 → 人形のようだ

formation.rule: ような + noun, ように + verb or adjective
formation.example: 夢のような話, 人形のようにきれい

usage: As "it seems", ようだ is a conclusion from what you see, hear or feel: 誰か来たようです (it seems someone has come, after hearing the door). It sounds careful and a little formal.
As "like", it compares or gives an example: 夢のような一日 (a day like a dream), 雪のように白い (white as snow).
ようだ and ようです are common in writing, the news, business and polite talk. In everyday conversation, most people say みたい instead.
どうも or どうやら before ようだ adds "somehow it seems", as in どうも風邪をひいたようです (I seem to have caught a cold).

examples.romaji: Dareka kita you desu.
examples.en: It seems someone has come.

examples.context: A team member talking about the manager
examples.romaji: Buchou wa kyou, sukoshi tsukarete iru you desu ne.
examples.en: The manager seems a little tired today.

examples.romaji: Kanojo wa ningyou no you ni kirei da.
examples.en: She is as beautiful as a doll.

examples.romaji: Doumo kaze o hiita you desu.
examples.en: I seem to have caught a cold.

compare.note: みたい has the same meanings but is casual, and it does not need な or の: 静かみたい, 雨みたい.
らしい leans toward information you heard from others. ようだ is more your own conclusion from evidence.
そう is about visible appearance and attaches to stems: 高そう. ようだ is a broader inference.

mistakes: Leaving out な or の: 静かようだ and 風邪ようだ are wrong. Say 静かなようだ and 風邪のようだ.
Using ようだ in very casual talk with friends sounds stiff. With friends, みたい is more natural.

faq.q: What is the difference between ようだ and みたい?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. ようだ is formal and written, and needs な or の before it. みたい is casual and attaches directly.

faq.q: What is the difference between ようだ and らしい?
faq.a: ようだ is usually your own judgment from evidence you noticed. らしい leans toward what you heard from others.

intro: つもり (tsumori) means "intend to" or "plan to". It follows the dictionary form or ない-form of a verb, usually with だ or です: 留学するつもりです (I plan to study abroad). After a past verb or a noun with の, it means "I believe I did" or "I meant it as".

formation.example: 行く → 行くつもり, 留学する → 留学するつもり
しない → しないつもり

formation.rule: dictionary form + つもりはない
formation.example: 行く → 行くつもりはない
説明した → 説明したつもり (I believe I explained)
冗談 → 冗談のつもり (meant as a joke)

usage: つもり is a plan you have already decided on in your own mind. It is firmer than ようと思う, which sounds like you are still thinking about it.
After a past verb or a noun, つもり means what you believe or meant, which may differ from how others see it: ちゃんと説明したつもりです (I believe I explained it properly), 冗談のつもりだった (I meant it as a joke).
つもりはない is a strong "I have no intention of": 謝るつもりはない. ないつもり is a calmer "I plan not to".
Asking a superior about their plans with つもりですか can sound blunt, as if you are questioning them. With superiors, use honorific forms instead.

examples.romaji: Rainen, Nihon ni ryuugaku suru tsumori desu.
examples.en: I plan to study abroad in Japan next year.

examples.context: A friend asks about your day off
examples.romaji: Kyou wa nani mo shinai tsumori.
examples.en: I plan to do nothing today.

examples.romaji: Joudan no tsumori datta n da.
examples.en: I meant it as a joke.

examples.context: A customer says they didn't understand
examples.romaji: Chanto setsumei shita tsumori desu.
examples.en: I believe I explained it properly.

compare.note: ようと思う (行こうと思う) is a plan you are considering or just decided. つもり is firmer and already settled.
予定 is a schedule or arrangement, often involving others: 会議の予定. つもり is your personal intention.
たい is just a wish (want to). つもり means you have decided to do it.

mistakes: Using the ます-stem: 行きつもり is wrong. Say 行くつもり.
Asking a superior 部長は行くつもりですか can sound rude. Ask 部長も行かれますか or いらっしゃいますか instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between つもり and 予定?
faq.a: つもり is your own intention. 予定 is a fixed schedule or plan, and it sounds more official and certain.

faq.q: What is the difference between つもりはない and ないつもり?
faq.a: つもりはない is a strong denial: I have no intention at all. ないつもり is a calm plan: I intend not to.

intro: たことがある (ta koto ga aru) means "have done" something before, at least once in your life. You attach ことがある to the past た-form of a verb: 行ったことがある (I have been there). The negative is たことがない (I have never done it), and the polite forms are ことがあります and ことがありません.

formation.example: 行く → 行ったことがある, 飲む → 飲んだことがある
食べる → 食べたことがある, 見る → 見たことがある

formation.rule: した / 来た + ことがある
formation.example: する → したことがある, 来る → 来たことがある
食べたことがない, 行ったことがない

formation.rule: dictionary form + ことがある = sometimes
formation.example: 遅れることがある (I am sometimes late)

usage: Use たことがある for life experience, not for a specific recent event. 日本に行ったことがある means you have been to Japan at some point. For "I went to Japan last week", just use the past: 先週日本に行った.
Words like 一度 (once), 何度も (many times) and 一度も〜ない (never once) go well with it: 一度も食べたことがない.
ことがありますか is the standard polite way to ask about someone's experience: 寿司を食べたことがありますか.
Be careful with the dictionary form. ることがある means "sometimes" or "there are times when", which is a different pattern.

examples.romaji: Nihon ni itta koto ga arimasu ka.
examples.en: Have you ever been to Japan?

examples.context: Talking about food with a friend
examples.romaji: Nattou wa ichido mo tabeta koto ga nai.
examples.en: I've never eaten natto, not even once.

examples.romaji: Fujisan ni nobotta koto ga aru yo.
examples.en: I've climbed Mt. Fuji.

examples.romaji: Kono eiga, mae ni mita koto ga aru ki ga suru.
examples.en: I feel like I've seen this movie before.

compare.note: Dictionary form + ことがある means "sometimes": 朝ご飯を食べないことがある (sometimes I skip breakfast). た + ことがある is past experience.
The plain past reports a specific event: 昨日寿司を食べた. たことがある is about experience at any time in your life.

mistakes: Using it for a specific recent event: 昨日寿司を食べたことがある is wrong. Say 昨日寿司を食べた.
Using the dictionary form for experience: 日本に行くことがある means "I sometimes go to Japan". For "I have been", say 行ったことがある.

faq.q: What is the difference between たことがある and ることがある?
faq.a: たことがある is life experience: I have done it before. ることがある means sometimes: there are times when I do it.

faq.q: How do I say "I have never" in Japanese?
faq.a: Use たことがない: 行ったことがない (I have never been). Add 一度も for emphasis: 一度も行ったことがない.

intro: ことにする (koto ni suru) means "decide to" do something, when you make the choice yourself. It follows the dictionary form or ない-form of a verb: 走ることにする (I'll start running). The past ことにした means "I decided to", and ことにしている means "I make it a rule to".

formation.example: 走る → 走ることにする, 作る → 作ることにした
食べない → 食べないことにする

formation.rule: dictionary / ない-form + ことにしている
formation.example: 見ないことにしている (I make it a rule not to look)
聞かなかった → 聞かなかったことにする (pretend I didn't hear)

usage: ことにする puts the focus on your own decision. ことにする is the moment of deciding ("I'll go with that"), and ことにした reports a decision you have already made.
ことにしている describes a personal rule you keep: 寝る前はスマホを見ないことにしている (I make it a rule not to look at my phone before bed).
With a past or negative past form, it can mean "treat it as if": 聞かなかったことにする (I'll pretend I didn't hear that). This is common in conversation and dramas.
The pattern works in both casual and polite speech. ことにしました is the polite past and is common for announcing personal choices.

examples.context: Telling a coworker about a new habit
examples.romaji: Raigetsu kara maiasa hashiru koto ni shimashita.
examples.en: I've decided to go running every morning starting next month.

examples.romaji: Kyou wa gaishoku shinaide, ie de tsukuru koto ni shita.
examples.en: I decided to cook at home today instead of eating out.

examples.romaji: Neru mae wa sumaho o minai koto ni shite imasu.
examples.en: I make it a rule not to look at my phone before bed.

examples.context: A friend lets a secret slip
examples.romaji: Ima no hanashi wa kikanakatta koto ni suru yo.
examples.en: I'll pretend I didn't hear that.

compare.note: ことになる is a decision made by others or by circumstances: 転勤することになった (I'm being transferred). ことにする is your own choice.
つもり is an intention you hold. ことにする is the act of deciding.
Noun + にする is choosing an item: コーヒーにする (I'll have coffee). ことにする is deciding on an action.

mistakes: Using the ます-stem: 走りことにする is wrong. Say 走ることにする.
Using ことにした when someone else decided: if your company is moving you, 転勤することにした sounds like it was your idea. Say 転勤することになった.

faq.q: What is the difference between ことにする and ことになる?
faq.a: ことにする is a decision you made yourself. ことになる is a decision made by someone else, or that came about naturally.

faq.q: What does ことにしている mean?
faq.a: It means you make something a regular rule or habit: 毎日歩くことにしている (I make a point of walking every day).

meaning: it has been decided that; end up
intro: ことになる (koto ni naru) means "it has been decided that" or "it will turn out that", when a decision comes from someone else or from circumstances. It follows the dictionary form or ない-form of a verb: 働くことになった (it has been decided that I'll work there). ことになっている means "it's the rule that".

formation.rule: dictionary form + ことになる / ことになった
formation.example: 働く → 働くことになった
行かない → 行かないことになった

formation.rule: dictionary / ない-form + ことになっている
formation.example: 脱ぐ → 脱ぐことになっている
やり直す → やり直すことになる

usage: ことになった reports a decision that was not just yours: a company transfer, a schedule set by a group, or a plan that came together. 来月から大阪で働くことになりました is a typical announcement.
Japanese speakers often use ことになりました even for their own choices, such as 結婚することになりました (we are getting married). It sounds modest and less self-centered than ことにしました.
ことになっている states a rule or standing arrangement: ここでは靴を脱ぐことになっている (you're supposed to take your shoes off here).
ことになる can also mean "it will end up that" as a logical result: このままだと遅れることになる (at this rate, we'll end up late).

examples.romaji: Raigetsu kara atarashii busho de hataraku koto ni narimashita.
examples.en: I'll be working in a new department from next month.

examples.context: Telling a teammate about the schedule
examples.romaji: Kaigi wa getsuyoubi ni yaru koto ni natta.
examples.en: It's been decided that we'll have the meeting on Monday.

examples.context: A host explaining a house rule
examples.romaji: Kono heya de wa kutsu o nugu koto ni natte imasu.
examples.en: In this room, you're supposed to take off your shoes.

examples.context: Warning a friend about a project
examples.romaji: Kono mama da to, mata saisho kara yarinaosu koto ni naru yo.
examples.en: At this rate, you'll end up having to start over again.

compare.note: ことにする is your own decision. ことになる is decided by others or by circumstances, or presented that way to sound modest.
ようになる is a gradual change in ability or habit: 話せるようになった. ことになる is about a decision or outcome.

mistakes: Using the ます-stem: 働きことになった is wrong. Say 働くことになった.
Using ことにする for a company decision: 転勤することにしました sounds like you chose it. If the company decided, say 転勤することになりました.

faq.q: Why do Japanese people say ことになりました about their own decisions?
faq.a: It sounds modest. Saying 結婚することになりました presents the news as something that came about, not as "I decided", which fits polite announcements.

faq.q: What is the difference between ことになる and ことにする?
faq.a: ことにする is a choice you make yourself. ことになる is a decision made by someone else or by the situation.

intro: ようになる (you ni naru) means "come to" do something or "become able to" do it, describing a change over time. It follows the dictionary form of a verb, or the potential form for new abilities: 話せるようになった (I became able to speak).

formation.rule: dictionary or potential form + ようになる
formation.example: 起きる → 起きるようになる, 泳ぐ → 泳げるようになる

formation.rule: dictionary or potential form + ようになる
formation.example: 食べる → 食べるようになる, 食べられるようになる

formation.rule: する / できる, 来る / 来られる + ようになる
formation.example: する → できるようになる, 来る → 来るようになる

formation.rule: ない-form → なくなる (more natural)
formation.example: 食べない → 食べなくなる

usage: ようになる describes a change from a state before to a state now. With the potential form it is a new ability: 漢字が読めるようになった (I became able to read kanji). With the dictionary form it is a new habit: 自炊するようになった (I've started cooking for myself).
It usually suggests a gradual change, often after practice or time, not a sudden one.
For a negative change, Japanese usually uses なくなる instead: 食べなくなった (I stopped eating it). 食べないようになった exists but sounds less natural.
ようになる only works with verbs. Adjectives and nouns use なる directly: 上手になる, 暑くなる.

examples.romaji: Nihongo ga sukoshi hanaseru you ni narimashita.
examples.en: I've become able to speak a little Japanese.

examples.context: A friend notices you seem healthier
examples.romaji: Saikin, maiasa hayaku okiru you ni natta.
examples.en: Lately I've started getting up early every morning.

examples.romaji: Renshuu shite, oyogeru you ni natta yo.
examples.en: I practiced and now I can swim!

examples.context: A parent chatting with a teacher
examples.romaji: Kodomo ga yasai o taberu you ni natte, ureshii desu.
examples.en: I'm happy that my child has started eating vegetables.

compare.note: ようにする means making an effort to do something: 毎日歩くようにしている (I try to walk every day). ようになる is a change that happened.
ことになる is a decision or outcome. ようになる is a gradual change in ability or habit.
Adjectives and nouns change with なる alone: 上手になる, 寒くなる. Only verbs take ようになる.

mistakes: Leaving out ように: 話せるになった is wrong. Say 話せるようになった.
Using it with a な-adjective: 上手ようになった is wrong. Say 上手になった.
Saying 食べないようになった for "stopped eating": it is understood but stiff. 食べなくなった is the natural way.

faq.q: What is the difference between ようになる and ようにする?
faq.a: ようになる is a change that came about, like a new ability or habit. ようにする is a conscious effort to do something.

faq.q: How do I say "I can now do" something in Japanese?
faq.a: Use the potential form + ようになった: 泳げるようになった (I can swim now), 読めるようになった (I can read it now).

form: なければならない / なきゃ
intro: なければならない (nakereba naranai) means "must" or "have to": you have no choice but to do something. Take the ない-form of a verb and change ない to なければならない, so 行かない becomes 行かなければならない. In casual speech it shrinks to なきゃ (nakya): 行かなきゃ.

formation.rule: ない-form minus ない + なければならない
formation.example: 行く → 行かなければならない, 書く → 書かなければならない

formation.rule: stem + なければならない
formation.example: 食べる → 食べなければならない, 起きる → 起きなければならない

formation.rule: し / こ + なければならない
formation.example: する → しなければならない, 来る → 来なければならない

formation.rule: drop い + くなければならない
formation.example: 安い → 安くなければならない
静か → 静かでなければならない, 学生 → 学生でなければならない

usage: The pattern is built from "if you don't do it" (なければ) and "it won't do" (ならない). Together they say something is required, because of a rule, a schedule or the situation.

There are several versions with the same core meaning. なければならない sounds formal and is common in writing and rules. なければいけない and ないといけない are more common in conversation. The polite forms are なければなりません and なければいけません.

In casual speech people shorten it to なきゃ or なくちゃ, often with the second half dropped: もう行かなきゃ (I have to go now). You can also say it in full: 行かなきゃいけない, 行かなくちゃならない. These short forms are very common among friends and family, but not in business emails.
Telling someone else what they must do can sound strict. For advice, ほうがいい (you should) is softer. To say something is not necessary, use なくてもいい.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa hayaku okinakereba narimasen.
examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.context: Checking the time at a friend's place
examples.romaji: Yabai, mou ikanakya!
examples.en: Oh no, I have to go now!

examples.context: A coworker talking about a deadline
examples.romaji: Kyoujuu ni repooto o dasanakereba naranai.
examples.en: I have to hand in the report by the end of today.

examples.romaji: Kusuri o nomanakya ikenai.
examples.en: I need to take my medicine.

compare.note: Same meaning, but more conversational. 行かないといけない is what many people actually say. なければならない sounds more formal or written.
ほうがいい is advice: 行ったほうがいい means you should go. なければならない means you have no choice.
The opposite: 行かなくてもいい means you don't have to go.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 行くなければならない is wrong. Start from the ない-form: 行かなければならない.
Dropping で after nouns and な-adjectives: 静かなければならない is wrong. Say 静かでなければならない.
Answering "Do I have to?" with a negative of this pattern. To 行かなければなりませんか, say いいえ、行かなくてもいいです (No, you don't have to).

faq.q: What is the difference between なければならない and なければいけない?
faq.a: The meaning is the same. なければならない is more formal and common in writing and rules. なければいけない is more common in everyday speech.

faq.q: What does なきゃ mean?
faq.a: なきゃ is the casual short form of なければ. 行かなきゃ means "I have to go". It is fine with friends but too casual for work or strangers.

faq.q: Is なければならない polite?
faq.a: The plain form is neutral and formal in tone. To be polite in speech, use なければなりません or なければいけません.

meaning: don't have to, it's OK not to
intro: なくてもいい (nakute mo ii) means "you don't have to" or "it's OK not to". Take the ない-form of a verb and change ない to なくてもいい, so 行かない becomes 行かなくてもいい. It is the opposite of なければならない (must).

formation.rule: ない-form minus ない + なくてもいい
formation.example: 行く → 行かなくてもいい, 使う → 使わなくてもいい
食べる → 食べなくてもいい, 見る → 見なくてもいい

formation.rule: し / こ + なくてもいい
formation.example: する → しなくてもいい, 来る → 来なくてもいい

formation.rule: drop い + くなくてもいい
formation.example: 高い → 高くなくてもいい

formation.rule: + じゃなくてもいい / でなくてもいい
formation.example: 日本人 → 日本人じゃなくてもいい

usage: The pattern literally joins "even if you don't" (なくても) and "it's fine" (いい). It tells someone that something is not necessary. It does not forbid anything: they can still do it if they want.
For polite speech, add です: なくてもいいです. なくても大丈夫です is a soft, friendly alternative, and なくてもかまいません is more formal, common at work and in shops.
As a question, なくてもいいですか asks if you can skip something: 靴を脱がなくてもいいですか (Is it OK if I don't take off my shoes?).
