In casual speech people often drop も: 来なくていいよ. The tone matters. Said warmly it is kind, but a cold 来なくていい! can mean "Don't bother coming."

examples.context: A manager talking to a part-timer
examples.romaji: Ashita wa konakute mo ii desu yo.
examples.en: You don't have to come in tomorrow.

examples.romaji: Keigo o tsukawanakute mo ii yo.
examples.en: You don't have to use keigo with me.

examples.romaji: Kutsu o nuganakute mo ii desu ka.
examples.en: Is it OK if I don't take off my shoes?

examples.romaji: Muri shinakute mo ii yo.
examples.en: You don't have to push yourself.

compare.note: The opposite. 行かなければならない means you must go. 行かなくてもいい means you don't have to.
てもいい gives permission to do something: 帰ってもいい (you may go home). なくてもいい says something is not needed: 来なくてもいい (you don't have to come).
ないでください asks someone not to do it. なくてもいい leaves the choice to them.

mistakes: Writing ないてもいい: 行かないてもいい is wrong. ない changes like an い-adjective, so it becomes なくて: 行かなくてもいい.
Confusing "don't have to" with "must not": 行かなくてもいい means going is optional. For a ban, use てはいけない: 行ってはいけない.

faq.q: What is the difference between なくてもいい and なくていい?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. なくていい drops も and is more casual and very common in speech. なくてもいい is a little more careful.

faq.q: How do I answer なければなりませんか?
faq.a: If the answer is no, say いいえ、なくてもいいです. For example, 行かなければなりませんか → いいえ、行かなくてもいいです (No, you don't have to go).

faq.q: Is なくてもいい rude?
faq.a: No. With です it is polite, and in a kind tone it often sounds considerate. Only a sharp tone makes it sound like "don't bother".

intro: てもいい (te mo ii) means "may" or "it's OK to". It is how you give or ask for permission. Attach もいい to the て-form of a verb, so 座る becomes 座ってもいい, and ask with てもいいですか (May I...?).

formation.example: 撮る → 撮ってもいい, 飲む → 飲んでもいい
開ける → 開けてもいい, 見る → 見てもいい

formation.rule: して / 来て + もいい
formation.example: する → してもいい, 来る → 来てもいい

formation.rule: drop い + くてもいい
formation.example: 小さい → 小さくてもいい
明日 → 明日でもいい, 簡単 → 簡単でもいい

usage: The pattern joins "even if you do" (ても) and "it's fine" (いい). Ask permission with てもいいですか and give it with てもいいですよ. A simple yes is はい、どうぞ or いいですよ.
For more politeness, say てもよろしいですか or てもかまいませんか, common with customers, teachers and bosses. Among friends, も is often dropped: 入っていい? (Can I come in?)
With nouns and adjectives, でもいい often means "X is fine too" or "X would do": 明日でもいいですか (Would tomorrow be OK?).
When you use it about your own actions, as in 手伝ってもいいよ, it can sound like "I don't mind helping" rather than an eager offer. To offer help warmly, say 手伝いましょうか.

examples.romaji: Shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.
examples.en: May I take a photo?

examples.context: On a crowded train, to a friend
examples.romaji: Koko ni suwatte mo ii?
examples.en: Can I sit here?

examples.context: A host talking to a guest
examples.romaji: Mado o akete mo ii desu yo.
examples.en: Feel free to open the window.

examples.romaji: Saki ni kaette mo ii yo.
examples.en: You can go home before me.

compare.note: The opposite. 撮ってもいい means you may take photos. 撮ってはいけない means you must not.
てもいい permits an action. なくてもいい says an action is not required: 来なくてもいい (you don't have to come).
Same meaning, but more formal. てもかまいませんか is a polite way to ask permission.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 食べるもいいですか is wrong. Use the て-form: 食べてもいいですか.
Refusing with てはいけません in polite talk. いいえ、撮ってはいけません is correct but sounds strict. A softer no is すみません、ちょっと…
Offering help with 手伝ってもいいです. It can sound reluctant. Say 手伝いましょうか (Shall I help?).

faq.q: How do you ask for permission politely in Japanese?
faq.a: Use て-form + もいいですか: 写真を撮ってもいいですか. For extra politeness, say てもよろしいですか.

faq.q: Is ていい casual?
faq.a: Yes. Dropping も, as in 座っていい?, is casual and common with friends. With strangers, keep も and add です.

faq.q: What is the difference between てもいい and てもかまわない?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. てもかまわない sounds more formal and a little more neutral, and it is common in polite requests at work.

intro: てはいけない (te wa ikenai) means "must not" or "you are not allowed to". It states a rule or a ban. Attach はいけない to the て-form of a verb, so 吸う becomes 吸ってはいけない, and in casual speech ては shrinks to ちゃ: 吸っちゃいけない.

formation.rule: て-form + はいけない (で-form + はいけない)
formation.example: 吸う → 吸ってはいけない, 飲む → 飲んではいけない
食べる → 食べてはいけない, 見る → 見てはいけない

formation.rule: して / 来て + はいけない
formation.example: する → してはいけない, 来る → 来てはいけない

formation.rule: ては → ちゃ, では → じゃ
formation.example: 食べちゃいけない, 飲んじゃいけない

usage: The pattern joins "if you do" (ては) and "it's no good" (いけない). It is used for rules, laws and things the speaker forbids. The polite form is てはいけません.
It sounds strong and direct. Parents, teachers and signs use it. Saying it to a customer, a boss or a stranger can sound bossy. A polite request like ないでください or ご遠慮ください works better there.
In casual speech, ては becomes ちゃ and では becomes じゃ: 走っちゃいけない, 飲んじゃいけない. ちゃだめ and じゃだめ are even more casual and common with children.
As a question, てはいけませんか asks if something is not allowed: ここで食べてはいけませんか (Am I not allowed to eat here?). In formal writing and laws you will also see てはならない.

examples.context: A staff member pointing at a sign
examples.romaji: Koko de tabako o sutte wa ikemasen.
examples.en: You must not smoke here.

examples.context: A teacher talking to a child
examples.romaji: Rouka o hashiccha ikenai yo.
examples.en: You mustn't run in the hallway.

examples.romaji: Shikenchuu wa jisho o tsukatte wa ikemasen.
examples.en: You can't use a dictionary during the exam.

examples.romaji: Miseinen wa osake o nonde wa ikenai.
examples.en: Minors must not drink alcohol.

compare.note: ないでください is a request: 吸わないでください (please don't smoke). てはいけない states a rule and sounds stronger.
Dictionary form + な, as in 吸うな, is a blunt command. It is much harsher than てはいけない.
The opposite. 吸ってもいい means you may smoke.

mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 吸うはいけません is wrong. Use the て-form: 吸ってはいけません.
Forgetting that some verbs take で: 飲んてはいけない is wrong. It is 飲んではいけない, with ではいけない after ん.
Using it with customers or superiors. ここで電話してはいけません sounds like scolding. Say ここでの電話はご遠慮ください or 電話しないでください.

faq.q: What is the difference between てはいけない and ないでください?
faq.a: てはいけない states that something is forbidden. ないでください is a polite request not to do it. In polite situations, ないでください is safer.

faq.q: What does ちゃいけない mean?
faq.a: It is the casual form of てはいけない. 食べちゃいけない means "you mustn't eat it". After ん, it becomes じゃいけない: 飲んじゃいけない.

faq.q: Is てはいけない rude?
faq.a: It is not rude in itself, but it is direct. It fits rules, signs and parents or teachers. Avoid it toward people above you.

intro: ことができる (koto ga dekiru) means "can" or "be able to". Put ことができる after the dictionary form of a verb, so 読む becomes 読むことができる. It means the same as the potential form (読める) but sounds more formal.

formation.rule: dictionary form + ことができる
formation.example: 読む → 読むことができる, 話す → 話すことができる

formation.rule: dictionary form + ことができる
formation.example: 食べる → 食べることができる, 寝る → 寝ることができる

formation.rule: する / 来る + ことができる
formation.example: 予約する → 予約することができる, 来る → 来ることができる

formation.rule: ことができた / ことができない
formation.example: 寝ることができなかった (couldn't sleep)
運転ができる, 日本語ができる

usage: こと turns the verb into a noun ("the act of reading"), and ができる says that act is possible. It covers both skill (I can read kanji) and possibility (you can pay by card here).

It sounds more formal and careful than the potential form. You will see it often in signs, announcements, manuals, websites and textbooks. In casual conversation, people usually say 読める or 話せる instead.
The past form ことができた often means "managed to": 合格することができました (I was able to pass). This sounds natural in speeches and formal reports.
With は in place of が, ことはできない adds emphasis or contrast: 行くことはできないけど… (I can't go, but...).

examples.romaji: Watashi wa kanji o yomu koto ga dekimasu.
examples.en: I can read kanji.

examples.romaji: Kono kaado de harau koto ga dekimasu ka.
examples.en: Can I pay with this card?

examples.context: Telling a friend about a bad night
examples.romaji: Kinou no yoru wa zenzen neru koto ga dekinakatta.
examples.en: I couldn't sleep at all last night.

examples.context: A notice on a hotel website
examples.romaji: Onrain de yoyaku suru koto ga dekimasu.
examples.en: You can book online.

compare.note: 読める and 読むことができる mean the same thing. The potential form is shorter and more common in speech. ことができる sounds more formal.
With a noun, drop こと: 日本語ができる (I can speak Japanese), 運転ができる (I can drive).

mistakes: Using the ます-stem: 読みことができる is wrong. Use the dictionary form: 読むことができる.
Using を instead of が: 読むことをできる is wrong. It is always ことができる.
Adding it to 分かる: 分かることができる is wrong. 分かる already means "understand", so just say 分かります.

faq.q: What is the difference between ことができる and the potential form?
faq.a: The meaning is the same. ことができる is more formal and common in writing and announcements. The potential form, like 話せる, is what people usually say in conversation.

faq.q: Is ことができる formal?
faq.a: It is neutral to formal. It is never wrong, but using it all the time in casual chat sounds stiff. With friends, use the potential form.

faq.q: What does ことができなかった mean?
faq.a: It means "couldn't" or "wasn't able to". 行くことができなかった means "I couldn't go".

meaning: have a feeling that, feel like
intro: 気がする (ki ga suru) means "I have a feeling that" or "it feels like". It expresses a vague sense or hunch, not a firm opinion. Put 気がする after the plain form of a verb or adjective, as in 会った気がする (I feel like I've met you).

formation.example: 降る → 降る気がする, 会った → 会った気がする
勝てない → 勝てない気がする
いい → いい気がする
静か → 静かな気がする

formation.rule: + のような / みたいな + 気がする
formation.example: 夢 → 夢のような気がする, 夢みたいな気がする

usage: Use it for a feeling or intuition you can't fully explain. It is softer and more uncertain than と思う (I think). Adding ような, as in 会ったような気がする, makes it even vaguer.
It is common in everyday conversation and works in both casual and polite speech. The polite form is 気がします.
Japanese speakers also use it to soften what they say, so a criticism sounds less direct: ちょっと高い気がします (It feels a bit expensive to me).
The negative 気がしない can mean "I don't feel like doing" when it follows a verb of action: 今日は勉強する気がしない (I don't feel like studying today).

examples.romaji: Mae ni dokoka de atta ki ga suru.
examples.en: I feel like I've met you somewhere before.

examples.romaji: Ashita wa ame ga furu you na ki ga shimasu.
examples.en: I have a feeling it will rain tomorrow.

examples.context: Lying on the couch on a day off
examples.romaji: Kyou wa nani mo suru ki ga shinai.
examples.en: I don't feel like doing anything today.

examples.context: Talking about a drama with a friend
examples.romaji: Kono dorama, saigo wa happii endo ni naru ki ga suru.
examples.en: I have a feeling this drama will have a happy ending.

compare.note: と思う states what you think, often with some reasoning. 気がする is a vaguer feeling or hunch.
気になる means something bothers you or catches your attention: あの音が気になる. It is not about a hunch.
みたい says how something seems from what you see or hear. 気がする is about your inner feeling.

mistakes: Adding の before 気: 会ったの気がする is wrong. Say 会った気がする.
Putting a noun right before 気がする: 夢気がする is wrong. Use のような or みたいな: 夢のような気がする.
Using it for things you know for sure. 明日は月曜日のような気がする sounds odd if you know the calendar. Just say 明日は月曜日です.

faq.q: What is the difference between 気がする and と思う?
faq.a: と思う gives your opinion or judgment. 気がする is a feeling or hunch you can't fully explain, so it sounds less certain.

faq.q: What does 気がしない mean?
faq.a: After an action verb, it usually means "don't feel like doing": 食べる気がしない (I don't feel like eating). It can also mean "I don't get the feeling that": 勝てる気がしない (I don't feel like I can win).

faq.q: Is ような気がする different from 気がする?
faq.a: The meaning is the same, but ような makes it a little vaguer and softer.

meaning: reason; that's why, it's not that
intro: わけ (wake) means "reason" or "the way things are", and it appears in several key patterns: わけだ (that's why, no wonder), わけではない (it's not that), わけがない (there's no way) and わけにはいかない (can't afford to). It follows the plain form of verbs and adjectives, as in 上手なわけだ.

formation.example: 行く → 行くわけ, 行った → 行ったわけ
高い → 高いわけ
上手 → 上手なわけ, 嫌い → 嫌いなわけ

formation.rule: + な / という + わけ
formation.example: 学生 → 学生なわけ, 学生というわけ

usage: わけだ states a natural conclusion: "so that's why" or "no wonder". You use it when a new fact explains something: それで上手なわけだ (So that's why you're good at it).
わけではない (casual わけじゃない) is a partial denial, "it's not that" or "it doesn't mean". It softens a statement: 嫌いなわけじゃない (It's not that I dislike it).
わけがない (casual わけない) is a strong denial, "there's no way". わけにはいかない means you can't do something because of duty or social reasons, even if you want to: 休むわけにはいかない (I can't just take the day off).

As a plain noun, 訳 also means reason or meaning: どういうわけ (for what reason), 訳が分からない (it makes no sense). The casual forms are very common in speech, and わけではない and わけにはいかない are standard in polite and written Japanese.

examples.context: Hearing that a coworker lived in Japan
examples.romaji: Sore de nihongo ga jouzu na wake desu ne.
examples.en: So that's why your Japanese is so good.

examples.romaji: Kirai na wake ja nai kedo, kyou wa ii ya.
examples.en: It's not that I don't like it, but I'll pass today.

examples.romaji: Ano hito ga uso o tsuku wake ga nai.
examples.en: There's no way that person would lie.

examples.context: Explaining to a doctor why you can't rest
examples.romaji: Ashita wa daiji na kaigi ga aru node, yasumu wake ni wa ikimasen.
examples.en: I have an important meeting tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.

compare.note: はずがない and わけがない both mean "it can't be". はずがない is based on reasoning, while わけがない is more emphatic and emotional.
んです explains a situation. わけだ draws a conclusion from facts you just learned: "so that's why".
から gives a reason directly. わけ talks about the reason behind something already known.

mistakes: Dropping な after な-adjectives: 好きわけではない is wrong. Say 好きなわけではない.
Mixing up わけではない and わけがない. 行くわけではない means "it's not that I'm going". 行くわけがない means "there's no way I'd go".
Putting a noun right before わけ: 学生わけ is wrong. Say 学生なわけ or 学生というわけ.

faq.q: What does わけじゃない mean?
faq.a: It means "it's not that" or "it doesn't mean". It is the casual form of わけではない and softens a statement: 嫌いなわけじゃない (It's not that I hate it).

faq.q: What is the difference between わけがない and はずがない?
faq.a: Both mean "there's no way". はずがない is a logical judgment. わけがない sounds stronger and more emotional, and is common in speech.

faq.q: What does 訳が分からない mean?
faq.a: It means "it makes no sense" or "I don't get it at all". Here 訳 is the noun for reason or meaning.
